Core course · Stop 1 · Foundations · about 35 minutes

How an AI model actually works

You don't need the math, but a clear picture of what's happening inside explains almost every piece of advice in this guide: why to give context, why to check citations, why to start fresh chats, and why the way you ask changes the answer. That's why it comes first. In about 35 minutes you'll watch a model write, see what it can and can't "see", and learn the six facts every later stop builds on.

7:58Start here · 3Blue1BrownLarge Language Models explained brieflyAnimated, made for the Computer History Museum.

At this stop you'll learn

  • How a model writes, one word at a time, and why that makes it fluent but fallible
  • The three stages that make a model, and the habit each one calls for
  • The context window: what Claude can "see," what goes into it, where to check it, and what lasts between chats
  • Six facts about how AI goes wrong, each with the habit that protects you
  • What AI is genuinely good at, and where it lets you down

The short version

A is a program that has read an enormous amount of text and learned one skill extremely well: given some text, predict what comes next. Do that one word at a time and you get fluent paragraphs, explanations, summaries and answers.

"Claude" is that model plus three things: instructions from Anthropic on how to behave, tools it can use (web search, reading your files, memory), and the conversation you're having with it. The model writes the words; the tools bring in information it didn't already have.

The key consequence: it produces what is likely to be said, not what has been checked to be true. Most of the time those are the same thing. Using it well means knowing when they aren't.

Watch it write interactive demo

Press Next word to step through, or click any word to choose it yourself. Then press Write it again and compare. Try both sentences.

Likely next words
Probabilities are illustrative; real models choose among tens of thousands of possible word-pieces.

Why the same question gets different answers slide it

You just saw it: press Write it again and the sentence comes out differently. Each next word is drawn from a list of likely ones, with a little randomness mixed in, and a setting called temperature controls how much. That's why asking Claude the same thing twice can bring back different wording, a different emphasis, and now and then a different answer.

Try it: press Sample 20 times at the middle setting. Then slide temperature all the way left and sample again, then all the way right. Watch the choices narrow to one word, then spread out.

When you want variety

Ideas, names, angles, wording

Spread helps here: you want options, not just the most typical one. Ask for several at once and say how different they should be: "Give me eight gift ideas for my dad, each a different price and style." Or ask again and compare.

When you want consistency

Facts, math, steps, code

Here, a different answer each time is a warning sign. Ask for one careful answer and narrow the target: the exact format, the file or source to work from, and "show your working" so you can check it. Once it's checked, save it (stop 4's verified/ folder) rather than asking again.

Claude's apps don't show a temperature setting: it's set for you (on the newest API models, sampling parameters such as temperature are no longer accepted). What you control is the request. Asking for several options gets you variety on purpose, and a specific request with your material attached leaves much less to chance.

The habit (fact 05, below): one answer is a sample, not the answer. For anything that matters, ask again in a new chat, worded differently. If the answers agree, trust goes up; if they don't, that's where to check.

Now with your own words mini playground

The demo above used whole words to keep things simple. Real models read tokens: common words whole, rarer ones in pieces, the space stuck to the front. Type anything to see the pieces, then let a tiny model guess the next one.

How a model is made tap each stage

Where does that next-word skill come from? Three stages, each of which leaves a fingerprint you can work with.

What it can "see": the context window

The model you just watched writes from whatever text is in front of it. That text has a name, and it explains most of the habits in this guide.

When you send a message, Claude doesn't remember you the way a person does. Instead, for every single reply, it is handed a bundle of text and reads all of it from the top before writing. That bundle is called the . Think of it as a desk: whatever is on the desk right now, Claude can use. Whatever isn't on the desk, it can't, however important it is.

The desk is large. With today's models it holds up to about a million tokens, very roughly 2,500 pages of text, on every plan including Free (Anthropic's pricing page says "up to 1M, varies by model"); some older models hold less, down to 200,000 (about 500 pages). A is a chunk of text a bit smaller than a word: 1,000 words come to roughly 1,500 tokens or more (a rule of thumb, not an Anthropic figure). But it isn't unlimited, and it isn't permanent: when the chat ends, the desk is cleared, and only a few things are put back on it next time: your standing instructions ("Instructions" in Settings, or "Instructions for Claude" in older layouts), memory if it's on, and project files when you're inside that project; past chats only come through memory or the "Search and reference chats" setting.

Why this matters: the quality of an answer depends heavily on what's on the desk. If your class's syllabus and notes are on it, Claude teaches your class; if your medications and history are on it, it reasons about you. If they aren't, it reasons about an average class or an average person and fills the gaps with what's typical. Most of the habits in this guide, and the whole folder method in stop 4, are really about putting the right things on the desk.

What goes on the desk open each layer

Five kinds of material can be in the context window when Claude answers. Each one gets there differently, lasts a different length of time, and is mostly something you can see and control. Open a layer to see what it is, where to find it on your screen, and how to use it well. Close it when you're done, or go straight to the next one.

InstructionsMemoryProject filesThis conversationUploads and searches
read in full before every replyClaude
Not on the desk, unless you put it there: your class materials, your medical records, your other chats (except through memory or the "Search and reference chats" setting), anything you said in an incognito chat, and anything newer than its training unless it searched the web for it.

When a conversation gets long drag the slider

Every reply re-reads the whole conversation, so a chat's length changes three things: how much of your usage limit each message costs, how reliably early details get attention, and, eventually, whether it fits at all. Drag to make the conversation longer.

Conversation length6 messages
Your messagesClaude's repliesFiles and project notes

Cost goes up

Message 40 costs more of your limit than message 4, because Claude re-reads the 39 before it. Long chats with big files are the usual reason people hit the limit early.

Attention thins out

Everything still fits, but a detail mentioned once, far back, is easier to overlook than one stated recently. If a fact matters, such as an exam date, a rule your class uses or a medication, restate it near your question.

Old parts get summarized

Near the limit, Claude may automatically summarize earlier messages to make room (when its code and file features are on). A summary keeps the gist and loses exact wording, numbers and nuance. Without that feature, the chat can't continue past the context limit, and you start a new one.

Habits that follow from this

  1. One topic per chat. A new question about a different problem gets a new chat, so the desk holds only what's relevant.
  2. Put lasting facts where they're reloaded automatically: your standing instructions, memory, or a project or folder (stops 3 and 4), not in a chat you'll lose track of.
  3. Restate what matters. In a long chat, repeat the critical facts with your question rather than trusting it to dig them up.
  4. Summarize and restart. When a chat gets long: "Summarize everything important we've established, including numbers and sources." Start a new chat, paste the summary, carry on.
  5. Check what it's working from. Ask: "Before you answer, list what you know about my situation and my material from this chat, my project and memory." Gaps and errors show up immediately.

Fill the desk yourself add things

The habits above, in your hands. Everything you add to a chat takes room on the desk, and big files and long answers fill it fastest. When it's full, the oldest material can't stay as it was: depending on your settings, Claude condenses it into a short summary or tells you the chat is full (the third card above). The two fixes are a fresh chat and a project.

Try it: add a big file and a few long answers until the desk overflows, and watch what leaves first. Then press Use a project, and then Start a fresh chat: the project notes stay, and everything else clears.

The habit: one topic per chat, and anything you need every time goes in a project or folder (stop 4), where it's put back on the desk for you.

Memory, files and learning: what lasts three common confusions

The desk empties when a chat ends. Three things last longer than one chat, and people often mix them up.

Lasts one chat

The conversation

Everything said in this chat stays on the desk until the chat ends. Open a new chat and none of it is there, unless it was saved to memory or a project.

Example: on Monday you explained what your class has covered so far. On Tuesday, in a new chat, Claude doesn't know it. Either continue Monday's chat, or keep that in your project or folder so every chat starts with it.

Lasts until you change it

Memory and project files

Memory is a short set of notes Claude writes about you from past chats ("taking Calc 2 this fall", "prefers sources cited"). Project files are documents you put in a project. Both are loaded into every relevant chat automatically. (Each project also keeps its own memory, so facts mentioned there stay with that project; a "Use account memory" switch on the project page sets whether its chats can also draw on your general memory.)

Example: memory might say your exam is on the 12th, from a chat last month. If it moved to the 9th and you never said so, memory is now wrong, and every plan it makes inherits the error. Check it in Settings now and then.

Doesn't happen

The model learning from you

Within a chat, Claude doesn't change the model. It doesn't "study" your class overnight or get better at your situation the more you ask. Each new chat starts from the same model, plus your loaded instructions, memory and files. If model improvement is on, chats may be used to train future models.

Example: if Claude made a mistake and you corrected it, the correction lives only in that chat (and in memory if it saves it). A new chat can make the same mistake again.

If you allow it in Settings, Anthropic may use your chats to train future models. That's separate from all of the above: Anthropic doesn't describe it as changing the Claude you're talking to now (stop 3 explains the setting).

Six facts to remember open each in turn

Everything so far boils down to six facts. Each fact explains a kind of mistake AI makes, why it happens, what it looks like in a real question, and the habit that protects you. The habits in stops 5 to 7, and in the health and school courses, all come from these six.

Which Claude? four model sizes

One more thing that changes the answer: which model you pick. Claude comes in a few versions that trade speed for depth. They share the same training approach and the same habits from the facts above; bigger models make fewer reasoning slips on complicated questions, but they still need context and still need checking. You pick one from a menu near the message box (stop 3 shows where), and the default is a sensible choice.

HaikuFastest · lightest

Quick, simple jobs: rewording, summarizing, sorting, short explanations. Uses the least of your limit. On Free.

SonnetBalanced · start here

Strong at explanation, reading documents, research and everyday coding. Anthropic's advice if you're unsure: start here. On Free.

OpusMost capable for most people

Deep analysis you'll build on, and problems Sonnet struggled with. Paid plans; uses your limit faster.

FableHeaviest · specialized

Long, many-step work where accuracy is critical. Included in the higher paid plans; on Pro it runs on extra usage credits.

Today's models also "think" before answering: they work through the problem before writing the reply. How much they think is set by an effort setting in the same menu (Low to Max; each model's recommended level is marked Default). Higher effort is slower and uses more of your limit, but is more careful on multi-step questions such as a hard proof, a tricky bug or weighing several options; lower effort is fine for routine work. (Older models have an on/off "extended thinking" switch instead.) Which model you pick matters much less than what you give it and how you ask.

Good at, bad at open any

Put the six facts together and you get a clear map of where Claude is reliably strong and where it lets you down.

Reliably good at

Explaining at your level

It can explain the same idea five ways, more simply or more technically, and never gets impatient. Ask "explain it again assuming I know X". Example: "Explain what a derivative is, first in two sentences, then the way a math professor would explain it to another mathematician." Useful because you can match the explanation to exactly what you already know.

Translating jargon

Decoding a dense textbook page, a legal letter, a lab report or a study abstract into plain terms is one of the most useful things it does. It works well because the meaning of technical terms is stable, well-documented knowledge, exactly the kind models get right. Still check that it read the numbers correctly, especially from a photo.

Showing you what you don't know

"What questions should I be asking about this?" often surfaces angles you'd never have thought to search for. It works because it plays to the model's breadth: it has read how experts, beginners and textbooks discuss a topic, so it can list the considerations you didn't know existed. Stop 6 turns this into a technique.

Summarizing and organizing

Long documents, several sources, your scattered notes: it can condense them and lay them out side by side, ready to check. Example: give it three weeks of lecture notes and ask for a one-page outline of what was taught, in order, with the terms you need to know. Check the summary against the originals for anything important, since summaries can drop a detail.

Finding sources, with search on

With web search or Research mode it can gather and cite sources quickly. Your job is to open the important ones. Searching changes what's on the desk: instead of recalling, it reads real pages and can show you which ones, which is why searched answers are far more checkable.

Unreliable at

Exact numbers from memory

Doses, statistics and dates recalled without a source can be wrong while looking precise. Always ask where a number comes from. This is fact 01 in action: a number is exactly the kind of precise detail that gets blurred in training.

Citations without search

From memory alone it can invent plausible-looking studies. With search on it does far better, but still check the ones that matter.

Your specific case

It can't see your class, your grades or your history unless told, and it can't weigh what a teacher or a doctor picks up in person. Even with all your material, it is reasoning about a written description of your situation.

Dates, times and arithmetic in its head

It can plan your week as if your exam were today when it's tomorrow, or add a column of numbers wrong, while sounding certain. It's much more reliable when it actually runs a calculation (with code) than when it works one out in its head. Double-check every date and total you'll rely on. (In health, the equivalent failure is judging urgency, which the health course covers.)

Disagreeing with you

Unless invited, it leans toward your framing. Ask for the case against, and it will make one. Fact 03 explains why; stop 5 shows how to word questions so the pull doesn't matter.

Spot the invented citation exercise

Now try the facts on a real-looking answer. Suppose Claude cited these three sources in one answer. One doesn't exist. Which? Choose before looking anything up.

Core course · Stop 2 · Foundations · about 15 minutes

Free or Pro: an honest comparison

The short answer: start free. Free Claude covers most of what this guide teaches. Pro ($20 a month) mainly adds one thing, a folder on your computer that Claude reads and keeps up to date itself, plus more usage and research extras. Which you need depends on what you'll use it for: for health research, Free is enough; for a full semester of classes, Pro earns its price. Here is everything, including the downsides.

At this stop you'll learn

  • What Free can really do, and where its limits bite
  • What Pro adds, what it costs, and its downsides
  • A four-question check: do you actually need it?
  • Why the recommendation differs for the health and school courses
Prices and features change. Anthropic's pricing page is the current authority; this page was checked in November 2026.

Pro$20/month · $17/month billed yearly

  • A folder on your computer that Claude reads and keeps up to date itself. One per class (every handout, transcript and practice exam, filed and indexed) or a health binder. Research extras
  • Research mode: many searches, one cited report
  • At least 5× more usage per 5-hour session than Free, plus a weekly limit

  • Claude in Chrome (help on websites) and computer use (operating apps). These are newer, early-stage features, and Anthropic itself advises against using them on health, banking or government sites.

What each difference means in practice open any

Now what those differences mean for you. Feature lists make every extra sound essential. Here is what each one actually changes, and what you'd do on Free instead.

More usage (at least 5× Free per five-hour session)

The limit is counted in computing, not messages (stop 3 explains how), so "5×" means at least five times as much reading and writing before you have to wait. Matters if you regularly run out partway through a session, which is common in long study sessions with big files the night before an exam. On Free instead: new chat per topic, upload only the pages you need, and put your background in a project so you don't resend it. Most people asking a few questions a week don't hit the limit often.

Research mode

Claude spends several minutes, sometimes longer, running many searches that build on each other, reading dozens of sources, and then writes a long report with citations. It's thorough, but uses a lot of your allowance. On Free instead: web search, one kind of source at a time, gets you a similar result in a few more messages, and you see each step, which makes it easier to check (the health course's seven-step method, stop H4, is built this way).

Opus, the larger model

Better at long, tangled reasoning: a hard proof, a big program, weighing several options against several constraints at once. For most questions (explaining, summarizing, finding sources, practice problems) Sonnet, on Free, does well, and the way you ask matters far more than the model. Bigger models like Opus generally use more of your limit.

Search your past chats

Claude can look through earlier conversations when they're relevant: "What did we decide about my spring schedule?" On Free instead: save what matters to your project files (stop 4), which is more reliable anyway, because you control exactly what's kept.

More projects and scheduled tasks

Free's five projects covers a health binder or four or five classes. Scheduled tasks run a request on a timetable, for example a Sunday list of everything due this week, or a weekly check for new research on a condition; on Free you'd simply ask when you want an update.

The folder on your computer, Chrome and computer use

The folder is Pro's real difference: Claude keeps your material filed and up to date itself, instead of you copying summaries into a project. For one health binder that's a convenience. For several classes, each with dozens of handouts, transcripts and practice files arriving every week, it's the difference between a system that keeps itself current and one you have to maintain by hand. It can also run your code and save practice files you open in your own editor. Chrome and computer use let Claude act on websites and apps; Anthropic advises against using them on health, banking or government accounts. Stop 4 covers all three.

G
Gavin's recommendation

For health research, I'd recommend Free. It does everything the health course teaches, and a Project makes a good health binder at no cost.

For school, I'd recommend Pro ($20 a month; not Max). The class folder (school course, stops S2 and S3) is the heart of the school course, and on Pro Claude keeps it itself: it files every handout word for word, keeps the summary current, runs your code, checks your math and saves practice files you open in your own editor. Pro's extra usage should also help with the long sessions before an exam. Start a class on Free if you're unsure; you can move it to Pro later.

I'd also recommend giving Claude most of the permissions it asks for. Turn on web search and memory, fill in your standing instructions (Instructions), add the connectors you'll use (PubMed for health, Google Drive if your notes live there) and, if your connector shows Tool permissions, set the read-only ones to "Always allow," and upload the documents that matter (with ID numbers removed). The more Claude can see and use, the more personal and accurate its answers get. Asking it to stop and check with you at every step mostly slows you down.

The exceptions: whether Anthropic can train on your chats is a privacy choice, not something Claude needs, so that one's up to you. And don't connect anything that can send messages, spend money or log into your health or bank accounts. Max (below) is probably more than either course needs. The quiz below helps decide.

Downsides and costs, plainly

Both plans have real costs and limits. Here they are without the sales gloss.

Free

  • You'll hit the usage limit if you do long research sessions with documents. Starting a new chat per topic and uploading only the pages you need helps.
  • No Research mode, so multi-source reviews take more back-and-forth.
  • You maintain your project files yourself (stop 4 shows the free method).
  • Five Projects maximum.

Pro

  • $240 a year paid monthly, or $200 paid yearly up front.
  • Still has usage limits; bigger models like Opus and tools like Research generally use more of your limit.
  • Working with files in a folder on your computer and computer use need the Claude desktop app open (Mac or Windows; Linux is in beta, without computer use); Claude in Chrome needs the Chrome browser. These are paid-plan features.
  • They're newer features: they make mistakes, need permissions you have to understand, and carry real risks (stop 4 explains).
  • The folder only works while the app is open and the computer is awake.
  • More to learn and set up.

The same on both

  • The AI can be wrong in the same ways, whatever you pay. The checking habits in stop 7 matter equally.
  • Privacy works the same: settings and habits for this are in stop 3. (For health: HIPAA, the medical-privacy law, doesn't cover chatbot companies by themselves.)

Do you actually need Pro? four questions

The sections above list every difference, but what decides it is how you'd actually use Claude. Answer four questions about your own week, and you'll get a suggestion with the reason for it.

The habit: if you're not sure, start on Free and use it for a couple of weeks. Hitting the limit most days you use it is the clearest sign Pro would be worth it.

Max Max ($100 a month) gives 5× Pro's usage, and Ultra ($200 a month) 10× Pro's weekly usage; both include Fable within limits. They're for people who use Claude frequently and need much more usage. Probably more than anything in this guide needs, including the school course: Pro should cover a full course load if you use the habits in stop 3.
What to do next: if you're unsure, start on Free and use the habits from the next three stops for a couple of weeks. If you hit the limit most days you use it, that's your sign to try Pro (for heavy school use, the recommendation above leans Pro). Stop 3 shows how to get the most out of Free in the meantime.

Eight free features, explained open any

Now that you know where things are, here's what each part does. For each feature: what it is, how it actually works, when it helps, what to watch out for, where to find it, and a prompt to try. Together they cover nearly everything the rest of this guide asks you to do.

Everyday jobs it's good at pick one

Features are easier to remember with a real job attached. Most of what people use Claude for isn't work or school: it's dinner, a confusing letter, a trip, a printer that won't print. Each one comes with a prompt to try, the one thing to check, and its limit.

Privacy: what happens to what you type

Before you use these features with your own material, it helps to know where that material goes.

Everything you send, including uploads, goes to Anthropic's servers to be processed; nothing runs only on your device. What matters is how long it's kept and what it can be used for. Three facts cover most of it:

  • No health-privacy law is written for what you type. HIPAA, the US medical-privacy law, covers doctors, hospitals and insurers, not chatbot companies by themselves (AP/PBS), and FERPA covers student records that schools (or vendors working for them) keep, not what you type into an app you use on your own. Your protection mostly comes from Anthropic's own policy plus what you choose to share.
  • How long chats are kept mostly depends on one switch (feedback you submit and safety-flagged chats are handled separately). With "Model Improvement" off, chats are kept in Anthropic's systems for up to 30 days after you delete them. With it on, chats can be kept, with identifying details removed, for up to five years and used to train future models.
  • Deleting works. A deleted chat disappears from your history at once and from Anthropic's storage within 30 days. Data already used in a completed training run is not removed from the trained model.
Decide once

Model training

Whether your chats can help train future Claude models. The setting only affects whether your chats may be used to improve future models; Anthropic's pages do not describe any change to the answers you get today. Many people turn it off if they discuss health or other private matters.

Click your name (bottom left) → Settings → Privacy → "Help Improve our AI models" (the Model Improvement setting). Applies to new and resumed chats. Anthropic's instructions

Check monthly

Memory

Memory makes answers more personal, which is why it's worth keeping on, but it's only useful if it's accurate. Read what's saved, correct anything out of date, and delete anything you'd rather it didn't know.

Settings → Your Claude (older layout: Settings → Memory). You can also pause it.

Every time

What you share

Share the details that make answers useful (your class material, your situation) deliberately. Never share ID numbers, student or account numbers, or passwords; Claude never needs them. Use incognito for one-off questions you don't want kept in your history.

Also: the thumbs up and down buttons send that whole conversation to Anthropic as feedback, kept for up to five years whatever your training setting. Skip them on sensitive chats.

Five situations worth thinking through

How the usage limit works, and making it last

The last thing that trips people up on Free is the usage limit. It's easier to manage once you know what it counts.

The limit isn't a fixed number of messages. Each message uses up an amount of computing that depends on how much Claude has to read and write to answer it: the whole conversation so far, any files, and the reply itself (stop 1's context window, again). A short question in a new chat costs very little; the 40th message in a long chat with a big PDF attached costs a lot.

The allowance refills on a five-hour cycle that starts with your first message, and every plan also has a weekly cap (Anthropic's pricing page lists one for Free too). On Free, the size of the allowance can vary with how busy Claude is. Paid plans see progress bars and reset times under Settings → Usage; on Free, Claude lets you know when you've reached the limit. Nothing is lost when you hit it; you just wait, or come back later.

Light
  • A focused question in a new chat
  • A follow-up in a short chat
  • Pasting a paragraph or one page
Medium
  • Uploading a few pages or a photo
  • Asking it to search the web
  • A chat that's run to 15 or 20 messages
Heavy
  • Long chats, especially with files attached
  • A 30-page PDF when two pages matter
  • High or Max effort on hard questions
1New topic, new chatA long chat is re-read with every message. When you change subject or a chat has run long, start fresh and paste a short summary.
2Upload only what's neededThe two pages that matter, not the whole 30-page packet. A clear photo of one page is cheaper than a whole scanned file.
3One good prompt beats five quick onesFive vague messages and their replies all pile up in the chat. Put your context and request in one message (stops 5 and 6 show how).
4Use a ProjectYour background lives there, so you don't retype it or re-upload it in every chat.

If you hit the limit often even with these habits, that's the honest signal that Pro might be worth it to you (stop 2).

The one habit from this stop: one topic per chat, with your background saved in a Project, so each message costs little and every answer starts from your material. Next, stop 4 turns that Project into the folder method.
Core course · Stop 4 · Setting up · about 40 minutes

The folder method

The most powerful habit in this guide is also the plainest: keep everything Claude should know about one subject in one place it reads every time, and let Claude keep that place organized. A class, your health, a job search, a house project. Once the folder exists, every answer is about your material instead of an average version of it. The health and school courses are built on this.

shortAnthropic · officialGetting started with projects in Claude.aiThe building block for the free version.

At this stop you'll learn

  • Why a folder of your own material changes answer quality so much
  • What goes in a good folder, file by file, and why each file exists
  • The free version (a Project) and the Pro version (a folder on your computer Claude keeps itself)
  • Ten rules for saving information so it stays findable and correct
  • Every setting involved, and the other Pro computer features

The idea

Stop 1 showed that Claude can only use what's on its desk, the context window, and that a new chat starts almost empty. So every question has a hidden first step: getting your situation onto the desk. Without a system, that depends on you remembering, each time, to paste the right syllabus, mention the right medication, or re-explain what you decided last week. People don't, and the answers quietly drift toward the generic.

The folder method fixes the first step once. You make one place per subject, put every original document in it, and keep a short "read this first" summary at the top. Every chat about that subject starts by reading it. Then you go further: you let Claude do the filing. When you hand it something new, it saves the original, adds it to the index, updates the summary, and tells you what changed. You never organize anything yourself, and nothing gets lost.

It's powerful for a simple reason: a model with your actual material on the desk is no longer guessing. Ask for practice questions and you get your class's questions, in your class's notation, at your exam's level. Ask about a symptom and the answer already accounts for your medications. The model didn't get smarter; its desk got better.

Same request, two desks switch the folder on and off

Pick a subject, then flip between No folder and With a folder. The request never changes. Watch what's on the desk, and what comes back.

Illustrative answers, written to show the typical difference. Real answers vary.

Why it works so well eight reasons, open any

Each of these comes from how models work (stop 1). Together they're why people who use this method get noticeably better results from the same model everyone else is using.

Anatomy of a good folder click any file

The same structure works for any subject. The school course (stop S2) and the health course (stop H2) each fill it in for their own use; here is the general shape and the reason each piece exists.

Other things a folder is good for

The same shape works far beyond classes and health. A few more places it pays off:

A job search

Your resume versions, each posting, cover letters and interview notes. "Tailor my resume to the new posting and tell me what I'm missing."

Free or Pro

A house or car

Manuals, receipts, warranty terms and a maintenance log. "When is the water heater's warranty up, and what does it cover?"

Free or Pro

A club or team role

Bylaws, meeting notes and the budget. "Draft the agenda from what's still open."

Free or Pro

A trip

Bookings, passport and visa rules, the plan and packing list. "What do I still need to book?"

Free or Pro

A writing project

Drafts, sources and feedback, with a log of what changed. "Which of my sources supports this paragraph?"

Free or Pro

Paperwork

Letters and bills explained in plain language, with a log of what's been resolved. Remove account numbers first.

Free or Pro

Two ways to build it

Ready to build one? The method is the same on both plans. What changes is who does the filing.

Free

A Project

One Project per subject. Its instructions hold the rules (how to teach or research, what to always do). Its files hold your material and the summary. Every chat inside it starts with both on the desk.

  • Works in the browser and the phone app
  • Up to five Projects
  • As far as we know, Claude can't save into it: when it writes an updated summary, you download it and replace the old file
  • Project files share a capacity limit (a bar on the project page shows how full)
Who files: you, with Claude writing the updates for you to drop in. About two minutes after each session.
Pro

A folder on your computer

A real folder (say, Desktop/Calc 2). In the Claude desktop app you connect that one folder, and Claude can read, create and edit files in it while you talk. It files new material itself, keeps the summary current, and saves anything it makes for you.

  • Needs the desktop app (Mac or Windows; Linux is in beta), open, with the computer awake
  • No project capacity bar: the folder is as big as your disk, and Claude reads only what each question needs
  • Claude can also run code on your files and read PDFs and images (zip files are not listed in Anthropic's upload article, so test yours)
  • You can open every file yourself; they're ordinary documents
Who files: Claude, as you go. You hand it things and ask questions.
School course · S3Build a class folder, step by stepHealth course · H2Build a health binder, step by step

Saving information so it stays useful ten rules

Building the folder is the easy part. Keeping it useful takes a few rules. A folder only helps if what's in it is complete, current and findable. These rules came out of real semesters of use; most were learned by getting them wrong first. Put them in your folder's instructions file so Claude follows them without being asked.

Every setting, explained open any

A few settings decide how well the folder works. Each setting that affects the folder method and everything else, with what it does, exactly where to find it, and a suggestion. Claude's menus have been rearranged more than once in 2026, so where a setting has moved, every current location is listed. If you still can't find something, the Help Center link under each one has screenshots.

The Pro computer features where it gets powerful

Once your folder exists, Pro can do more than read it. These let Claude act, not just talk: on websites as you, in the apps on your computer, and on a schedule while you're away. They're where Claude goes from helpful to actually doing the work, and they're worth setting up. Pair them with two habits: give automated browsing its own browser profile without your bank and health logins (Anthropic advises keeping those out, because a web page can hide instructions meant to trick an AI, called prompt injection), and keep backups on. The advanced section's first stop, Full power, safely, walks the whole access ladder.

Claude in Chrome

Helps on websites
  • A Chrome extension: Claude reads the page you're on, clicks, fills forms and moves between pages.
  • Choose Manually approve (it asks before every action) or Automatically approve (it still pauses for high-risk steps such as downloads, entering sensitive information or opening financial sites). A third mode, Skip all approvals, removes even those pauses; it isn't worth the risk for everyday use. You are responsible for purchases it makes.
  • Manage allowed sites in the extension's settings.
Good uses
  • Gathering details from several pages (a course catalog, program requirements) into one table
  • Comparing prices or opening hours across sites
Don't use it on patient portals, pharmacy accounts or banking. Anthropic suggests a separate Chrome profile without those logins. Sign in to sites yourself; never give Claude a password.Use Claude in Chrome safely →

Computer use

Operates your apps
  • Beta. Claude moves the mouse, types and opens apps to finish a task when there's no better tool.
  • Pro, Max and Ultra. Turn it on in the desktop app: Settings → Capabilities → Enable computer use (on some versions, Settings → System). It asks permission for each app, and some financial apps are blocked by default.
  • The computer must stay awake with the app open.
Good uses
  • Software with no other way in, such as a calculator's desktop app or design software (stop S8 has a real example)
  • Moving information between two programs
Don't grant it access to health, banking or government apps (Anthropic's advice). Close private documents before starting.Let Claude use your computer →

Scheduled tasks

Runs on a timetable
  • Describe a task once and pick how often it runs: hourly, daily, on weekdays, weekly, or only when you start it.
  • Runs in the cloud; to read a folder on your computer, the desktop app needs to be open there.
Good uses
  • "Every Sunday at 7 pm, list everything due this week across my class folders, hardest first."
  • "Every Monday, search for new systematic reviews on [condition] and add a short summary to my research folder."
Schedule recurring tasks →
What to do next: set up one folder this week for whatever you ask Claude about most, with a short "read this first" summary at the top that stays current: on Pro, Claude updates it after each addition; on Free, you ask Claude for the new version and replace the old file yourself. Asking well

The gap between a mediocre answer and an excellent one is mostly in the question. Six habits do most of the work. Each one answers one of the six facts from stop 1, so once you know why it works you'll use it without thinking.

shortAnthropic · AI FluencyIntroduction to AI FluencyTreating AI as a partner you direct and check.

At this stop you'll learn

  • Six habits that produce sharper, more honest answers
  • How to spot a leading, vague or permission-seeking question and rewrite it
  • A one-line test to run on any prompt before you send it

Six habits what, why, and an example of each

Each habit shows the fact from stop 1 it counters, then the same request asked without and with it. The health and school courses apply these to their own subjects (stop H3 for health, stops S4 to S6 for school).

1Give the context an expert would ask forCounters: Fact 04 (it only knows what you tell it)

Before you ask, give what a good tutor, doctor or colleague would want to know first: who you are in this situation, what you already know, what you've tried, what it's for, and any rules you're working under.

Why it works

Claude answers whatever is on the desk. Every missing detail gets filled with what's typical, so the answer quietly becomes about someone else: a different class, a different level, a different goal. The folder method (stop 4) supplies most of this automatically; for one-off questions, you supply it.

Instead ofExplain recursion.
TryI'm in an intro Python class. We've covered loops, functions and lists, but not classes. Explain recursion using only those, with one short example I can run, then give me one small problem to try myself.

Notice the last line: it says what you'll do with the answer. That changes the answer as much as the background does.

2Make it interview youCounters: Fact 04

When you're not sure what details matter, ask Claude to question you first, one question at a time.

Why it works

It turns Claude into the expert taking notes. It asks about things you didn't think were relevant, and it can't skip the questions, because you've told it not to answer until it has asked them.

Instead ofMake me a study plan for finals.
TryHelp me make a study plan for finals. Before you write anything, ask me questions one at a time: my exams and dates, what each covers, where I'm weakest, my fixed commitments, and how long I can really focus. Then propose the plan.

Answer honestly, including "I don't know." The plan you get is built around your actual week.

3Ask neutral questionsCounters: Fact 03 (it leans toward agreeing)

Ask what's true or what's weak, rather than asking it to confirm what you hope.

Why it works

Models lean toward the answer the question signals (sycophancy). "It's good, right?" gets "Yes, with a few small suggestions." A question that doesn't reveal your hopes gets a straighter answer.

Instead ofMy essay's argument is pretty convincing, right?
TryRead my essay as a skeptical grader using this rubric. What are the three weakest points in the argument, and what would a strong counter-argument say?

If you want honesty every time, put it in your standing instructions: "Give harsh, realistic assessments, not encouraging ones."

4Demand evidenceCounters: Facts 01 and 02 (predicts text; has a cutoff)

For anything factual you'll rely on, ask for sources, with links, and for how strong each one is.

Why it works

From memory alone, Claude can blur details or invent sources. Asking for named, linked sources (with web search on) changes how it answers and gives you something to check. Asking how strong each source is tells you how much weight a claim can bear.

Instead ofDoes listening to music help you study?
TryWhat does research show about studying with background music? Search for reviews and controlled studies, give each with its year and link, say how strong the evidence is, and keep settled findings separate from mixed ones.

For your own class material, "evidence" means the file: "Quote the line from my notes that says this."

5Say what you want backCounters: generic, padded answers

Name the format, length, level and purpose: a table, three bullets, a worked example, LaTeX for the math, under 200 words, "for an exam tomorrow", "to explain to my parents".

Why it works

Without a target, Claude writes the most typical answer: a few paragraphs, a list, a friendly wrap-up. Telling it what the answer is for lets it choose what to include and leave out, which is most of what makes an answer good.

Instead ofSummarize this article.
TrySummarize this article for a 10-minute class discussion: a three-sentence overview, the author's main claim and evidence, one weakness, and two discussion questions. Plain language, under 200 words.

Formats you'll use constantly: tables to compare, numbered steps to follow, "each math step on its own line with the rule named", "code I can run", and "end with one question to test me".

6Push back and cross-checkCounters: Facts 03, 05 and 06

Ask for the case against the answer, then check it another way: a new chat with different wording, a source opened yourself, or the calculation actually run.

Why it works

A single answer is one sample (fact 05), stated with more confidence than it may deserve (fact 06). The case against brings out the weak spots; a second, independently worded answer shows whether the first was stable.

Instead of(accepting the first answer)
TryWhat's the strongest argument against what you just said? Which of your claims are you least sure of? If any step involved arithmetic, redo it with code.

If it changes its answer when you push, ask what new evidence changed it. If there isn't any, the first answer may have been sounder. Stop 7 covers checking in depth.

Three questions to catch yourself asking tap to see the rewrite

Three kinds of question quietly undo those habits: leading, vague and permission-seeking. Tap each to see the rewrite.

LeadingPython is the best first language, right?
NeutralWhat are the trade-offs between Python, JavaScript and Java as a first language for someone heading into engineering? Where would each be the wrong choice?

The first invites agreement (fact 03). The second asks for trade-offs and for the case against each option, so no answer is favored in advance.

VagueIs my resume good?
SpecificHere's my resume and the job posting. As a recruiter for this role, what would you notice in the first ten seconds, what does the posting ask for that I don't show, and which three lines would you rewrite?

"Good" has no standard. Naming the reader, the goal and the output gives Claude a standard to judge against, and gives you something specific to act on.

Looking for permissionThe grading on this assignment was unfair, wasn't it?
BalancedHere's the rubric and my submission. Grade it against the rubric as strictly as the instructor would, and explain each point I lost. Then tell me if any deduction looks inconsistent with the rubric.

The first sets up a conclusion and the model will tend to supply it. The second gets an honest grading first, and only then a fair look at whether you have a case.

Weak prompt, strong prompt flip each card

Real requests usually need several of the six habits at once. Each card starts as the one line most people type. The back is the same request with the missing pieces added: who it's for, the details that matter, the format, and a way to check the answer.

Try it: before you flip a card, guess what you'd add. Then tap it and compare; the highlighted parts are what changed.

The habit: you don't need every piece every time, only the ones the answer depends on. The test below tells you which ones are missing.

A test to run before you send

All six habits fit into one quick test.

“

If I handed this message to a smart stranger who knows nothing about me, could they do exactly what I want, without asking me anything?

Adapted from Anthropic's prompting guide; stop 6 builds on it

If the answer is no, add what they'd ask for, or add "Ask me what you need to know first." That one line fixes most weak prompts.

The one habit from this stop: run the smart-stranger test before you send anything that matters. If a stranger would need to ask you something, add it. Next, stop 6 shows how to get Claude to help you write the question itself.

The golden rule

Stop 5 ended with the smart-stranger test, and it's no accident: Anthropic's own prompting guide puts the same test above all others, with a smart colleague who knows nothing about your situation. If they'd need to ask you questions, Claude needs those answers too. Every technique below is a way of passing that test, or of getting Claude to help you pass it.

Prompt surgery switch on each upgrade

Here is the golden rule in action. Start from a typical first attempt and add one improvement at a time. Watch the prompt grow, and notice which additions change the answer most: usually your situation, the "ask me first" line, and the standards you set. Pick a scenario first.

The prompt
Strength10%

      

      

    


    

      
Worked example: let Claude fix your prompt first

      
Surgery shows what to add. You don't have to add it all yourself, though. The most advanced move is also the simplest to use: write your question however it comes out, then ask Claude to critique and improve it before answering. It works because Claude knows what information a good answer needs, so it can spot what's missing faster than you can. You stay in charge: you approve or edit the improved version before it runs.

      

        
1 · Your draft
Help me study for my chem exam.
Before you answer, critique this prompt: what's missing or unclear? Then suggest a better version and wait for me to approve it.

        
→

        
2 · Claude's critique
Missing: which course and exam, the date, what it covers, the format (multiple choice, written, calculations), what's allowed in the room, how much time you have, and where you're weakest.
"Help me study" doesn't say what help looks like: a plan, an explanation, practice questions, or a check of your understanding. Each gets a very different answer.

        
→

        
3 · Improved prompt
My General Chemistry Exam 2 is Thursday at 8 pm: 25 multiple-choice questions plus 3 written ones, covering acids and bases, pH and buffers (learning objectives attached). Calculator allowed, no notes. I have about 6 hours before then and I'm weakest on buffers. Make a plan that puts most of the time on buffers, then give me 5 exam-style questions on it, harder than the practice exam, one at a time. Don't show answers until I've tried.

      

      
The critique is illustrative of what Claude typically says. Approve it (or edit it), and Claude answers the improved version. With a class folder (stop S2), most of the missing details are already on the desk, which is why the folder method and this technique work so well together. For a fully guided version, use the "Help me write the prompt" goal in the health prompt studio (stop H5), or the kit builder for classes (stop S9).

    


    

      
Thirteen techniques roughly easiest first

      
Everything else, in one list. Each technique is another way to pass the golden rule, or to get Claude to help you pass it. Start at the top; the later ones are for when the first few are habits.

      

    


    
The one habit from this stop: when a question matters, ask Claude to critique and improve your prompt before it answers, then approve or edit the better version. Next, stop 7 covers checking what comes back.



    

    

  








  

    

    

      

        
Core course · Stop 7 · Using it well · about 25 minutes

        
Checking the answers

        
You don't need to check everything Claude says. You need to check the few things you'll act on, hand in or repeat to someone, and to know which kind of check catches which kind of mistake. A date gets checked differently from a quote, and a quote differently from a calculation.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The kinds of mistakes AI makes most, and how each one looks
  • The right check for each kind, from running the math to finding the quote
  • The two-minute check for any citation
  • The second-opinion check, and prompts that make Claude check itself

        
The rule of thumb: the more it matters and the more precise it is (a number, a date, a quote, a name), the more it needs checking.

      

    

    


    

      
Spot the mistakes exercise

      
Here's a realistic answer to a student planning their week. It reads well. Three of its six highlighted claims are wrong in ways AI answers often are. Tap each highlighted claim and decide: fine or needs checking.

      

    


    

      
The right check for each kind of claim open any

      
The mistakes you just found are typical. Most mistakes fall into a few types, and each type has a quick check that actually catches it. Asking Claude "are you sure?" isn't one of them: it may just agree with whatever you seem to expect (fact 03).

      

    


    

      
The two-minute check, for any citation

      
Citations deserve their own check, because an invented one looks exactly like a real one. For any source Claude cites that a decision or an assignment rests on. You don't need to read the whole thing: the abstract or the relevant page is usually enough to catch most problems.

      

        
    
          
  1. Get the exact reference. Ask: "Give me the exact title, author, year and a link for that source, and quote the sentence that supports your claim."
    2. 
          
  2. Find it yourself. Paste the exact title into Google Scholar or a regular search engine (for medical papers, PubMed: stop H6). For your class, open the file it named. Nothing found: treat the claim as unverified. A different paper under that title is a red flag too.
    3. 
          
  3. Find the quoted sentence. Use your browser's find (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F) on the page. If the sentence isn't there, Claude paraphrased or invented it.
    4. 
          
  4. Compare with the claim. Same people or situation as yours? Same outcome? Same size of effect? Claims most often go wrong by stretching a result to a different group, or by overstating how big it was.
    5. 
          
  5. Decide: supported, overstated, or not supported. If it's off, tell Claude what you found and ask it to correct its answer.
    6. 
        

        
      

    


    

      
The second-opinion check

      
When you can't check a claim directly, a second source can still tell you something.

      

        
Different AI systems are trained differently and make different mistakes. When something matters, ask a second one the same question, worded neutrally, and compare. You can also ask Claude itself again in a fresh chat with different wording: a stable answer comes back the same; a shaky one changes.
Agreement isn't proof, since they can share the same wrong source, but disagreement is a reliable signal to go to a primary source: the textbook, the official page, the instructor, the doctor.

        
Other assistants worth knowing
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI), with its own free tier and study features.
  • Gemini (Google), available as an app and inside Google's other products.
  • Each has its own privacy settings and limits. The habits in this guide work on all of them.
This guide uses Claude because it's what you're learning, not because the others can't do this.

      

    


    

      
Make Claude check itself copy any

      
You can also put Claude to work on its own answer. Claude rarely volunteers its weak spots, but it's good at finding them when asked the right way. These prompts ask for something specific to check against, which works far better than "are you sure?"

      

    




    

      
When the fake is aimed at you sort them

      

        

          
Everything above is about Claude being wrong by accident. Scammers use the same technology on purpose. A few seconds of someone's voice from a video is enough to clone it; a fake photo or video no longer has tell-tale glitches; and a scam email can now be written in perfect, personal English.

          
The good news: the defenses don't depend on spotting the fake. Urgency + secrecy + an unusual way to pay (gift cards, crypto, wire transfer, a payment app, cash by courier) is a scam, whoever's voice it is. And you can always hang up and call back on a number you already had.

        

        
Set a family safe word today. Pick a word or phrase only your family knows, and agree that anyone calling in an emergency asking for money has to say it. The FBI recommends exactly this against voice-clone calls. It takes two minutes and works against every version of the trick.

Claude can help, too: paste a suspicious text or email (without clicking anything in it) and ask "What are the red flags here, and how would I check this safely?"

      

      
Sort each message: probably fine, check it another way, or scam signs.

      

    


    

      
The right tool for the job sort them

      
Last, the simplest check of all: whether to ask AI in the first place. Knowing when not to ask is part of using AI well. Some things a calculator or an official site answers faster and more reliably; some decisions need a person who is accountable to you. Sort each one.

      

      
The pattern: AI is best at explaining, drafting, planning and helping you think. Facts that change by the minute come from the source. Decisions with money, law or health on the line end with a person who answers for them.

    


    
The one habit from this stop: check only what you'll act on, hand in or repeat, and match the check to the claim: recompute numbers, find quotes in the source, and look up citations yourself. Next, stop 8 zooms out to the bigger picture.

The bigger picture

        
You now know how to use one AI well. This stop zooms out: where today's AI came from, what the word "AI" can mean, what happens between pressing send and seeing an answer, the vocabulary you'll hear in the news, the AI that's already built into things you use, and the big open questions, presented fairly, without telling you what to think.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Seventy years of AI in a two-minute timeline
  • How "AI", machine learning and chatbots fit together
  • The journey of one message, step by step
  • Sixteen terms from the news, in plain language
  • The AI you didn't choose to use, and the big questions about all of it

      

    

    


    

      
Seventy years in two minutes click through

      
Chatbots seemed to appear overnight in 2022. They didn't: they're the latest step in a long line of ideas, dead ends and breakthroughs. Pick any moment, or use the arrows.

      

    


    

      
What "AI" can mean tap a ring

      
That history produced many kinds of AI. "AI" is a big umbrella. Your spam filter, your phone's face unlock and Claude are all AI, but they're very different things. Each ring sits inside the one around it.

      

    


    

      
How an answer travels press play

      
What actually happens in the second or two after you press send. Stop 1 showed the middle step, writing one token at a time; here is the whole journey.

      
Try it: it plays by itself once it's on screen. Click any step to stop and read it, or press Play it to start again.

      

      
Where you come in: two steps are yours to shape. What's on the desk (step 2) comes from what you give it, and tools (step 6) are how it gets facts it never learned, which is why a searched answer comes with sources you can check.

    


    

      
Attention, in one sentence hover a word

      
Step 4 above mentioned "attention": while reading, every word looks back at the earlier words that help explain it. Hover or tab to "it", "was" or "hungry" to see which words it leans on. The weights here are illustrative, drawn to show the idea, not measured from a real model.

      
The cat ignored the dinner because it was not hungry
Why it matters to you: the model decides what "it" means from context. When your prompt is vague, there's less good context to attend to, which is why the details you give change the answer so much.

    


    

      
Words you'll hear open any

      
With the journey in mind, the news vocabulary is easier to place. The vocabulary from headlines and product announcements, each with what it means and why it matters to you.

      

    


    

      
The AI you didn't choose

      
Plenty of AI arrives without you opening an app. Everything from stop 1 applies to it too: it predicts plausible text, it can be confidently wrong, and it's only as current as what it can see.

      

        
Search summaries
The AI overview at the top of search results is a model summarizing a few pages, fast. It's handy for a quick orientation and sometimes wrong. Click through to the source for anything you'll act on, especially health, money and law.

        
Company chatbots
Support bots on airline, bank and store sites can be wrong, and what they tell you may still count. In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024), a Canadian tribunal made the airline pay a customer who relied on a refund policy its chatbot had made up. Screenshot what a bot promises, and get it confirmed.

        
Summaries everywhere
Email apps, phones and shopping sites now summarize messages, notifications and reviews. A summary can drop the one detail that matters (a date, a "not"). For anything important, read the original.

        
Your feeds
Recommendation algorithms (the older kind of AI in the rings above) choose what you see on video and social apps, tuned to keep you watching. Not good or bad on its own, but worth knowing that the feed isn't neutral.

      

    


    

      
The other assistants, fairly

      
This course uses Claude, but the habits work with any of them. Here's how the major ones compare on the things that matter day to day. Prices and settings change, so this is a snapshot, dated below.

      

    


    

      
How much energy is one question? slide it

      
Two last questions people ask most: what it costs the planet, and what it means for everyone. First, energy. The honest answer has two halves: a single text question is tiny, and the total across the world is large and growing fast.

      
Try it: slide to about how many questions you ask in a day, and see what that adds up to in everyday terms.

      

    


    

      
The big questions open any

      
Reasonable, well-informed people disagree about most of these. Each one gives you what's known, where the disagreement is, and what you can do. That includes criticism of Anthropic, the company that makes Claude.

Using Claude well · cheat sheetThe habits and prompts from every course, on one page.

        

          
Before you ask
  1. Start inside the right project or folder, so your material is on the desk.
  2. Search on for anything current.
  3. Give the context an expert would ask for, or: "Ask me what you need to know first."
  4. Ask neutrally: "What are the weakest points?", not "It's good, right?"
  5. Say what you want back: format, length, purpose.

          
Power phrases
  • What don't I know about this that I should?
  • Before answering, critique my prompt and suggest a better one.
  • Rate your confidence in each point.
  • Quote the line that supports that, and say which file.
  • Recompute that with code.
  • What's the strongest case against this?

          
Checking
  • Numbers: recompute. Dates: check the calendar.
  • Quotes: find the exact words in the source.
  • Citations: find it yourself; can't find it, treat it as unverified.
  • Code: run it on the sample. Math: verify a different way.
  • Second opinion: new chat, different wording.

          
The folder method
  • One folder or project per subject.
  • Originals word for word, one index row each.
  • "Read this first" at the top of the summary, edited in place.
  • One source of truth; dates as 2026-11-06.
  • A short report after every addition.

          
Health: the method
  1. Map what you don't know
  2. Learn the key terms
  3. Find the best evidence (guidelines, then reviews)
  4. Weigh it: who was studied, absolute numbers
  5. Cross-check the claims you'd act on
  6. Write a dated summary
  7. Bring questions to your doctor

          
Health: never
  • Ask AI in an emergency. Call 911.
  • Change a medication because of an AI answer.
  • Share ID, Medicare, bank or card numbers.
  • Let Chrome or computer use into health or banking accounts.
  • Trust a citation that isn't on PubMed.

          
School: the system
  1. Check the class's AI policy.
  2. One folder per class; syllabus first.
  3. Learn by doing: try first, then line-by-line feedback.
  4. Practice harder than the exam, prompt only.
  5. Verify every answer by computation; save to verified/.
  6. Ask for a harsh readiness check.

          
School: exam prep
  1. Pin down the facts (date, format, allowed).
  2. Gather intel, labeled as guesses.
  3. Learn each question type: basic, sample, harder.
  4. Timed practice with only what's allowed.
  5. Stop, write reference notes, sleep.

Health research · Stop H1 · Why method matters · about 25 minutes

        
What the research shows

        
What rigorous studies and major medical bodies have found about the public using AI for health questions: where it helps, and exactly where it breaks down.

      

      

      

        ~14 minTED · Eric Topol, MDCan AI Catch What Doctors Miss?A cardiologist makes the optimistic but evidence-minded case.
        
At this stop you'll learn
  • What a large randomized trial of the public using AI found
  • The three reasons people did worse than the AI alone, and the habit that fixes each
  • Where six expert sources agree, and where they differ

      

    

    


    

      
The Oxford trial Nature Medicine · Feb 2026

      
Oxford researchers and doctors wrote ten medical scenarios, from a common cold to a bleed on the brain. 1,298 UK adults were randomly assigned either to use an AI model (GPT-4o, Llama 3 or Command R+) or whatever they'd normally use. The same models were also tested alone, given the full scenario.

      

        
The model alone
given the complete scenario text

          
Named a relevant condition94.9%

          
Chose the right next step56.3%

        

        
People using the model
describing the scenario in their own words

          
Named a relevant condition<34.5%

          
Chose the right next step<44.2%

        

      

      
"Next step" means stay home, see a GP, go to A&E, or call an ambulance. Figures for people are upper bounds across the three models; they did no better than the comparison group (who used search engines and health websites) at choosing the next step, and worse at naming the condition. Abstract on PubMed.

    


    

      
How much weight to give this study

      
This trial is worth a whole stop because it's the kind of evidence stop H6 teaches you to look for. Here is how to weigh it, the same way you'd weigh any study Claude cites.

      

        
Why it's strong
  • Randomized: people were assigned to AI or no AI by chance, so the groups were alike except for the AI.
  • Preregistered: the researchers declared their methods and measures before starting, so they couldn't pick flattering results afterwards.
  • Large and independent: 1,298 people, run by a university, published in a leading peer-reviewed journal.

        
Its limits
  • People described written scenarios, not their own symptoms.
  • It tested 2024 models from other companies, not Claude, and models have improved since.
  • Participants were UK adults recruited online, not trained in using AI for health.

        
What it means for you
The medical knowledge was there; what failed was the conversation. That's the part you control. Every habit in stops H2 to H5 targets one of the failure points below, so this study is less a warning against AI than a map of how to use it well.

      

    


    

      
Why it failed, and the fix for each

      

        
People left details out
Participants often didn't give the information the model needed.
Fix: your health binder (stop H2)

        
The model didn't ask
The models didn't reliably ask for what was missing before answering.
Fix: "ask me first" (stops 5 and H3)

        
Answers mixed good and bad advice
Two people describing similar symptoms of a brain bleed got opposite advice.
Fix: the stoplight test and checking (stops H3, H6)

      

      
The study used 2024 models, and newer ones are better. The lessons about briefing the model, asking neutral questions and checking still hold.

    


    

      
What the experts advise

      

        
AMA
American Medical AssociationMay 2026 · patient guide
  • Use AI to learn, compare options and prepare for appointments.
  • Not for emergencies, diagnosis or treatment decisions, or to replace a doctor.
  • AI can't know your full history, may use outdated or unvetted information, and sounds confident even when wrong.
  • Add context: "Given my situation [age, lifestyle, goals], what do I need to know?"
One-page guide (PDF)Article

        
HH
Harvard Health PublishingOctober 2026 · reviewed by Adam Rodman, MD
  • The green/yellow/red guide from stop H3.
  • Explaining reports and preparing for visits is green; new symptoms are yellow; treatment and medication decisions are red.
  • Bottom line: AI is not a replacement for health care professionals.
Full article

        
HG
Dr. Adam Rodman, Harvard GazetteMay 2026 · interview
  • A stricter stoplight: test results and appointment prep are yellow; managing a condition or choosing medications is red.
  • Give enough health context, because the quality of the question drives the answer.
  • People tell chatbots more personal details than they'd type into a search engine, which makes privacy a bigger concern.
Interview

        
AP
AP / PBS NewsHourMarch 2026 · "5 things you should consider"
  • Chatbots tailor answers better than search but still hallucinate.
  • Serious symptoms need immediate care, not a chatbot.
  • HIPAA doesn't cover the companies that build chatbots.
  • A second chatbot can work like a second opinion.
Article

        
UB
University of Birmingham: "Ask SMART"Health Chatbot User Guide · no AI-industry funding
  • Slow down · Make questions clear · Ask yourself what you're sharing · Remember to check the facts · Talk to a real person.
  • Citations don't always match the answer, and chatbots can be sycophantic and biased.
  • Talk to a professional before starting or stopping a medicine.
The guide"Check the facts"Full PDF

        
F
Forbes: an emergency physician's guideSeptember 2026 · Jesse Pines, MD
  • How to upload lab results and scans safely.
  • Sycophancy: "Is this just stress?" invites reassurance, while "What else could this be?" gets a differential diagnosis.
Article

      

    


    

      
Where the experts agree, and where they don't

      

        
Broadly, all six agree
  • AI is good for understanding: explaining terms, reports and options, and preparing for appointments.
  • It is not for emergencies, and not the one to decide on a diagnosis or treatment.
  • Give it context, because the quality of the question drives the quality of the answer.
  • Check facts and sources; confident answers can be wrong.
  • Be deliberate about what you share. In the US, HIPAA doesn't cover chatbot companies (AP).

        
Where they differ
  • Interpreting your own results: Harvard Health calls it green; Rodman, in the Gazette interview, calls it yellow, best done with your doctor involved.
  • Second chatbot: AP's guide suggests a second AI as a second opinion; the Birmingham guide puts more weight on talking to a real person.
  • Optimism: Topol (in the video above) emphasizes what AI can catch; the Oxford trial shows how easily that gets lost in the conversation. Both are true, which is why this guide teaches the conversation.

      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
Health research · Stop H2 · Setting up · about 35 minutes

        
Your health binder

        
This is the folder method from core stop 4, built for your health. A health binder keeps your medications, conditions, appointment notes, questions and research in one place Claude reads every time, so every health question is answered for you, not for an average adult. There's a free way and a Pro way.

      

      

      

        shortAnthropic · officialGetting started with projects in Claude.aiThe building block for the free binder.
        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Why a binder makes answers more accurate
  • The free binder: a Project plus memory
  • The Pro binder: a folder on your computer Claude reads and updates
  • How to remove identifiers from a document without losing what matters

      

    

    


    

      
Why it makes such a difference

      

        
Stop 4 showed why a folder of your own material changes answers. In health the stakes are higher, because the missing detail is often the one that matters: a medication that causes the symptom, a kidney problem that makes a common drug unsafe. Without a binder, getting those onto the desk depends on you remembering every relevant detail, every time. People don't, and that was one of the main problems in the Oxford trial (stop H1): the models knew the medicine, but people often left out key details and the AI didn't reliably ask.

        
A health binder is simply a set of documents about you that Claude reads automatically. Once it exists, a question like "Is this new cough worth worrying about?" is answered for someone your age, with your conditions and your medications, not for an average adult. It also builds over time: after each research session the useful findings go back in, so next month's question starts where this month's ended.

      

      
What goes in it, and why each part matters

      

        
Medication listEvery prescription, supplement and over-the-counter drug, with dose and timing. The single most important page: interactions, side effects and dosing questions all depend on it.

        
Conditions and historyDiagnoses with the year, past surgeries, relevant family history. Changes what's likely, what's risky and which guidelines apply to you.

        
Allergies and bad reactionsWhat happened, not just the name ("penicillin: rash"). Keeps suggestions safe.

        
Recent resultsLab values with ranges and dates. Dates matter: a trend over three tests says much more than one number.

        
Visit notesWhat each doctor said, changed or planned. Lets Claude answer in line with your actual care, and spot conflicting advice.

        
Questions logQuestions waiting for a doctor, and the answers you got. Nothing gets forgotten between appointments.

        
Research summariesWhat you found, with sources and confidence (the worksheet in stop H4 produces these). Stops you redoing the same research.

        
Leave outName, birth date, addresses, phone, record, insurance and account numbers. Claude never needs them; the medical content is what helps.

      

    


    

      
Before anything goes in redaction trainer

      
Whichever binder you use, every document that goes in should have what identifies you removed, and keep everything that's medically useful. The rule of thumb: remove anything that points to who you are (name, birth date, address, phone, record and insurance numbers); keep anything about your health (age, sex, results, ranges, dates of tests, diagnoses). Your age does the work your birth date would, without identifying you. Blacking out on paper before photographing works; so does retyping just the results. Tap every detail you'd black out on this sample, then press Check my redaction.
