The free binder Free

      
On Free, the binder is a Project. A project has two parts, and they do different jobs: instructions tell Claude how to work with you (always cite sources, ask before assuming, flag anything urgent), and files tell it about you (your summary, medication list, key reports). Both are loaded into every chat you start inside the project.

      

        
        
Why the answer above is different
The same question asked outside the project gets a general answer about coughs. Inside it, Claude already knows the conditions and medications in the files, and follows the instructions about citing and flagging urgency, without you typing any of it. (A dry cough is a known side effect of lisinopril, for example; Claude can only raise that if it knows you take it.)
The capacity bar shows how much of the project's room your files use. A summary and a few reports use very little; dozens of long PDFs fill it.

      

      

        
Set it up once (15 minutes)

          
    
            
  1. Sidebar → Projects → New project. Name it "My Health".
    2. 
            
  2. Paste the "My Health" instructions from the prompt studio (stop H5) into the project's instructions.
    3. 
            
  3. Ask Claude, inside the project: "Interview me to build a one-page health summary: conditions, medications with doses, allergies, surgeries, family history, my doctors." Answer its questions.
    4. 
            
  4. Save the summary it writes as a file and add it to the project's files.
    5. 
          

        

        
Keep it current (2 minutes)

          
    
            
  1. Start every health chat from inside the project.
    2. 
            
  2. At the end of a useful session: "Update my health summary with anything new from today and give me the full updated version."
    3. 
            
  3. Replace the old file in the project with the new one.
    4. 
            
  4. For small facts, memory is enough: "Remember I started magnesium 250 mg." (Memory inside a project stays with that project, so the important facts still belong in the summary file.)
    5. 
          

          
The catch: you do the copying. That's the manual step Pro automates.

        

      

    


    

      
The Pro binder: a folder on your computer try the simulator

      
On Pro, the Claude desktop app (Mac or Windows) can be given access to a folder you choose (older versions call this Cowork, a separate mode you choose first; in the newer version rolling out since September 2026 it's part of every chat in the desktop app). Claude can then read, create and edit files in that folder as you talk, so the binder updates itself: tell it your dose changed and it edits the medication list; finish some research and it files a summary. The files are ordinary documents on your computer that you can open, print or back up yourself (the ".md" ones are plain text). Tap the requests below and watch the folder change.

      

        
Health Binder

        

        

      

      
A demonstration with example content. In the real app you type or speak the requests yourself; Claude shows what it plans to change and, depending on your settings, asks before doing it.

      

        
Set it up (Pro)

          
    
            
  1. Install the Claude desktop app from claude.com/download and sign in.
    2. 
            
  2. Make a new, empty folder called "Health Binder". Don't point Claude at your whole Documents folder.
    3. 
            
  3. In the desktop app, ask Claude to set up your health binder in that folder and connect the folder when it asks. (In older versions, first choose Cowork at the bottom left of the message box.)
    4. 
            
  4. Set the permission mode to Manual ("Manually approve") for the first day or two so you can watch what Claude does, then switch to Auto ("Automatically approve", Gavin's suggestion) so it can keep the binder current without stopping to ask each time. Anthropic suggests staying on Manually approve for sensitive files, so stay there if you'd rather check each change.
    5. 
            
  5. Ask: "Set up my health binder: create files for medications, conditions, a questions log, and folders for visit notes and research."
    6. 
          

        

        
How it behaves

          
    
            
  • Claude can only reach the folders you connect, and only while the desktop app is open on that computer.
    • 
            
  • It asks your explicit permission before permanently deleting anything.
    • 
            
  • The folder stays on your computer, but any file Claude opens is sent to Anthropic to process, the same as an upload. Anthropic advises caution about giving it personal records, which is one more reason to remove identifiers first.
    • 
            
  • You can see what it plans and stop it at any point.
    • 
            
  • Back the folder up like any important documents.

Other health jobs a binder handles

      

        
Appointment prep
A folder per doctor: last visit's notes, your questions, what changed since. "Prepare me for Thursday."
Free or Pro

        
Family health history
Who had what, at what age. Useful for screening questions and to share with relatives.
Free or Pro

        
Meals around your health
Your dietary needs and favorite foods stored once; ask for a week of meals or a shopping list.
Free or Pro

        
Insurance and bills
An explanation-of-benefits letter or an itemized hospital bill, decoded line by line: what each code means, what you owe, and anything that looks billed twice. Remove account numbers first.
Free or Pro

        
Travel
Medication schedules across time zones, packing lists, and questions to ask before a trip.
Free or Pro

        
A reading log
Summaries of articles and studies you've read, so you never research the same thing twice.
Free or Pro

      

    


    

    

  






  

    

    

      

        
Health research · Stop H3 · Research skills · about 30 minutes

        
Asking health questions

        
Core stop 5 taught six habits and why they work. Health questions raise the stakes on every one of them, and add one habit of their own: asking for absolute numbers. This stop shows each habit in its health form, drawn from the AMA, Harvard Health, the University of Birmingham and the Oxford trial, then gives you a question checker and the green/yellow/red test for how far to trust an answer.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The six habits in their health form, including absolute numbers
  • Three common health questions, rewritten
  • A checker that grades your own health questions
  • The stoplight test: how far to trust each kind of answer

        
Haven't done core stop 5 yet? Start there: it explains why each habit works. This stop doesn't repeat it.

      

    

    


    

      
The habits, health edition open each

      
Five of these are the core habits with the health-specific reason they matter; number 5 replaces "say what you want back" with the habit medicine needs most. Each shows the same question asked without and with it.

      

        
1Brief it like a specialistCore habit 1 · Counters: Facts 04 and 01
          
Give the context a specialist would ask for before answering: age, sex, conditions, every medication and supplement with dose, allergies, when this started and how it has changed, what's been tried, and what your doctor has said.
Why it works
Claude answers whatever is on the desk (stop 1). Every missing detail gets filled with what's typical for an average person, and the answer quietly becomes about someone else. Missing context was a key failure in the Oxford trial (stop H1).

          
Instead ofMy ankles are swollen. Why?
TryI'm 64, with high blood pressure. I take amlodipine 10 mg (started six weeks ago) and metformin. Both ankles have been swollen for about a month, worse in the evening, no pain or redness. What could explain this?

          
Your binder (stop H2) supplies most of this automatically. Amlodipine, a common blood-pressure drug, often causes ankle swelling, which the short version would likely miss.

        
2Make it interview youCore habit 2 · Counters: Fact 04
          
Ask Claude to question you before it answers, one question at a time.
Why it works
It turns Claude into a history-taker. It asks about things you didn't think were relevant, including the symptoms you aren't having, which often matter as much as the ones you are.

          
Instead ofI've been getting headaches. What's causing them?
TryI've been getting headaches. Before answering, ask me any questions you need, one at a time, the way a careful doctor would take a history. Then give me your assessment.

          
Answer each question honestly, including "I don't know." The final answer is usually far more specific.

        
3Ask neutral questionsCore habit 3 · Counters: Fact 03
          
Ask what could explain something, rather than asking it to confirm what you suspect or hope.
Why it works
Models lean toward agreeing with the person asking (sycophancy). A question that signals the answer you want tends to get that answer, with the alternatives underplayed.

          
Instead ofThis is probably just stress, right?
TryWhat could explain this, from most to least likely, including anything serious that shouldn't be missed?

          
If you do have a guess, say it separately: "I wondered about stress, but don't assume that."

        
4Demand evidenceCore habit 4 · Counters: Facts 01 and 02
          
Ask for sources, and for how strong each one is: a clinical guideline, a randomized trial, an observational study, or expert opinion.
Why it works
From memory alone, Claude can blur details or invent sources. Asking for named, linked sources (with web search on) changes how it answers, and gives you something to check. Asking for the type of evidence tells you how much weight each claim can bear.

          
Instead ofIs magnesium good for sleep?
TryIs magnesium supplementation effective for sleep in older adults? Search for systematic reviews and randomized trials, give each with its year and link, say how strong the evidence is, and keep settled findings separate from preliminary ones.

          
Stop H6's evidence pyramid explains why a guideline or systematic review outweighs a single study.

        
5Ask for absolute numbersHealth only · Counters: misleading percentages
          
When a benefit or risk is given as a percentage, ask what it means in actual people.
Why it works
"Cuts risk by 30%" sounds large, but if the risk was 10 in 1,000 it becomes 7 in 1,000, so 3 people in 1,000 benefit. Percentages alone make small effects look big and hide side-effect rates.

          
Instead ofDoes this drug reduce stroke risk?
TryOut of 1,000 people like me taking this drug for five years, how many would avoid a stroke, and how many would have a significant side effect? Who was studied, and how similar are they to me?

          
The answer is often the clearest single thing to take to your doctor.

        
6Push back and cross-checkCore habit 6 · Counters: Facts 03, 05 and 06
          
Ask for the case against the answer, then check it another way: a new chat with different wording, and one of the sources opened yourself.
Why it works
A single answer is one sample (fact 05), stated with more confidence than it may deserve (fact 06). The case against brings out weak spots; a second, independently worded answer shows whether the first was stable.

          
Instead of(accepting the first answer)
TryWhat's the strongest argument against what you just said? Which of your claims rest on the weakest evidence?

          
If it changes its answer when you push, ask what new evidence changed it. If there isn't any, the first answer may have been sounder.

      

    


    

      
Leading vs. neutral, in health tap to see the rewrite

      
LeadingThis rash is probably just an allergy, right?
NeutralWhat could cause a rash like this, from most to least likely, including anything serious that shouldn't be missed? Ask me what you need to know first.
The first invites agreement (sycophancy, fact 03). The second asks for a ranked list of possibilities and a proper history.

      
VagueIs fish oil good for my heart?
SpecificWhat do randomized trials and systematic reviews show about fish-oil supplements for preventing heart disease in adults over 70? Give absolute numbers and say where the evidence disagrees.
Naming the population, the outcome and the kind of evidence keeps marketing claims out of the answer.

      
Looking for permissionMy doctor says I need surgery but I don't think I do. What are the alternatives?
BalancedMy doctor recommended [procedure] for [condition]. Lay out all the options, including surgery and watchful waiting, with the benefits and risks of each, so I can discuss them with her.
The first sets up a conclusion and the model will tend to supply it. The second gets a fair comparison to take back to the doctor.

The stoplight test

      
Harvard Health's guide, reviewed by Dr. Adam Rodman, an internist and AI researcher at Harvard Medical School, sorts health questions by how far you can rely on the answer.

      
Why the colors fall where they do: green tasks rely on stable, well-documented knowledge (what a term means, what a test measures), where AI is strong and mistakes are easy to spot. Yellow tasks depend on details about you that may be incomplete, so the answer is a starting point for a clinician. Red tasks are decisions that need an examination, your full record and someone accountable for the outcome, which no chatbot has.

      

        
Green
Explaining a condition or term; decoding a doctor's note, lab report or imaging report; diet planning around a known condition; preparing for an appointment.
Generally fine. Remove identifiers from documents first.

        
Yellow
New symptoms and possible diagnoses: "Interview me like a doctor about this new headache."
A first step only. Take the result to a clinician.

        
Red
"Is this the right treatment plan for me?" "Should I take this medication?" "Is this the correct chemotherapy regimen?"
Don't rely on AI. Use it to prepare questions for the person who decides.

      

      
In a Harvard Gazette interview, Rodman is stricter: appointment prep and interpreting test results are yellow (best with your doctor involved), and managing a condition or choosing between medications is red.

Health research · Stop H4 · Research skills · about 45 minutes · the heart of the course

        
Researching a topic, start to finish

        
A seven-step method for going from "I've just heard about this" to "I understand the evidence and know what to ask my doctor." Each step has a prompt to copy, what a good answer looks like, and the warning signs of a bad one. Work through it once with a real topic and the worksheet below.

      

      

      

        ~3 minAnthropic · officialGetting started with research in Claude.aiResearch mode, which speeds up step 3 on Pro. Free works too, with web search.
        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Why you map a topic before asking specific questions
  • How to find the best evidence, not just any evidence
  • How to weigh, cross-check and record what you find
  • How to turn research into a better conversation with your doctor

      

    

    


    

      
Why a method beats a single question

      

        
Most people ask one question and accept the answer. That gets you an answer to the question you thought of, framed the way you framed it. The most important things are often the ones you didn't know to ask about.

        
The method runs from wide to narrow and back out again: first map what you don't know, then learn the vocabulary, then find and weigh the strongest evidence, then try to knock it down, then write it up and take it to someone who can examine you. It mirrors how good researchers and good doctors think, and every step is designed around a known weakness of AI.

      

    


    

      
The seven steps tap a step or use Next

      
Each step comes with a prompt to send Claude, written so it works around one of AI's known weak spots. Put your own topic in the box and every prompt fills it in for you.

      
Try it: type a topic you care about, open step 1 and copy its prompt into Claude. Then use Next step to go on, and note what each step turns up in the worksheet below.

      

      

      

      
The habit: don't stop at the first answer. Step 1 (map what you don't know) and step 5 (try to knock the answer down) are the two a single question always skips.

Health research · Stop H6 · Trust and checking · about 30 minutes

        
Checking health claims

        
Core stop 7 covered checking in general. Medical claims need three extra skills: tracing a claim back to its study on PubMed, judging how strong a piece of evidence is, and knowing which trusted medical source answers which kind of question.

      

      

      

        ~13 minPeter Attia, MDThe various types of scientific studies and how they differCase reports through meta-analyses.
        
At this stop you'll learn
  • How to trace a claim back to its study, in a guided exercise
  • The two-minute check, done on PubMed
  • How to judge evidence strength, with the pyramid
  • Which trusted source answers which kind of question

      

    

    


    

      
Check this claim 4-step exercise

      
A realistic AI answer that cites a real study. Work through it the way you would for real.

      

        

        

      

    


    

      
The two-minute check, on PubMed

      
The general check from core stop 7, done the medical way: the exercise above as a routine you can use on any health claim that would change a decision. You don't need to read the whole paper: the abstract (a one-paragraph summary at the top) is enough to catch most problems.

      

        
    
          
  1. Get the exact reference. With web search on, ask Claude: "Give me the exact title, first author, journal, year and PubMed ID (PMID) for that study, and quote the sentence of the abstract that supports your claim."
    2. 
          
  2. Find it yourself. Go to PubMed and paste the PMID or the exact title into the search box. If nothing comes up, try the title in a regular search engine. Still nothing: treat the claim as unverified. If the ID brings up a different paper, that's a red flag too.
    3. 
          
  3. Read the abstract for four things: who was studied (age, health), what was compared, what was measured, and how big the difference was.
    4. 
          
  4. Compare with the claim. Same kind of people as you? Same outcome? Same size of effect? Claims most often go wrong by stretching a result to a different population or overstating its size.
    5. 
          
  5. Decide: supported, overstated, or not supported. If overstated or unsupported, tell Claude what you found and ask it to correct its answer.
    6. 
        

        
      

    


    

      
The evidence pyramid tap a level

      
Finding that a study is real is half the check. The other half is how much that kind of study can prove: a review of many trials outweighs one small study, and both outweigh one expert's opinion. Knowing the levels tells you how much weight a cited study deserves.

      
Try it: tap each level, from the strongest at the top down to the weakest, to see what it is, how it sounds in a headline, and what to ask Claude about it.

      

      
The habit: when Claude cites research, ask what kind of study it is. One small study, an animal or lab study, or one expert's view is a reason to keep looking, not a settled answer.

Health research · Stop H7 · Trust and checking · about 5 minutes

        
Hard limits

        
The short list of situations where AI is the wrong tool, however good the answer sounds. The first four draw on the medical sources in stop H1; the fifth is Anthropic's own advice.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The emergency signs that mean call 911, not ask a chatbot
  • Five rules: medications, reassurance, privacy, citations and computer features

        
A screenshot of the card below is worth keeping on your phone.

      

    

    


    

      
Emergency? Don't ask AI.
Call 911

      
Outside the US, use your local number: 999 or 112 in the UK, 112 across the EU, 000 in Australia.

      

        

          
Chest pain, pressure or tightness

          
Trouble breathing

          
Worst headache of your life

          
Sudden confusion

          
Severe bleeding that won't stop

          
Fainting or unresponsiveness

        

        
Stroke signs, remembered as F.A.S.T.: any one of these means call 911 right away, even if it passes.

        
FFace drooping
AArm weakness
SSpeech difficulty
TTime to call 911

        
A model can misjudge urgency. In the Oxford trial, people using AI chose the right level of care less than half the time. Not an emergency, but not sure? Call your doctor's office, or a 24-hour nurse advice line if your insurance has one (the number is often on the back of your card). A nurse can judge urgency with the right questions.

        
988Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US). Call or text 988, any time, for yourself or someone you're worried about. AI is not the place for this.
1-800-222-1222Poison Control (US): swallowed the wrong pill, a double dose, a child into the cleaning cupboard. Free, 24 hours, or online at poison.org.

      

    


    

      
Medications
Don't start, stop or change a medication because of an AI answer. Bring what you found to your prescriber or pharmacist. Why: the right dose and the risks of stopping depend on your full record, and some medicines (certain blood-pressure drugs, steroids, antidepressants, seizure medicines) are risky to stop suddenly.

      
Reassurance
Don't let a reassuring answer delay care. The Birmingham guide warns specifically against waiting because a chatbot said a symptom was probably harmless. Why: AI leans toward reassurance (stop 1, fact 03) and misjudges urgency. If you're worried enough to ask, that's reason enough to call your doctor's office.

      
Identifiers
Never share Social Security, Medicare, bank or card numbers, or your full address. They add nothing medically, and they're the details that do real harm if they ever leak.

      
Citations
If a cited paper isn't on PubMed by title or ID, treat the claim it supported as unverified (stop H6).

      
Computer features
Don't let Claude in Chrome or computer use operate patient portals, pharmacy, banking or government accounts. Anthropic advises against it: a website can hide instructions that trick Claude into actions you didn't ask for, and it sees everything on screen.

    


    

    

  








  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S1 · Ground rules · about 25 minutes

        
AI in school: the rules and the research

        
The same tool can be the best tutor you've ever had or a way to skip the learning and get caught. The difference is what your class allows and whether you do the thinking. This stop settles both, then shows what decades of learning research say about which study methods actually work, because the whole course is built around them.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • How to find out exactly what each class allows, and what to do when it's unclear
  • Which uses are almost always fine, which depend, and which usually aren't
  • The study methods research rates highest and lowest, and how Claude does each
  • How university students actually use Claude, from Anthropic's own data
  • Learning mode: what it does and when to switch it on

        
Not legal or academic advice. Your syllabus and your instructor decide. When in doubt, ask them in writing before you use AI on anything graded.

      

    

    


    

      
Tutor or shortcut

      

        

          
Grades are supposed to measure what you can do. Exams are taken without Claude, so anything Claude did for you instead of with you is something you'll have to do alone later, under time pressure. That's the practical reason, apart from the rules, to use AI to learn, not to produce.

          
The rest of this course is built that way on purpose: Claude teaches from your class's own material, gives you problems instead of answers, marks up your attempts, and checks its own work. Used like that, it's allowed in more classes, and it builds the skills exams test.

        

        
Shortcut
"Solve problem 4." You copy the answer. It's on the homework; it isn't in your head.
Tutor
"Give me a problem like number 4, don't solve it, and mark up my attempt." You do the work; it shows you exactly where you went wrong.

      

    


    

      
Allowed or not? sort eight real situations

      
For each situation, choose where it usually falls. Policies really do differ, so the answers are "usually", and the explanation says what changes it.

      

    


    

      
Find your class's actual rule five places to look

      

        
    
          
  1. The syllabus. Look for "AI", "generative", "ChatGPT", "outside help", "collaboration" or "academic integrity". Many syllabi now have a section just for AI.
    2. 
          
  2. Each assignment's instructions. A class that allows AI for studying may ban it on a specific project or take-home exam.
    3. 
          
  3. Course site announcements (D2L, Canvas, Blackboard). Policies get clarified mid-semester.
    4. 
          
  4. Your school's academic integrity page. It sets the default when a class says nothing.
    5. 
          
  5. Ask, in writing. A two-line email ("Is it OK to use AI to generate practice problems and check my understanding, as long as I don't use it on graded work?") gets you a clear answer you can point to later.
    6. 
        

        
Let Claude find it for you
Here's my syllabus. Quote, word for word, every sentence about AI tools, outside help, collaboration or academic integrity, with the section each one is in. Then summarize in three lines what I may and may not use AI for in this class. If anything is ambiguous, say so and draft a short email asking the instructor.

      

      
Some classes ask you to say when and how you used AI. If yours does, keep a line in your class folder's log (the session log in INDEX.md, stop S2) each time, so writing the note later takes ten seconds.

    


    

      
AI detectors, and how to protect yourself

      

        

          
Some instructors run work through an "AI detector". Know what those tools can and can't do. No detector can prove a piece of writing came from AI. They estimate how predictable the text looks, and predictable isn't the same as machine-written: clear, formal writing gets flagged, and so do people writing in a second language. A 2023 Stanford study found popular detectors flagged more than half of essays by non-native English speakers as AI-written. OpenAI withdrew its own AI-text detector in 2023 because it wasn't accurate enough, and several universities have switched detection off.

          
That cuts both ways. A detector score alone shouldn't get you in trouble, and it also won't save work that broke your class's rules. The rules are what matter, which is why the policy check above comes first.

        

        

          Protect yourself
          
    
            
  • Write in Google Docs or Word with version history on, so your drafting is visible over time.
    • 
            
  • Keep your notes, outlines and early drafts, not just the final file.
    • 
            
  • Keep the short AI-use log described above: what you used it for, and when.
    • 
            
  • If you're accused, stay calm, ask what the process is and what evidence it rests on, and show your history. Most schools require more than a detector score.
    • 
          

        

      

    


    

      
What research says about studying tap a method

      
In 2013, a team of cognitive psychologists led by John Dunlosky reviewed hundreds of studies on ten popular study techniques and rated how useful each one is. The two rated highest take more effort, so students use them less than they should. Three of the five rated low (rereading, highlighting and summarizing) are what most students actually do. Tap any method to see why it landed there, and how Claude makes it easier.

      

      
Source: Dunlosky et al., "Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques," Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013; summary from the Association for Psychological Science. "Low" doesn't mean useless: it means the evidence for it helping across students and subjects is weak.

    


    

      
How students actually use Claude

      
In April 2025 Anthropic published an analysis of 574,740 anonymized conversations from accounts tied to university email addresses. Three findings are worth knowing:

      

        
~47%of conversations were direct: asking for an answer or a finished piece of work with little back-and-forth. The report notes some of that "might also be cheating," and that it can't tell without knowing each class's rules.

        
39.8%of Claude's responses involved creating, the top level of Bloom's taxonomy, and 30.2% analyzing. The report flags a concern: students may be handing Claude the higher-order thinking that learning depends on.

        
36.8%of conversations were about computer science, though only 5.4% of US degrees are in it. Coding help was the single biggest use.

      

      
Source: Anthropic Education Report: How university students use Claude (April 8, 2025). The lesson this course draws: keep the conversation collaborative, and keep the creating and analyzing for yourself.

    


    

      
Learning mode a switch worth knowing

      

        

          
Claude has a Learning style that makes it teach instead of answer: it asks how you'd approach the problem, points you toward the next step, and asks you to explain your reasoning, the Socratic method. It was built for Claude for Education and opened to everyone in August 2025.

          
Use it when you're learning something new and tempted to just read the answer. Switch it off when you want a fully worked example to study, or when you're checking work you've already done. The class folder's teaching rules (stop S4) give you the same effect with more control, so many people use those instead.

          
Anthropic's current help pages list only Normal, Concise, Explanatory and Formal, so Learning may not be in your menu. If it isn't, just ask: "Use a Socratic, learning style: guide me with questions and don't give me the answer until I've tried."

        

        
      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S2 · The class folder · about 35 minutes

        
The class folder: why it works

        
One folder per class. Every syllabus, slide deck, lecture transcript, practice exam, answer key and announcement goes in, word for word, and Claude keeps it organized. From then on, Claude stops being a generic tutor and becomes a tutor for your class: your instructor's notation, your exam's format, your learning objectives, what's been taught so far and what hasn't. For school, this is the single most useful thing you can set up.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Why a folder of real class material makes practice questions so much more exam-accurate
  • Nine specific things it does that a generic chat can't
  • What every file in the folder is for, using a real class folder
  • The boot rule: how every new chat loads the class without you asking

        
This is the folder method from core stop 4, built out for a class. Stop S3 shows how to set it up on Free and on Pro.

      

    

    


    

      
Feed the folder, watch the questions change drag the slider

      
The request stays the same: "Give me one practice question for Exam 2." Drag to add class material to the folder, one kind at a time, and watch the question Claude can write get closer to the real exam.

      

    


    

      
Why it's so good nine reasons, open any

      
Core stop 4 gave the general reasons. These are the ones that matter for a class, each with what it looks like in practice.

      

    


    

      
Inside a real class folder click any file

      
This is the structure from an intro Python class (CSE 231) that was then reused, with a few improvements, for Calculus 2. Click each file or folder to see what's in it, why it exists, and an excerpt.

      

    


    

      
The boot rule how every chat loads the class

      

        

          
A folder only helps if Claude reads it. You could start every chat with "read my class folder first", but you'll forget. The fix is a short boot rule saved where every chat sees it (memory, or the Project's instructions), that tells Claude what to load the first time you mention the class.

          
Three details make it reliable:

          
    
            
  • A narrow trigger. "When I mention Calc 2" rather than "whenever we talk about school". A broad trigger fires in the wrong chats and wastes your limit loading files you don't need.
    • 
            
  • One source of truth. The boot rule only says where the folder is and which file to read first. Your preferences and teaching rules live in the folder, not in memory, so there's one copy to keep current.
    • 
            
  • Save it first. Save the boot rule before anything else in the setup chat, so it exists even if later steps get interrupted.
    • 
          

        

        

          
Boot rule (saved to memory)
Calc 2 boot rule: once per chat, the first time I mention Calc 2, open ~/Desktop/Calc2, read prompt/PROMPT.md and follow it. PROMPT.md loads my learner profile, SUMMARY.md ("read this first" section) and context/INDEX.md. My learner profile overrides the default teaching rules.

          
Free version (in the Project's instructions)
This project is my Calc 2 class. Before answering anything, read SUMMARY.md (start with "Read this first"), then LEARNER_PROFILE.md, then check INDEX.md for the files that matter to my question. Teach only from these files.

          
On any plan, a skill can act as a backup trigger: a saved instruction file that Claude loads when its description matches, even if memory misses it. Turn on code execution (Settings → Capabilities), then manage skills under Customize → Skills. One more reason for it: memory saved inside a project stays with that project, so a skill is how the class loads when you mention it elsewhere.

        

      

    


    

      
One folder per class, not one for everything

      

        
Why separate
Nothing bleeds across
Chemistry notation doesn't leak into calculus answers, and a question about one exam never pulls in another class's dates.

        
Why separate
Cheaper to load
Each chat reads one class's summary, not five. Your usage limit lasts much longer (core stop 3).

        
Why separate
Easy to reuse
When a class ends, the folder is a finished study guide. Next semester, copy the structure, not the content (stop S8).

      

      
Material from an earlier course (say, Chem 1 notes while taking Chem 2) can go in a background/ folder marked "context only", so Claude uses it to fill gaps but teaches from the current class.

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S3 · The class folder · about 40 minutes

        
Building it: Free and Pro

        
The class folder works on both plans. On Free it's a Project, and you drop in the files Claude writes for you. On Pro it's a real folder on your computer that Claude reads, files into, runs code in and keeps current by itself. Pro is the recommendation for a full semester; this stop sets up both, step by step, then shows what to feed it and how to save it well.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Which plan fits your semester, and why Pro (not Max) is the usual pick
  • The Free setup and the Pro setup, step by step
  • Exactly what computer access lets Claude do, and its limits
  • What to feed the folder, and what Claude does with each item
  • Lessons to apply from day one, so the folder stays trustworthy

        shortAnthropic · officialGetting started with projects in Claude.aiThe building block for the free version.
      

    

    


    

      
Free or Pro, for a semester of classes

      

        
Free A Project per classPro A folder per class

        
Who files new materialYou upload it; Claude writes the updated summary for you to download and swap inClaude saves the original, updates the index and summary, and reports what changed

        
How much fitsThe project's capacity bar (dozens of documents; big slide decks fill it)As much as your disk; Claude opens only what a question needs

        
Code and math checksClaude can run code in the chat and make files to downloadAlso runs your lab code against the class's test files, and saves practice files you open in your own editor

        
UsageFine for a class or two; long pre-exam sessions can hit the limitAt least 5× Free per five-hour session

        
Where it worksBrowser and phoneDesktop app (Mac or Windows) for the folder; phone and browser for everything else

        
Cost$0$20 a month, or $200 a year paid up front

      

      
Why not Max? Max (from $100 a month) mostly buys more usage, plus priority access and API credits. Pro has the folder, computer access, code and Opus. If you hit Pro's limit often, the efficiency habits in core stop 3 usually fix it before Max would.

    


    

      
The Free setup Free about 15 minutes

      

        
    
          
  1. Make the Project. Sidebar → Projects → New project. Name it after the class ("Calc 2").
    2. 
          
  2. Paste the instructions. Use the master prompt from the setup kit (stop S9) or write your own: how to teach, what to always do, and the Free boot rule from stop S2.
    3. 
          
  3. Upload the syllabus first, then ask: "Read the syllabus. Write SUMMARY.md with a 'Read this first' section at the top: exam dates and formats, what's allowed in the room, grading, and topics in order. Also write INDEX.md with one row for the syllabus." Download both and add them to the project's files.
    4. 
          
  4. Add materials as they come. Upload the file, then: "File this: add a row to INDEX.md and merge its key facts into SUMMARY.md. Give me both updated files and tell me what changed." Replace the old versions in the project.
    5. 
          
  5. Tell it how you learn. "Interview me, then write LEARNER_PROFILE.md." (Stop S4 has a builder.) Add it to the project.
    6. 
        

        
      

      
Saving originals on Free: keep the original files in a folder on your own computer too (same names as in INDEX.md). The project is where Claude reads them; your computer is the backup.

    


    

      
The Pro setup Pro about 20 minutes

      

        
    
          
  1. Make one folder for the class somewhere easy, such as Desktop/Calc2. Empty is fine; Claude builds the structure.
    2. 
          
  2. Install the Claude desktop app from claude.com/download and sign in.
    3. 
          
  3. Make a "Calc 2" Project and start a chat in it from the desktop app. The project keeps class-specific memory together; the folder holds the files.
    4. 
          
  4. Ask for exactly that folder. "Set up my Calc 2 system in Desktop/Calc2." Approve access to just that folder when asked. A narrow request (one class folder) gets approved smoothly; asking for your whole Desktop and Downloads is broader than it needs and may be refused.
    5. 
          
  5. Give it the plan. Attach the setup message from the kit (stop S9), or a handoff from another class (stop S8): "Set up my Calc 2 system from this handoff." It creates the folders, saves the boot rule first, writes PROMPT.md, and asks for your syllabus.
    6. 
          
  6. Choose how often it asks. Start in the mode where it asks before each change, watch for a session or two, then let it work more freely so filing doesn't interrupt you. (Core stop 4 explains every setting.)
    7.

What computer access lets Claude do open any

      
Linking the desktop app to your computer is what makes the Pro version work: Claude works directly in your class folder instead of you uploading files every chat. Here's everything it can do there, with the limits.

      

    


    

      
What to feed it drop materials into the folder

      
Tap a material to hand it to Claude. Watch where it's filed, the row it gets in INDEX.md, what changes in the summary's "Read this first" section, and the short report Claude gives back. The order on the left is the order to send things in.

      

    


    

      
Do these from day one a checklist that saves itself

      
Each of these was learned the hard way during a real semester. Tick them off as you set up a class; the list remembers on this device.

      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S4 · Studying · about 35 minutes

        
Learning by doing

        
Reading a perfect explanation feels like learning. It mostly isn't. What builds the skill is doing it yourself first and getting checked: typing the code, working the step, writing the program from a blank file, then seeing exactly where you went wrong. This stop sets Claude up to work that way, shows a real calculus session, and explains how to get math written properly with LaTeX.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The active recall loop, and why it beats reading answers
  • What a good tutoring session looks like, step by step, in calculus
  • Line-by-line feedback on your own attempt, with ❌ and ✅
  • Teaching rules that make Claude explain the way you learn
  • LaTeX: how to get clean math in chat, and into your documents
  • Your learner profile, built in two minutes

        
From a real semester: "Writing programs from a blank file, with only the prompt" and "asking for an honest assessment" were the two biggest wins. "You're not ready yet, here's why" was more useful than encouragement.

      

    

    


    

      
The active recall loop tap each step

      
Four steps, repeated. Basics first, then deeper. Each step has the line to send Claude.

      

    


    

      
A real session: learning calculus step through it

      
Integration by parts, taught the way the teaching rules below ask for: the formal rule first, each step on its own line with the rule named, a check question, an attempt, inline feedback, a re-teach, then a harder one. Press Next to play the session.

      

    


    

      
Feedback on your own work flip between attempt and markup

      
Ask Claude to rewrite your attempt exactly, then mark each wrong line inline: ❌ what's wrong and why, ✅ what it should be. It's the fastest feedback to read, because your own work is the map. Pick an example, then flip the switch.

      

      
The line to send with your attempt
Here's my attempt. Rewrite it exactly as I wrote it, then mark each wrong step inline: ❌ what's wrong and why, ✅ what it should be. Don't fix lines that are right. Then tell me which single idea I'm missing, and give me one new question that tests it.

    


    

      
Teaching rules that work open any

      
Put the ones you like in your learner profile (below), and Claude follows them in every chat for that class. Each came from what worked, or failed, across a semester of chemistry, Python and calculus.

      

    


    

      
LaTeX: clean math, everywhere see the source and the result

      

        

          
LaTeX is the standard way to write math as plain text: \frac{a}{b} becomes a fraction, x^2 a superscript, \int an integral sign. Claude's chat renders it automatically, so math shows up properly typeset instead of as a jumble of slashes and carets.

          
Why it matters for studying: you read math faster and misread it less when it looks like your textbook, and you can reuse the source in your own documents: Overleaf takes it directly, Word's equation editor has a LaTeX mode, and Google Docs needs an add-on. Your notes can look as clean as the chat.

          
Put this in your learner profile: "Always use LaTeX for math. Each step on its own line, with the rule name and formula in italics between steps. Never put math inside code blocks, where it shows as raw source."

        

        

      

    


    

      
Build your learner profile two minutes

      
LEARNER_PROFILE.md tells Claude how you learn. It overrides the general teaching rules, and it's loaded in every chat for the class. Choose what fits; the file updates as you go and saves on this device.

      

    


    

      
Ask for the truth about where you stand

      

        
By default, Claude is encouraging (fact 03: it leans toward what you seem to want). Before an exam, encouragement is the most expensive thing it can give you. Ask for a harsh, realistic read, based on evidence: what you got wrong, what you haven't practiced, and how the exam is weighted.
Say it once in your profile ("Harsh, realistic assessments of where I stand") and it sticks.

        
Readiness check
Based on SUMMARY.md, my practice results and the exam's format and point values, give me a harsh, realistic assessment: if the exam were tomorrow, what score range would I most likely get, and why? List the three topics costing me the most points, how many hours each needs, and the order to do them in. Don't soften it.

      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S5 · Studying · about 35 minutes

        
Study artifacts

        
An artifact is a small interactive page Claude builds beside the chat: a practice exam you can take and submit, a drill that re-teaches what you miss, a worked-solutions page, a diagram, a schedule. It works on every plan, you can reuse it as often as you like, and the best ones let you copy your results back to Claude so the next session targets your mistakes. This page you're reading is one.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • What makes a study artifact good, by taking one
  • The kinds of things you can ask Claude to make, with examples you can see
  • Prompts for each kind of study artifact
  • How to save, reuse and share them

        
Some people don't like quiz cards, and that's fine: for code, the better "artifact" is an editable code box you type into and run, then your own program (stop S4). Use what makes you do the work.

      

    

    


    

      
Take one: a practice exam 7 questions · intro Python

      
Built in the format that worked best across a semester: answer everything first, then Submit. Each miss opens with the question restated, "how do I know", and the trap. Then a topic table tells you what's solid and what to re-learn, and Copy results for Claude gives you a summary to paste into your class chat. The questions are the tiny details multiple choice really tests. No Python experience? Take it anyway and read the explanations: you'll see why the format works.

      

    


    

      
Things you can ask it to make real examples

      
Claude draws diagrams, charts and pictures by writing them as code (SVG, the same format as the drawings on this page), so they're crisp, editable and labeled. Pick a kind to see an example of what comes back, and the prompt that makes it.

      

    


    

      
Study artifacts, and the prompt for each open any

      
Every prompt assumes you're in your class project or folder, so Claude builds from your real material. Each says how the artifact should behave, which is what separates a useful one from a pretty one.

      

    


    

      
Saving, reusing and sharing

      

        
Close the loop
Ask for a "Copy results for Claude" button in every quiz. After you finish, paste the results into the class chat: "Re-teach every miss in depth, then give me a new quiz on the weak topics." Each round targets exactly what you got wrong.

        
Keep them with the class
Artifacts are saved to Artifacts in the sidebar, and you can reopen them from any chat. On Pro, also ask Claude to save each one's file into the class folder (artifacts/) with a row in INDEX.md, so they're with everything else and you can open them offline.

        
Share carefully
An artifact can be published with a link. A practice exam you made from your own notes is usually fine to share with classmates; one built from an instructor's copyrighted exam or keys usually isn't. Check the syllabus.

      

      
Ask for the best format, in one line
Make this an interactive artifact: I answer every question first, then press Submit. For each miss, restate the question, explain "how do I know", show the work and the trap. Then a topic table (Solid / Review / Re-learn) with links to the missed questions, and a "Copy results for Claude" button.

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S6 · Studying · about 40 minutes

        
Exam prep

        
A repeatable process for any exam, from pinning down the facts to the night before. It leans on everything so far: the class folder supplies the real material, practice is prompt-only and harder than the real thing, and every answer gets verified by computation before you study it, so you never memorize something wrong.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The five-phase exam process, with the prompt for each
  • How to write practice problems that are harder than the exam, on purpose
  • A seven-step method for reading a long exam question
  • Memorizing patterns instead of answers, with "if you see → do → because"
  • How to verify math and code answers before you trust them

        
Double-check every date the AI states. In a real semester it once planned as if an exam were today when it was tomorrow. Exam facts go in the summary's "Read this first" section, and you confirm them against the syllabus.

      

    

    


    

      
The process, in five phases tap each

      
This spreads exam prep over five phases, from the first week of class to the last few hours. Doing them in order means nothing you study is built on a wrong date, format or topic list, and nothing important is left for the last night.

      
Try it: tap each phase to see when it happens, what to do, and the prompt to copy into your class chat.

      

      
The habit: phase 1 comes first for a reason. Until the date, format and topics are confirmed against the syllabus, every plan Claude makes is built on a guess.

    


    

      
Practice problems, the right way

      

        

          

            
Written like the real thing. For code: a story, a sample data file, and a full sample run. For math: the wording, notation and point style your instructor uses.

            
Prompt only. No solution until you ask. Reading solutions doesn't build the skill; producing them does.

            
Harder than the practice exam. If an example looks like one you've already seen, it's too shallow. For coding exams, ask for prompts with no starter functions, so you decide the structure.

            
Only what the class taught. Every problem uses patterns and tools from the class, never outside methods.

            
All the material, not just the mock. Draw from recitation keys, learning objectives and slides too: the real exam tests the same ideas in different forms.

          

        

        
Practice problem prompt
Write one new practice problem for Exam 2 in exactly the style of the real exam questions in my folder, on [topic]. Make it harder than the practice exam, use only what the class has taught, and include everything the real thing would (for code: a story, a sample data file and a full sample run; no starter functions). Give me only the prompt. No hints and no solution until I send my attempt.

      

    


    

      
Reading a long exam prompt seven steps, try them

      
Long coding or word problems are mostly a reading test. This method turns a wall of text into a plan. Step through it on a real-style prompt: each step highlights what to look at and adds to your plan.

      

    


    

      
Memorize patterns, not answers two examples

      
Don't memorize code or worked answers. Memorize the handful of patterns that cover most questions, by writing each one from a blank page until it comes out on its own. Then drill the small details that multiple choice tests.

      

      

    


    

      
Verify every answer before you study it open any

      
Claude is far more reliable when it computes an answer than when it works one out in its head (core stop 7). Make verification a standing rule for the class: every code example is run, every math answer is checked by a method that doesn't depend on how it was found, and verified solutions are saved to verified/ so they're never regenerated wrong.

      

    


    

      
Spot what needs checking tap the claims

      
Math and code can be checked by running them. Facts in a study sheet can't, and a wrong fact you memorize costs you points. So before you study from notes Claude wrote, find the claims that could be wrong and check them against your class material.

      
Try it: tap every claim you'd check before studying it, then press I'm done: score me. Each catch shows where to check it.

      

      
The habit: a fact goes on your flashcards or reference sheet only after you've found it in your notes, slides or textbook. Ask Claude: "Quote the line from my class files that says this, and name the file."

    


    

      
Reference sheet, and the last 24 hours

      

        
If your exam allows a reference sheet
  • Get the official sheet early: it defines what you can rely on, so you don't waste time memorizing what's printed on it.
  • Add short notes on what each method does, in words, not code blocks or dense symbols you can't read under stress.
  • Check your notes against exactly what the instructor said is allowed.
  • If a calculator with stored notes is allowed (some accommodations allow it), keep drafts separate and save to the device only when you say so, then test every page.

        
The last 24 hours
  • Timed practice in exam-sized sets, reference sheet only, as the instructor suggests.
  • Ask for a harsh readiness check (stop S4) the evening before, while there's still time to act on it.
  • Stop new material a few hours before. Write your reference sheet notes, eat, sleep.
  • Get there early, with exactly what you're allowed to bring.

      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S7 · Planning · about 30 minutes

        
Classes and degree planning

        
Choosing classes is a puzzle with a lot of pieces: graduation requirements, prerequisites, which terms each class is offered, a transfer school's rules, credit loads, and your actual week. Claude is very good at puzzles like this when it has every piece in writing, and very bad when it fills gaps from memory. This stop shows what to give it, builds the planning prompt for you, and lists what to verify before you register.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Exactly which documents to give Claude for degree and transfer planning
  • A plan builder that turns your goals into a complete prompt
  • How to get several plan options (fastest, balanced, lightest) and compare them
  • Building a weekly schedule around practice, work and sleep
  • What to verify with the official degree audit and an advisor

        
Claude drafts; the registrar decides. Use the plan to walk into your advisor meeting prepared, not to skip it. Course catalogs, prerequisites and transfer credit change.

      

    

    


    

      
What to give it tick what you have

      
Every gap here becomes a guess. Gather these into a "Planning" folder or project first; most are downloadable PDFs or pages you can save.

      

    


    

      
Plan builder fill in, copy, paste

      
Choose your goal and constraints. The prompt on the right builds itself, asking for several options so you can compare them instead of accepting the first plan. Nothing you type leaves this page.

      

    


    

      
What good options look like an illustration

      
Ask for options side by side, each with its trade-offs. This is the shape of a useful answer for a student planning two more terms before transferring. The numbers are illustrative.

      

      
The real answer depends on your documents. What matters is the shape: options, each labeled with what it costs you, every requirement accounted for, and anything it couldn't confirm flagged.

    


    

      
A weekly schedule that fits your life

      

        

          
Once you know which classes, the next puzzle is which sections. Give Claude the section list (times and days) and your fixed commitments, such as team practices and lifts exported from your team app, a work schedule or a commute, plus the rules you care about. Ask for every valid combination ranked by your rules.

          
Rules that worked for a student athlete:

          
  • Classes only bump practice if there's no other way
  • At least 10 minutes between classes, and between class and practice
  • No early mornings if possible
  • A whole free day if possible

        

        
Schedule prompt
Here are the sections offered next term for [classes], and my fixed weekly commitments (attached). Rules, in priority order: 1) classes only overlap practice if there is no other way; 2) at least 10 minutes between any two commitments, including walking time between buildings if you can find it; 3) no classes before 10 am if possible; 4) one fully free weekday if possible. List every valid combination, ranked by how well it follows the rules, as a weekly grid for the top three. Flag any rule a combination breaks. Check every time conflict with code rather than by eye.

      

    


    

      
Transfer planning

      

        
Step 1
Find what transfers
The target school's transfer equivalency table, or a shared database: Transferology covers many US schools, and ASSIST covers California's public colleges. Save the pages for your courses into the planning folder.

        
Step 2
Find what the major needs
The target program's admission requirements for transfer students: required courses, minimum grades, GPA, and deadlines. These are often stricter than general admission.

        
Step 3
Plan the overlap
Ask Claude for the classes that count at both schools and keep you on track for the major, and flag every class it can't find in the equivalency table. One real example: a spring plan settled on Calc 3, Physics 2, Statics and an intro engineering course, all chosen to transfer.

      

    


    

      
Verify before you register where AI plans go wrong

      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
AI for school · Stop S8 · Power user · about 30 minutes

        
Running your class system

        
Once a class folder is running, a few habits turn it from a tutor into a system: handoffs that let any new chat pick up exactly where the last one stopped, several chats working at once without stepping on each other, independent fact-checks on anything high-stakes, and reusing the whole setup for the next class, improved each time.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Handoff files: when to write one, and what goes in it
  • Running a main chat and a side chat on the same class safely
  • Independent fact-check passes on keys and solutions
  • Reusing your setup for a new class, and the seven improvements from a real one
  • Computer use with real software, and what to do when usage runs low

      

    

    


    

      
Handoffs never lose a chat's progress

      

        

          
Long chats get slow, expensive and forgetful (core stop 1). Side jobs come up mid-session. The fix is a handoff: a short file Claude writes that lets a brand-new chat continue exactly where this one stopped. You open a new chat and say "Read HANDOFF_exam2.md first."

          
Write one when: a chat is getting long; you're switching to a side job; you're about to stop for the day mid-topic; or you're starting a new class from an old one's setup.

          
A handoff isn't a transcript. It's what the next chat needs to act: where things stand, what's been decided, what's next, and where the files are. The summary's "Read this first" section is the permanent version; a handoff is for work in progress.

        

        
Ask for a handoff
Write HANDOFF_[topic].md in the class folder so a new chat can continue exactly where we are. Include: what we were doing and why; what's done; what's decided (including my preferences from this chat); the next three steps; my unanswered work; which files matter; and anything you were unsure about. Keep it under one page. Then add a line to the session log in INDEX.md.

      

    


    

      
Several chats at once tap each part

      
Sometimes one chat should keep teaching while another builds something, such as a set of calculator reference pages or a big practice exam. Two chats editing the same files will overwrite each other, so give each one its own territory.

      

    


    

      
Independent fact-check passes

      

        
For anything high-stakes, such as an answer key you'll study from or reference pages you'll use in the exam, ask for a separate, independent check against the official source. A check that starts fresh isn't anchored on the first answer. The simplest way, on any plan: a new chat that's given only the official key and the draft does the same job.
Say quality must not drop: a check that only skims is worse than none, because it gives false confidence.

        
Fact-check prompt
Before I study from this, have an independent check done: compare every answer and every step in worked-solutions.md against the official key and the class notes in context/. Recompute every number. List each disagreement with which source says what, and don't change anything until I confirm.

      

    


    

      
Reusing the setup for a new class CSE 231 → Calc 2

      
The first class folder (intro Python) worked, but grew messy. When it was reused for Calculus 2, through a handoff that copied the structure and not the content, seven changes made it leaner and more reliable. Tap each to compare.

      

      
Start the next class from this one
Write a handoff that lets a new chat set up the same system for [new class] in Desktop/[folder]: the folder structure, the master prompt, my learner profile, and everything we learned about what works. Don't copy any [old class] content. Add checks specific to [new class] (for math: verify every answer by computation). Then I'll start a "[new class]" project chat in the desktop app, attach the file, and say "Set up my [new class] system from this handoff."

    


    

      
Sharing it with classmates

      

        
Share the master prompt
Write PROMPT.md so it's the same for every student, and keep your personal rules in LEARNER_PROFILE.md. Then the master prompt can be shared as-is.

        
Share a setup message
A ready-made message a classmate forwards to their own Claude, which then interviews them and builds their folder (stop S9 makes one).

        
Don't share the content
Your folder holds the instructor's materials and your own work. Each student should feed their own folder from their own copies.

      

    


    

      
Working with real software

      

        
Translation
When the class teaches a different program
A CAD class taught in MicroStation, done in AutoCAD: Claude translates the instructor's steps and terms into the other program, and keeps the submission rules in the summary (for example, native drawing file plus an 11×17 PDF, named Lastname-Firstname-HW#), so every homework is handed in right.
Prompt
The instructor's steps below are for [program A]; I use [program B, version]. Translate each step into [program B], with the exact command or menu path, and flag anything that has no direct equivalent.

        
Computer use
Operating an app for you
With computer use (core stop 4), Claude can operate desktop software that has no other way in. A real example: building reference pages for a graphing calculator in its official desktop software. Lessons:
  • Some parts of an app refuse automated clicks and typing (here, the script editor), so you paste that part yourself.
  • Keep the app on the visible screen; automation can fail when it's on another desktop or Space.
  • Seeing the real screen caught layout bugs a test missed.
  • Use only official software, never an unknown converter.

      

    


    

      
When usage runs low near a deadline

      

        
1Ask for the cheapest way"I'm low on usage. What's the cheapest way to get this done?" It will often batch steps, skip re-reading big files, or suggest doing a step yourself.

        
2Hand off, then start freshA new chat that reads a one-page handoff costs far less per message than message 60 of a long one.

        
3Point it at one file"Only read context/exam2-review.pdf pages 3–5" instead of letting it search the whole folder.

        
4Lighter model for choresFiling, renaming and formatting don't need the most capable model; save it for the hard explanations.

Copy them into Claude (Free) or hand Claude the setup message and let it create them (Pro).

  • Free: paste PROMPT.md into the Project's instructions, and add the other files to the Project.

Advanced: work smarter · Stop A1 · Start here · about 35 minutes

        
Full power, safely

        
The more Claude can reach, the more it can do for you. With your files, your accounts, a browser and your computer, it stops being a chatbot you copy from and becomes an assistant that does the work. This stop starts with what that kind of access makes possible, then how to ask for the best way to do anything, and only then the honest risks and the layers of protection that keep them close to zero. Set up well, the benefits outweigh the risks almost every time.

      

      

      

        
G
Gavin's take
I let Claude use my computer every day: it reads and files my class folders, runs my code, and works in apps for me. It's that useful. I do it with the habits on this page: one folder per job, backups, official sources only, and a look before anything gets deleted or sent. That's all it takes.

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The access ladder: what each level of access unlocks, and what to set up
  • How to always get the best workflow, by asking for it
  • The seven real risks, from most to least likely, with honest numbers
  • Layers of protection you can stack, as many as the job needs
  • What plugins, skills and connectors can do, and why where you get them matters so much
  • The safeguards already built in

      

    

    


    

      
The access ladder climb it

      
Each rung gives Claude more reach, and each one multiplies what it can do. Pick a rung to see what it unlocks, what you set up on your end, and the one safety layer that goes with it. Most people stop at rung 1 and never see what the top looks like.

      

    


    

      
Always ask for the better way

      

        

          
Most people use AI the way they first met it: typing into a chat box, copying the answer out, pasting it somewhere else. Very often there's a much better way to do the same job, and the person just doesn't know it exists: a connector that lets Claude send the email itself, a browser it can sign in to, a scheduled task that does the chore every Monday, a small program it can write to reach data that's stuck in some app.

          
AI models also tend to work around a missing permission quietly, giving you a weaker result, instead of telling you what would make it better. So make it a rule: tell Claude you want the best workflow, and that you're happy to set things up or grant access on your end. Then decide, knowing the trade-off.

        

        
Put this in your instructions
"Before you start, tell me if there's a better way to do this: a connector, a setting, more access, a tool you could build, or something I could set up on my end. Explain the benefit and what I'd need to do. Don't quietly work around a missing permission; ask for it."
Where: Settings → Your Claude → Instructions (older layout: Settings → Account → "Instructions for Claude"), so it applies to every chat. Or in a project's instructions.

      

      

    


    

      
The right way to think about it

      

        

          
Treat an AI agent like a capable new assistant: give it the keys it needs for the job, not the keys to everything, and glance at anything that can't be undone before it happens. That's the whole philosophy. Everything below is a specific case of it.

          
Some perspective: documented incidents are rare next to the hundreds of millions of AI sessions people run every week. Almost all of them involved at least one of three things: software from an unofficial or look-alike source, an "approve everything" mode with access to the whole computer, or no backups. Avoid those three and you've removed most of the risk.

          
Honest caveat: nobody publishes an overall incident rate, so "rare" here means "few documented cases compared with enormous use", not a measured percentage. Anthropic itself says the risk is "non-zero", which is the honest answer, and a reason to trust its safeguards rather than fear them.

        

        

      

    


    

      
Seven risks, most likely first open any

      
Notice the order. The two most likely problems aren't hackers at all: they're a wrong answer you trust, and leaning on AI so much you stop learning. The dramatic ones are the rarest.

      

    


    

      
Plugins, skills and connectors: where you get them is everything

      

        

          
A plugin is a bundle of extras for Claude (stop A5 explains them fully). Some parts are just instructions; others, such as hooks and local connectors, run programs on your computer with your permissions. That's what makes them powerful, and why the source matters.

          
The data on this is striking. When the security firm Snyk scanned about 4,000 skills from open marketplaces in February 2026, 13.4% had a critical issue and 76 contained confirmed malicious code. But in the curated top 100 of one directory, the rate of hidden instructions was zero. The worst incidents happened on open marketplaces anyone could publish to, or through look-alike packages with a familiar name.

          
Anthropic's own directory works differently: every version gets automated validation and a security scan, and a person reviews a new listing before it goes live. That review doesn't cover something you add from a link or upload yourself, which is exactly why those deserve more care.

        

        

          

          
Sources: Snyk "ToxicSkills" report (Feb 5, 2026); Anthropic plugin directory documentation. ClawHub belongs to an unrelated assistant, not to Anthropic.

For each situation, decide. Most real uses are a confident "go", sometimes with a small habit attached.

      

    


    

      
Layers of protection stack what you need

      
Security people call this "defense in depth": no single layer has to be perfect, because something only goes wrong if it gets through every layer at once. Low-stakes jobs need one or two; anything touching money, health records or your whole computer deserves more. Tap a layer to switch it on and see what it stops.

      

    


    

      
Eight habits that cover nearly everything a checklist

      
Tick the ones you already do. The list saves on this device.

      

    


    

      
What's already protecting you

      

        
Trained to refuse
Claude is trained to ignore instructions hidden in web pages and files, and classifiers scan untrusted content as it comes in. In Anthropic's latest published tests (August 2026), with safeguards on, prompt-injection attacks on Claude in Chrome succeeded 0.3% of the time against Fable 5 and 0% against Sonnet 5, Opus 5 and Mythos 5.

        
It asks first
Claude always asks before permanently deleting files, in any mode. It asks before visiting financial sites, refuses stock trading, and computer use asks permission per app, with sensitive apps blocked by default.

        
Reviewed sources
Directory plugins get an automated security scan on every version, and an Anthropic reviewer approves at least the first version. Official marketplace names can only come from Anthropic's own repositories, so a third party can't pretend to be official.

      

      
No safeguard is perfect, and Anthropic says so: its Chrome safety page says "The risk is not zero." Your habits are the second layer. Sources: Use Claude in Chrome safely, Use Cowork safely, Let Claude use your computer in Cowork, Claude in Chrome is generally available (August 26, 2026; the 0.3% and 0% test results).

Advanced: work smarter · Stop A2 · How usage works · about 30 minutes

        
Tokens, limits and usage

        
Your limit isn't a count of messages. It's a budget of tokens: every piece of text Claude reads and writes, every file, every search result and every bit of thinking. Once you can see what's being counted, you can make the same budget go several times further. Core stop 3 gave the basics; this is the full picture.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • What a token is, and how to estimate them
  • Why every message re-reads the whole conversation, and the surprising math that follows
  • Which features use the most, and why
  • How the 5-hour and weekly limits work, where the meter is, and what happens when you hit it
  • Caching: why coming back after a break can cost more

        
The one idea to take away: a long chat costs roughly the square of its length. Forty messages in one chat can use nearly four times what the same forty messages cost spread over four fresh chats.

      

    

    


    

      
What a token is

      

        

          
A token is the small chunk of text a model actually reads and writes: a short word, part of a longer word, a punctuation mark. Think of Scrabble tiles rather than whole words: "unbelievable" might be three or four tiles.

          
On today's Claude models, a rough rule of thumb (not an Anthropic figure) is 1,000 words ≈ 1,500 tokens or more. (Anthropic says its newer models produce about 30% more tokens for the same text than older ones did.) Code, numbers, tables and non-English text use more.

          
Tokens come in two kinds. Input is everything Claude reads: your message, the conversation so far, files, search results. Output is everything it writes, including its thinking. At Anthropic's published prices, output costs five times as much as input. So a request for a shorter answer saves twice: less writing now, and less history to re-read later.

        

        

      

    


    

      
Why long chats cost so much drag the sliders

      
The model remembers nothing between messages. To answer message 40, the whole conversation, all 39 earlier exchanges, is sent and processed again. Anthropic puts it plainly: "nothing gets sent just once." So the total grows much faster than the chat does.

      

      
Ignores caching, which softens this when you work in quick bursts (below). The shape is the point: split long work into fresh chats with a short handoff note, and the same work costs a fraction.

    


    

      
What uses the most open any

      
Anthropic lists what affects usage: message length, file size, conversation length, tools like web search and Research, model choice, effort level, artifacts, and multi-step tasks. Here they are from heaviest to lightest, with why.

      

    


    

      
Where one message's tokens go change the setup

      
Your new message is usually the smallest part of what Claude reads. Everything below is sent again with every message in a chat. Change the setup and watch the bar. (Sizes are illustrative but realistic.)

      

    


    

      
How the limits work

      

      

        
Two windows
5 hours, and a week
Paid plans have a limit that resets five hours after your first message; there is also a weekly limit on top, reset at a fixed time shown in Settings → Usage. Free has a five-hour limit and a weekly limit too. Usage in claude.ai, the desktop app and Claude Code all counts toward the same limits.

        
Where to look
Settings → Usage
Click your name (bottom left) → Settings → Usage: bars for the current session and the week, with reset times. In Claude Code, /usage shows the same and breaks it down. On Free, limits also reset every five hours, and Claude lets you know when you've hit one.

        
At the limit
Wait, or use credits
Nothing is lost: you wait for the reset. On paid plans you can turn on usage credits (Settings → Usage), billed at API rates, and keep working. If you do, set a monthly spending cap so there are no surprises.

      

      

        
PlanPriceUsageModels

        
Free$0Limited, every 5 hours and every week (varies with demand)Sonnet, Haiku

        
Pro$20/mo, or $200/yrAt least 5× Free per 5-hour session, plus a weekly limit+ Opus; Fable on usage credits

        
Max$100/mo5× Pro, every 5 hours and every week+ Fable, up to half the weekly limit

Checked November 6, 2026 on claude.com/pricing and the Help Center. Ultra is the plan formerly called Max 20x.

    


    

      
Caching: the waiter who remembers your order

      

        

          
When the start of a conversation or a Project hasn't changed, the system can reuse the work it already did on it instead of processing it again from scratch. That's caching, and it makes re-reading much cheaper. Anthropic says Project content "is cached and counts less against your limits when reused."

          
The catch: caches can expire after a period of inactivity, so after a long break your first message may count that content in full again (Anthropic documents cache expiry for Claude Code; its Projects pages do not spell out the timing). Like a waiter who remembers your usual if you come back within the hour, but not next week.

        

        
What this means in practice
  • Work in focused bursts. A session of related questions close together is cheaper than the same questions spread across a day.
  • Don't change the start. In Claude Code, switching models mid-session breaks the cache (each model has its own), and connecting tools can too when tool search is off; pick your model at the start.
  • Big chat, long break? Start a new chat with a handoff note instead of reopening the giant one.
