Choosing a model and effort

        
Two dials decide most of what a message costs: which model answers, and how much effort it puts in. The biggest model at the highest effort isn't the best choice for everything. For most tasks it's slower, uses your limit far faster, and gives the same answer. Here's how to match the dials to the job.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The four models, what Anthropic says each is for, and how heavy each is
  • What effort does, and when to turn it up or down
  • How to see the price differences, and why the smartest model is sometimes cheaper overall
  • A task-by-task cheat sheet, and a practice round

        
Anthropic's own advice for chat: "If you're not sure which model to pick, start here," about Sonnet. Move up when Sonnet struggles; move down for quick, simple jobs.

      

    

    


    

      
The four models lightest to heaviest

      

      
Model names and descriptions from Anthropic's model guide and announcements (checked November 2026). All four current models can hold up to a million tokens in their context window on paid plans and the API (Haiku gets 500,000 in long hand-off tasks). Older models stay selectable for a while after new ones arrive.

    


    

      
How different the costs are

      
Anthropic doesn't publish how much faster each model uses a subscription limit, but it labels them Lightest, Moderate, Heavy and Heaviest, and its API prices (what developers pay per token) show the relative sizes. Treat this as a rough guide to how fast each eats your limit.

      

      
But cheaper per token isn't always cheaper per job. A smarter model often finishes in one pass where a smaller one needs three tries. Anthropic's own example: a smaller model at high effort missed a detail and needed a follow-up; a frontier model at medium effort got it in one go. Judge by the whole job.

    


    

      
The effort dial drag it

      
Current models think adaptively before they answer (in the Claude apps it can’t be turned off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 or Fable 5.1); effort sets how much. You'll find it in the model menu next to the send button, with each model's recommended level marked Default. Phrases like "think hard" in your message don't change it; they're just text.

      

    


    

      
Practice: pick the model eight tasks

      
For each task, choose the model you'd start with. There's often more than one reasonable answer; the explanation says why one is the best start.

      

    


    

      
Cheat sheet

      

        
Haiku · low to medium
Fix grammar, rewrite an email, summarize an article, translate a paragraph, sort a list, file and rename things, quick definitions.

        
Sonnet · default
Explain a concept, a study guide or practice questions, a cover letter, everyday coding and debugging, spreadsheet formulas. Your everyday model.

        
Opus · medium to high
A long contract or research paper, comparing options with real trade-offs, a hard bug, anything Sonnet got wrong. Health questions where accuracy matters (with search on, and checking).

        
Fable · high
Rarely needed: long, many-step work where accuracy is critical, carried through to a finished document. Or when Opus has struggled.

Working efficiently

        
Anthropic puts it well: being efficient with tokens "doesn't mean using fewer of them overall." It means spending them on the task, not on noise: stale history, files you didn't need, corrections piled on corrections. These habits, ranked by how much they save, get you the same results for a fraction of your limit, and usually better results too, because a focused desk gives better answers.

The handoff note

      

        
The most useful single habit: when a chat gets long, have Claude compress it into a short note, then continue in a fresh chat. You swap a history of tens of thousands of tokens for a few hundred, and lose nothing that matters, because you chose what to keep.
This is the same idea as the school course's handoff files (stop S8), and Claude Code's "write a spec, then start a fresh session".

        
Handoff prompt
Summarize this conversation as a handoff note for a fresh chat: the goal, decisions made, key facts and numbers, what's done, what's left, and any exact text I'll need. Keep it under 300 words.

Advanced: work smarter · Stop A5 · Extending Claude · about 30 minutes

        
Plugins, skills and connectors

        
Claude on its own is a capable new employee. Extensions are what you hand that employee: a handbook for how you like things done, keys to your other apps, speed-dial buttons, specialist helpers, automatic rules. A plugin is a bundle of those, installed in one go. Here's what each piece is, which ones only advise and which ones run programs, what they cost you even when idle, and how to choose them well.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Skills, connectors (MCP), commands, agents and hooks, in plain language
  • What's inside a plugin, by opening one up
  • Which parts only give instructions and which run code, and why that matters
  • Where to find trustworthy ones, and what the labels mean
  • When to build your own: six signals

        
Where they live in the app: one Plugins page in the sidebar, with filters for skills and connectors. (It replaced Customize and its Skills, Connectors and Plugins tabs from late October 2026; some accounts may still show Customize.) Skills and connectors work on every plan, Free included; plugins need a paid plan. In Claude Code, type /plugin. Menus move; the Help Center has the current paths.

      

    

    


    

      
Open up a plugin click each compartment

      
This is a typical plugin for a sales job, the kind Anthropic publishes for knowledge work. Each compartment is one kind of extension. The badge says whether it only advises Claude (instructions) or runs a program on your computer.

      

    


    

      
Why skills are so light

      

        

          
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: a short name and description at the top, instructions below, and optionally more files. Anthropic compares building one to "putting together an onboarding guide for a new hire."

          
The clever part is progressive disclosure. Claude always sees only each skill's name and one-line description. It reads the full instructions only when a task matches, and the extra files only when a step needs them. So a long reference costs almost nothing until it's used. That's why the school course uses a skill as the boot rule's backup, and why "make a skill" beats pasting the same long instructions into every chat.

          
Anthropic published skills as an open standard in late 2025, and in October 2026 donated the format to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, which also looks after MCP; dozens of other AI tools now read the same files.

        

        

      

    


    

      
Connectors and MCP

      

        

          
MCP (the Model Context Protocol) is the open standard Anthropic launched in November 2024 for connecting AI to other systems. The MCP documentation's analogy: "Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications." A connector links Claude to another service through MCP, such as Gmail, Google Drive, GitHub, PubMed. It gives Claude tools that can read data, and sometimes create, change, delete or send things.

          
Remote connectors run on the service's own servers; local ones run as a program on your computer (desktop extensions package these for easier install). For each tool a connector offers there are permission settings such as Always allow, Needs approval or Blocked (on Team and Enterprise, owners set these for everyone): allow "read email", block "send email".

        

        
The three labels
  • Verified Tested by Anthropic. Not a security audit or a guarantee, and the developer can change tools later.
  • Community Screened, but not reviewed in depth.
  • Custom You added it yourself; nobody reviewed it. (Free accounts can add one.)

      

      
What happens when Claude uses a connector press play

      

    


    

      
Advises, or runs code? sort them

      
The single most useful question about any extension. Instructions can only influence Claude, inside its usual permission prompts. Programs run with your full user permissions, outside those prompts. That's where trust in the source matters most.

      

    


    

      
The always-on cost

      

        
An enabled plugin is part of every session, not only the ones where you use it. The name and description of each of its skills and agents sit in Claude's context on every turn, and its local servers run in the background. Each one is small; twenty add up. Anthropic's tool-search feature already keeps unused connector tools out of the way, but descriptions still load.
So: install what you'll use, and disable the rest. Claude Code's marketplace even shows a "context cost" estimate before you install.

        

      

    


    

      
Choosing good ones

      

        
Start in Anthropic's directory or official marketplace. Directory plugins get an automated security scan on every version, and an Anthropic reviewer approves the first version (and later ones too if flagged or if the plugin's setting requires it).

        
Prefer well-known publishers (Anthropic, GitHub, Microsoft, Slack, Atlassian), many installs, and a verified badge.

        
Check the spelling and the source. Look-alike names are the classic trick. Install from the vendor's own page or repository, not a forum link.

        
Read the "will install" list. Skills-only plugins are low risk. Hooks, local servers and executables run code: give them the extra look.

        
Never paste a "prerequisite" command from an unknown guide into your terminal. That was the trick behind the biggest skills malware wave of 2026.

        
Fewer is safer and cheaper. Remove what you don't use.

      

      
Examples worth knowing from Anthropic's marketplace: Context7 (current library documentation), the official GitHub server, language-server plugins for code navigation, Code Review, and Anthropic's knowledge-work plugins for roles such as legal, finance and sales. Outside the marketplace, Graphify is a standout for big projects: it gives Claude a map of your code and documents (stop A6).

    


    

      
When to build your own six signals

      
Anthropic's Claude Code guide suggests building your setup over time, in response to what keeps happening. Tap a signal to see what to build.

Maps and indexes: Graphify

        
Once a project grows past what fits on Claude's desk, the slow part is finding things. Graphify is one of the best plugins for that: it turns a project into a map Claude can ask before it goes reading files. It's the folder method's index file, grown up and drawn as a graph. Here's how it works, a real map to explore, the commands worth knowing, and how to read the savings numbers honestly.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Why a map saves tokens, in a demo
  • What Graphify builds, and how
  • How to explore a map in 3D: clusters, god nodes, inferred links
  • The handful of commands you'll actually use
  • How to read the savings claims, and where it really pays off

      

    

    


    

      
Why a map saves tokens run both

      
The question: "Where is the code that handles logging in?" in a project with 40 files. Run it without a map, then with one.

      

    


    

      
What Graphify is

      

        

          
Graphify is a free, open-source tool (a paid Graphify Cloud also exists), released in spring 2026, that turns a folder of code and documents into a knowledge graph: every file, function, class and idea is a dot, and every "calls", "imports", "uses" or "mentions" is a line between dots. It installs as a /graphify skill for Claude Code and many other coding assistants. It appeared days after Andrej Karpathy shared his idea of an AI keeping an organized wiki of your sources, and is often described as building on it.

          
Code (about 40 languages) is read by a deterministic parser called tree-sitter, on your own computer: no AI, no credits, nothing sent anywhere. Documents, PDFs, images and recordings get an optional second pass with an AI model, so a design PDF or a whiteboard photo can join the map. It then groups the dots into clusters (the project's subsystems), and marks every link EXTRACTED (written in the code) or INFERRED (worked out by graphify).

          
It writes three things into a graphify-out folder: graph.html, the map you can click around; GRAPH_REPORT.md, a one-page summary of the key concepts, surprising connections and good questions to ask; and graph.json, the whole graph as data. Claude reads the report and queries the JSON instead of opening dozens of files, and a hook reminds it to ask the graph before it starts searching.

        

        

      

      
Installing it safely: the Python package is spelled graphifyy, with a double y. That's exactly the kind of detail look-alike packages exploit, so install from the project's own repository page, read what the hook does, and remember the graph goes stale until it's rebuilt (the commands below fix that). Privacy: code stays on your computer. Documents and images go to whichever AI the second pass uses, which is your assistant by default; you can switch it off or point it at a local model. Queries are logged in a file on your own computer, and you can turn that off too.

    


    

      
Explore a map drag, zoom, click

      
This is what a Graphify map looks like, built for Campus Planner, a made-up student app with a course catalog, a schedule builder and flashcards. Each colour is a cluster. Bigger dots have more connections; the biggest are god nodes, the parts most of the code flows through. Dashed lines are inferred. Diamonds came from documents and images. Try the questions underneath: they're the same kind Claude asks the graph. (Graphify's own graph.html is a flat, clickable 2D map; this demo adds depth so you can turn it around.)

      

      

        
Look for
God nodes
The few big dots. Change one and a lot can break, so they're where to be careful and where tests matter most.

        
Look for
Bridges between clusters
Lines that cross colours are how features depend on each other. "Surprising connections" in the report point you straight at the odd ones.

        
Look for
Dashed links
Inferred, not written in code. Usually right, sometimes not. If an answer rests on one, Claude should check that link in the actual files.

      

    


    

      
The commands you'll use

      
You type these in Claude Code, or you just ask Claude in plain words and it runs them. In Codex the slash becomes $graphify.

      

        
OnceInstalluv tool install graphifyygraphify install
The package, then registering the skill with your assistant. pipx or pip work too. Needs Python 3.10 or newer.

        
First runBuild the map/graphify .
Maps the current folder and writes the three outputs. Open graphify-out/graph.html in a browser to explore it.

        
Any timeAsk it something/graphify query "how does signing in work?"
Answers from the graph and names the files involved, so Claude reads two files instead of twenty.

        
DebuggingHow are two things connected?/graphify path "ExamCountdown" "db.session"
The shortest chain between them, with the confidence of its weakest link.

        
Learning a codebaseExplain one part/graphify explain "scheduleEngine"
What it is, what it uses and what uses it. Great on day one of a new project.

        
After changesKeep it freshgraphify update .graphify hook install
Update re-reads only what changed. The hook rebuilds on every commit, so you never think about it.

      

    


    

      
Reading the savings claims

      

        

          
Graphify's materials have claimed 71.5× fewer tokens per query than reading the raw files on one benchmark (reportedly 52 files: three of Karpathy's code projects, five papers and four images). The same table reportedly showed about 1× for a small 6-file project: "6 files fits in a context window anyway." The 71.5× figure is no longer in the GitHub README, which as of November 2026 advertises "80%" savings for the paid Graphify Cloud.

          
That 71.5× compares one graph lookup against reading every file, which Claude rarely does anyway. It's a best case for a single question, not a measure of your bill. The real win grows with size: the bigger and more tangled the project, the more searching a map saves, and the more it helps Claude find the right file instead of a plausible one.

          
An independent test by KubeBlogs (August 2026) built real features over three rounds, each with one session using Graphify and one without. The table shows what happened: the first round cost more with Graphify, later rounds slightly less, and quality was about the same (44/50 vs 45/50). Their conclusion: it "did not support a large session-level token cut," and how the work was organized mattered more than the tool. One small test, but the only independent one so far, and it fits the pattern: the map costs a little to build and pays back over many questions.

Tick each question for both claims. A careful claim answers all five; a marketing claim answers one or two.

Where it shines
Large projects
Hundreds of files, a codebase you're new to, or a big pile of mixed code and documents you keep asking about. Build the map once, keep it fresh with the hook, and watch your usage page for a week.

      

    


    

      
Quick check three questions

      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
Advanced: work smarter · Stop A7 · Putting it together · about 25 minutes

        
Power workflows

        
The habits that separate people who get a little out of AI from people who get a lot. Most aren't about prompts at all: they're about picking the right tool for the job, giving Claude a way to check its own work, and setting things up so good work repeats itself. Ranked by how much difference they make for most people.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • Which surface to use: chat, a hand-off task, the browser, or Claude Code
  • Interview, then brief, then a fresh chat
  • Verification loops: giving Claude a check to pass
  • Reusable tools: skills, templates, artifacts and scheduled briefings
  • What a 2026 Anthropic study found about learning with AI

      

    

    


    

      
Pick the right surface tap a job

      
Since September 2026, chat and Cowork are one Claude on paid plans: you can hand off a long task and it keeps running even after you close your laptop. Different jobs still suit different surfaces.

      

    


    

      
Interview, brief, fresh chat

      

        
1Interview
"Interview me, one question at a time, until you could write a one-page brief for this."

        →
        
2Brief
"Now write the brief: goal, constraints, what done looks like, and how we'll check it."

        →
        
3Fresh chat
Open a new chat, paste the brief, and do the work there, with a clean desk.

      

      
Anthropic recommends the same pattern for coding ("write it to SPEC.md, then start a fresh session"). It saves tokens and improves quality at once: the work starts from a written definition of done instead of a long, messy conversation.

    


    

      
Give Claude a check to pass

      

        

          
Anthropic's advice for agents: "Give Claude something it can run that comes back pass or fail. Once it has that, it can keep going on its own." For code, that's a test. For everything else, it's a checklist or rubric written into the request.

          
Its own guide to reducing made-up answers adds four moves that work in any chat: let Claude say "I don't know"; for long documents, have it pull direct quotes first; require a citation for each claim and have it withdraw anything it can't support; and restrict it to the documents you gave it.

        

        

          
A check for any task
Before you finish, check your work: every number against the source table, every quote word for word against the document, every date against the calendar. List anything you couldn't verify instead of guessing, and say "I don't know" where the documents don't say.

          
A fresh-eyes reviewer
(in a new chat) Here's a draft someone wrote and the brief it was written to. Critique it against the brief: what's missing, what's wrong, what's weakest. Be specific.

        

      

    


    

      
Make good work repeat itself open any

      

    


    

      
Learn, don't just delegate

      

        
In a January 2026 randomized study, Anthropic had developers learn a new coding library, with or without AI help, then tested them. The AI group scored 17 points lower on the follow-up quiz on average. But how they used it mattered: those who asked conceptual questions and explanations kept most of their learning, while those who simply handed over the work did worst. It's the school course's whole philosophy, in data: use AI to understand, and do the work yourself.
Source: Anthropic research, "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills" (January 29, 2026).

        

      

    


    

      
Quick check three questions

      

    


    

    

  







  

    

    

      

        
Advanced: work smarter · Stop A8 · Putting it together · about 30 minutes

        
Teams of agents

        
One Claude can do a lot. Several, working in parallel under a lead that hands out the work and checks the results, can do in an hour what one would take a day to finish. This stop shows how that works, lets you run a team yourself in a simulator, and tells the true story of how this course's video notes were made by a team of agents, including everything that went wrong.

      

      

      

        
At this stop you'll learn
  • The lead-and-workers pattern, and why it's so effective
  • How team size, model choice and checking trade off, in a simulator
  • A real case study: 32 videos summarized from their transcripts
  • A copy-paste template to run a team yourself
  • When one agent is better than many

      

    

    


    

      
The lead and the workers

      

        

          
Think of a good editor with a team of researchers. The lead agent plans the job, splits it into pieces that don't depend on each other, and writes each worker a clear brief. The workers (Claude calls them subagents) each take a piece, work in their own fresh context, and send back a short result. The lead checks, merges and decides what's next.

          
It works for three reasons. Pieces run at the same time, so a 30-video job takes the time of a few videos. Each worker starts with a clean desk holding only its piece, so nothing gets crowded out. And the lead's own desk stays clear for judgment, because it reads summaries, not every page.

          
You've already used one: Claude's Research mode is a lead agent sending out search workers. In Claude Code and the desktop app you can ask for subagents directly.

        

        
The honest cost
Teams use a lot more
Anthropic reports that a single agent uses about 4× the tokens of a chat, and its multi-agent research system about 15×. In return, a lead on Opus with Sonnet workers beat a single Opus agent by about 90% on its internal research tests. Workers' usage counts toward the same plan limits, so savings come from picking cheaper models for workers, not from running more of them. Use a team when the job is wide, valuable and splittable; use one chat when it isn't.
Sources: How we built our multi-agent research system, Building effective agents, Claude Code subagents.

      

    


    

      
The loop every agent runs scroll or play

      
Before teams, one agent. An agent is Claude doing a job in steps on its own: it plans, acts, looks at what happened, checks, and goes round again until the job is done. Knowing the loop shows you where to step in, because each stage is also where something can go wrong.

      
Try it: press Play the loop (or just scroll past it), then press What could go wrong? to see the risk at each stage.

      

      
The habit: ask any agent to show you its plan before it starts, and to check with you before it pays, sends, books or deletes anything. A team, below, is this same loop, with the lead checking each worker's result.

    


    

      
Run a team change the setup

      
The job: summarize 24 videos. Choose how many workers run at once, which model they use, and whether you add a pilot run and a checker. Watch time, usage and mistakes trade off.

      

    


    

      
Case study: how this course's video notes were made

      
Every summary on the video shelf was written by a team of agents from the video's real transcript. Here's what happened, mistakes included, because the mistakes are the useful part.

      

        
1
One brief for everyone
The lead wrote a single instruction sheet: how to open a video in the Claude app's browser, pull the transcript, save it, and write a summary in a strict format (one-line summary, key moments with timestamps, takeaways, a "two-minute version"). One rule above all: every timestamp must come from the transcript.

        
2
Find first, then summarize
A separate worker searched for new videos and confirmed each one actually exists and loads before anyone spent effort summarizing it. Then the videos were split by topic across three workers, later three more.

        
!
Workers grabbed the same browser tab
The first instruction opened videos in a way that handed every worker the same tab, so they briefly overwrote each other's page. Fix: each worker opens its own tab and closes it after.

        
!
Doubled lines, and a site redesign
On some videos the script captured every line twice, and YouTube had quietly changed its transcript panel on others. Fix: remove duplicates and look for both versions. One video had no captions at all; it's marked "notes coming" rather than guessed.

        
!
Too many at once hit the usage limit
Six workers on the most capable model ran through the plan's five-hour allowance mid-task, and everything stopped for twenty minutes. Fix: fewer workers at a time, cheaper models for the mechanical parts, and the strongest model only where judgment matters.

        
✓
The result
31 of the shelf's 32 videos got careful notes with key moments, each pointing to a real moment in the video; the one with no captions is labelled rather than guessed. The team then moved to separate "worker" chats on the owner's computer that pick up jobs from a shared folder, so work keeps going without one conversation holding everything.

      

    


    

      
Run one yourself

      

        
Paste this into Claude Code, Research or the desktop app, and fill in the brackets. It bakes in the fixes from the case study.

        
You're the lead on this job: [the goal, e.g. "compare 20 apartment listings I'll paste"].
1. Plan: split it into independent pieces. Show me the plan before starting.
2. Brief: write one instruction sheet every worker follows, with a strict output format and the rule "never guess; mark anything you couldn't verify."
3. Pilot: run ONE piece yourself first, show me the result, and fix the brief.
4. Fan out: use subagents for the rest, at most [3] at a time, on the cheapest model that does the job well.
5. Check: review every result against the brief (spot-check the facts), and redo any that fail.
6. Merge: give me one combined result, plus a short list of anything uncertain.

        
      

    


    

      
Where a team pays off

      

        
A semester of lectures
One worker per recorded lecture: notes, key moments, likely exam topics. The lead merges them into one study guide.

        
A big purchase
Workers read reviews, specs and complaint threads for each option; the lead builds the comparison table and flags disagreements.

        
Job or apartment hunting
Each worker checks a batch of postings against your must-haves; the lead ranks the shortlist and drafts your questions.

      

    


    

      
When one is better than many

      

        
Anthropic's own guidance is to start with the simplest thing that works and add agents only when they clearly help. Teams shine when the work is wide: many similar pieces that don't depend on each other. They struggle when the work is deep and connected, like writing one essay or fixing one tricky bug, where every part depends on the last. Splitting those creates pieces that don't fit together. They also aren't worth the extra usage for small jobs. Rule of thumb: if you'd hand it to one careful person, use one agent; if you'd hand it to a team with a coordinator, use a team.

    Your own AI assistant · Stop B1 · Understand it · about 30 minutes
    
        
    Assistants, agents and workflows
    
        
    By the end of this stop you'll be able to look at any AI product and say what it can actually do for you: just answer, act when you ask, follow a fixed recipe, or figure out the steps on its own. You'll also know what the big 2026 assistants offer and cost, what "MCP" means, and when it's worth building your own.
    
      
    
      
    
      
    At this stop you'll learn
    • The spectrum from chatbot to agent, and who decides the steps at each level
    • The four building blocks: tools, memory, computer use and MCP
    • What ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Siri, Alexa+ and others offer (checked Nov 2026)
    • When to buy an assistant and when to build one
    • How much access to give, and the safety layer that goes with each step up
    
    
    
    
    

    
    
      
    One job, six kinds of AI slide through it
    
      
    These words get used loosely, so here is one everyday job handled at every level. Watch two things change as you move right: who decides the steps, and what can go wrong.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    
          
    The short version. A chatbot answers. An assistant is a chatbot with tools, memory and your personal context, so it can act when you ask. A workflow runs the model along steps someone fixed in advance. An agent chooses its own steps and tools, in a loop, until the goal is met.
    
          
    Anthropic calls both workflows and agents "agentic systems". The difference is who holds the map: in a workflow the path is written in code, in an agent the model directs its own process. OpenAI describes an agent the same way: a model plus tools plus instructions, running in a loop.
    
        
    
        
    Our reading: in 2026 these are modes, not products. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are all assistants with agent modes built in. So the useful question isn't "is this an agent?" but "in this mode, who decides the next step, and what is it allowed to touch?" Rule of thumb from the research: if you can draw the flowchart, use a workflow. Save the agent for the "figure it out" box.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: Anthropic, Building effective agents, OpenAI, A practical guide to building agents, IBM, What are AI agents?, TechCrunch on Alexa+, SiliconANGLE on ChatGPT Dots.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    The four building blocks open a tile
    
      
    Every assistant and agent is a language model plus some of these. Knowing which ones a product has tells you what it can do, and what it could do wrong.
    
      
    
    
    

    
    
      
    MCP in five minutes flip the switch
    
      
    You'll see "MCP" on connector pages and in every build guide in this course. It's the plug standard that lets one AI app talk to many services.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    
          
    How it fits together. The app you use (Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor) is the host. For each service it connects to, it runs a client that talks to that service's MCP server. A server offers tools (actions), resources (things to read) and prompts, and the app can ask it at any time what it offers. Many servers simply wrap an existing API, like GitHub's, so MCP sits on top of APIs rather than replacing them.
    
          
    Where it stands now. Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation's new Agentic AI Foundation on December 9, 2025, co-founded with Block and OpenAI; at that point there were over 10,000 public servers. The current spec, dated 2026-07-28, is stateless: no sessions and no start-up handshake, every request carries what it needs, and "Streamable HTTP" replaced the older SSE transport.
    
        
    
        
    
          
    What it means for you: when Claude offers a "connector" or a voice platform says "add an MCP server", this is what's happening. One connection gives the AI a whole menu of actions, which is powerful and is exactly why you should read that menu before you plug it in.
    
          
    Update box (Nov 2026): every MCP video in our library was made before the donation or before the 2026-07-28 spec. Anything they say about sessions, SSE or "initialize" is out of date; the ideas still hold.
    
          
    The catch: MCP's co-creator points out that a tool's description is itself text the model reads, so a hostile server can hide instructions there, and a public registry carries supply-chain risk. Install servers only from the vendor or an official directory.
    
        
    
      
    
      
    Sources: MCP introduction, Anthropic on donating MCP, 2026-07-28 changelog, IBM: MCP vs API (0:35), pixegami: the N×M problem (1:18), Why we built and donated MCP: security (20:34).

We checked every price on November 6, 2026; each card shows the date and kind of source the price comes from, because some makers don't publish prices on their own page. Pick what you already use to see the natural fit.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: Claude pricing, Claude Dispatch, ChatGPT pricing, GeoToolbox ChatGPT prices, TNW on ChatGPT Work, Gemini plans, TechCabal on I/O 2026, GeoToolbox Copilot prices, MacRumors on Siri, Beebom on the Siri app, TechCrunch on Alexa+, Notebookcheck on Meta AI, CloudZero on Perplexity, CloudZero on Grok, Home Assistant voice, OpenClaw known vulnerabilities.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Buy one, or build your own? decide
    
      
    
        
    Buy when it already exists
    For most personal use, a $20-a-month assistant already has the apps, voice and agent mode you need. Follow your ecosystem: Google Workspace points to Gemini, Microsoft 365 to Copilot, an Amazon home to Alexa+, an iPhone to Siri plus a chatbot app. Try the built-in agents first (ChatGPT Work or Dots, Claude Cowork and scheduled tasks, Gemini Spark, Perplexity Computer), then a no-code tool such as n8n or Zapier.
    
        
    Build when you need your own channel or rules
    Build when you want a phone number you can call, tools that touch your own files or accounts, strict privacy, or your own limits on cost, speed and safety. Building means pay-as-you-go API prices instead of a flat plan, and you own the maintenance: OpenAI's Agent Builder, for example, is shutting down on November 30, 2026, after roughly 14 months.
    
      
    
      
    Why this course exists: as of November 2026, no off-the-shelf product lets you dial a phone number and reach your assistant with your tools. Claude's Dispatch takes texts, not calls, and ChatGPT's GPT-Live voice is now also available through OpenAI's API (GPT-Live 1, $0.05/min). That gap is what stops B3 to B10 fill.
    
      
    Sources: Building effective agents, Claude Dispatch, Introducing GPT-Live, MCP Directory on the Agent Builder shutdown.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    How much should it be allowed to do? benefits, costs, safety
    
      
    The more an assistant can touch, the more it can do for you, and the more a mistake costs. Here is the top of the ladder first, then the honest downsides, then the layers that make it safe.
    
      
    
        
    The full-access version
    An agent that works while you don't
    • Hours of work across apps: ChatGPT Work can use a browser and your computer (with approval) and run scheduled tasks; Claude Dispatch takes a text from your phone and works on your desktop, files and connected apps.
    • Always on: ChatGPT Dots each get their own cloud computer and thousands of app connections, and can reach your laptop if you allow it.
    • Untested promise: Google's Gemini Spark demo shows a 24/7 agent that keeps going while your phone is locked, turns a voice brain-dump into tasks and asks before sending. That's a marketing demo; availability after the May 2026 beta isn't confirmed.
    
        
    The honest downsides
    More steps, more ways to go wrong
    • It costs more: Anthropic measured a single agent at about 4× the tokens of a chat, and its multi-agent system at about 15×.
    • Errors compound: one study of seven multi-agent systems found failure rates between 41% and 86.7% across tasks.
    • It can claim it did something it didn't, or obey instructions hidden in a web page, email or tool description.
    • Some tools are unsafe by default: OpenClaw, a popular open-source agent, has more than 700 published security advisories (count from a community tracker).
    
        
    Safety layers, scaled to the risk
    Add one per step up the ladder
    1. Read-only first. Connect calendar and email with read access before anything can send.
    2. Approve anything you can't undo. OpenAI's guide rates each tool by how reversible it is and how much money is involved; payments, cancellations and sends get a human yes. Every major assistant ships an approval step; switch it on for those tools.
    3. Separate the blast radius. A spare email address, a virtual card with a monthly cap, one folder per job.
    4. Official sources only for connectors, skills and MCP servers.
    5. Check the log. Look at what it actually did, not what it said it did.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: TNW on ChatGPT Work, Claude Dispatch, SiliconANGLE on Dots, Google: Gemini Spark (0:07), Anthropic multi-agent research system, MAST study, OpenAI agents guide, OpenClaw vulnerability tracker.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Name that kind sort each one
    
      
    Six real setups. Is it a fixed recipe, an assistant acting when asked, or an agent choosing its own steps?

    Your own AI assistant · Stop B2 · Understand it · about 30 minutes
    
        
    What a personal assistant can do
    
        
    A good assistant can screen your calls, wait on hold for you, keep your lists, phone you with reminders and quiz you on the bus. Some jobs it does reliably today, some need you watching, and a few are still experiments that mostly lose money. This stop sorts eighteen real uses by the evidence, so you know which to hand over first.
    
      
    
      
    
      
    At this stop you'll learn
    • Which everyday, business and ambitious uses work today, with the evidence for each
    • A four-question test to rate any job before you hand it to an AI
    • What happened when AIs ran a shop, traded stocks and booked appointments
    • The rules when your assistant talks to other people (AI-voice rules, recording consent)
    • Which safety setting to use at each level of stakes
    
    
    
    
    

    
    
      
    How well does it actually work? pick a use
    
      
    Each use gets one of four ratings, from the strongest evidence we found. Vendor claims are labelled as vendor claims.
    
      
    
      
    An honest caveat: nobody has published an independent benchmark of how often personal-assistant actions succeed, or of AI receptionists' accuracy. These ratings combine platform documentation, published failures and the pattern below: one action you can see and undo is safe; chains of steps, other people and money are not.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Rate any job in four questions try one
    
      
    The pattern behind every rating above fits in four questions. Answer them for a job you have in mind, and you get a rating and the safety setting to match.
    
      
    
    
    

    
    
      
    The best places to start
    
      
    The jobs with the strongest evidence are also the ones that save the most small moments in a week. Turn these on first.
    
      
    
        
    Screen calls and skip hold music
    On a Pixel, turn on Call Screen and Hold for Me (Phone app → Settings). On an iPhone with iOS 26 or later, turn on Call Screening, and use Hold Assist when a queue starts. Google's have shipped on Pixels since the Pixel 3; Apple's arrived with iOS 26 in 2025. Both run on the phone itself.
    
        
    One-step jobs by voice
    "Add eggs to the list", "log $12 for lunch", "what's on Saturday?" One action, a result you can see, and easy to undo. Ask it to read the item back, and glance at the list the first few times.
    
        
    Reminder calls and quizzing
    A phone call at 6:30 a.m. ("bus in 40 minutes, math quiz today") or a ten-minute quiz from tonight's notes. Scheduled calls are a documented feature of voice platforms; a quiz uses no tools at all, so there's nothing to fail.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: Google Hold for Me, Google Call Screen, TechCrunch on iOS 26 Hold Assist, Vapi outbound and scheduled calls, Zapier MCP.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    When AIs ran the shop and the portfolio true stories
    
      
    The ambitious uses get the headlines. Here's what happened when they were tried with real money, in order. The mistakes are the useful part.
    
      
    
        
    1
    An AI shopkeeper in an office (Project Vend)
    Anthropic let Claude agents run a small office shop, with a "CEO" agent overseeing the shopkeeper. Money-losing weeks mostly stopped, but the agents nearly signed an illegal onion-futures contract, offered a wage below California's minimum, and were talked into deals by staff. Against a quarterly target of $15,000 they reached $2,649.20, about 18%. A human still approved the purchases.
    
        
    2
    A real store with an AI manager (Andon Market)
    A San Francisco store opened in April 2026 with an AI manager named Luna. It lost about $13,000 early on, ordered 1,000 toilet-seat covers, and closed for three days because of its own scheduling error. Humans still stock the shelves and open the doors, and the rent is covered for three years.
    
        
    3
    AI traders with real money (Alpha Arena)
    In a series of live trading contests on US stocks (as reported by ThinkAdvisor), eight models' combined portfolio lost about a third of its value, and only 6 of 32 results made a profit. The organiser's conclusion: language models can't make money by themselves without a sophisticated system around them. A separate benchmark found most trading agents struggle to beat simply buying and holding.
    
        
    ✓
    What does work: the AI drafts, you decide
    Interactive Brokers' approach is the safe pattern: the AI researches and drafts an order, and a human enters it. Robinhood's agent accounts require approval for some trades and put a limit on the agent's card. Practise with paper trading (Alpaca's official tools default to it) before any real money.
    
      
    
      
    How big a job can an agent take on? The research group METR measures the longest task (in human working time) an AI finishes half the time. METR measured its top 2026 model at about 11 hours at a 50% success rate (METR says these figures aren't precise and stopped updating them in Sep 2026), and secondary summaries put the 80% figure at only about 1 to 3 hours. That gap is why long jobs still need checkpoints and a human review. (The 11-hour figure is from METR's own report; the 80% figure comes from a secondary summary.)
    
      
    Sources: Anthropic, Project Vend phase two, Axios on Andon Market, The Star on Andon Market, ThinkAdvisor on Alpha Arena, StockBench, Interactive Brokers, TNW on Robinhood agents, Alpaca MCP server, METR (Wikipedia summary). Nothing here is financial advice.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    When your assistant talks to other people the rules
    
      
    Calling yourself is simple. The moment your assistant calls or records someone else, a few rules apply. This is a plain summary, not legal advice.
    
      
    
        
    Say it's an AI
    Open every call to someone else with "this is an AI assistant calling for…". Google's own calling feature announces itself this way. A 2024 WIRED test found some business voice bots claiming to be human, which is exactly the trust problem to avoid.
    
        
    AI voices count as robocalls
    In February 2024 the FCC ruled that AI-generated voices are "artificial" under the federal robocall law (TCPA). Calls to consumers need their prior consent (written consent for marketing), must say who is responsible for the call, and must offer a way to opt out. It isn't a ban, and calling yourself carries minimal risk.
    
        
    Recording needs consent
    Federal law and most states are one-party, but some states require everyone on a call to agree to recording. One 2024 law-firm survey lists thirteen (CA, CT, DE, FL, IL, MD, MA, MT, NV, NH, OR, PA and WA); other lists differ, because some states depend on the situation. Across state lines the rule varies, so the cautious habit is to follow the stricter state. Michigan is generally treated as one-party, which a 2026 federal ruling reaffirmed, but its supreme court hasn't decided it. Check your own state, and announce recording anyway.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: TechCrunch on Google's AI calling, WIRED on bots claiming to be human, Wiley on the FCC ruling, Orrick: not a ban, Kilpatrick on wiretap laws, Mondaq on the Michigan ruling (from the winning firm).

    Your own AI assistant · Stop B3 · Understand it · about 35 minutes
    
        
    How a phone assistant works
    
        
    You dial an ordinary phone number from any phone, say "add milk to the list", and a moment later it's on the list on your own computer. This stop follows one call through every link in that chain, shows what each link costs, and ends by picking which of five build paths fits you.
    
      
    
      
    
      
    At this stop you'll learn
    • The four links: a phone number, a voice platform, tools, and your computer
    • What happens, step by step, during one real call, and where it can break
    • The two kinds of voice "brain", and why Claude always uses one of them
    • How to let a call reach your home computer without opening it to the internet
    • Which of the five build paths (A to E) to choose
    
    
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Follow one call play it
    
      
    Press play, or step through. Then try the two other versions: what happens when your computer is asleep, and when a stranger rings your assistant's number.
    
      
    
      
    Status: this order of events is assembled from the platforms' documentation and our tested tool server (72 automated tests, run with simulated calls). No real end-to-end phone call has been tested yet. Sources: Vapi phone quickstart, Vapi custom tools, LiveKit turn detection, Vapi call timeouts, ElevenAgents caller personalization, Vapi caller check.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    The four links, with prices open a link
    
      
    Every callable assistant, from a no-code one to a fully home-made one, has these four parts. Prices are US list prices checked on November 6, 2026.
    
      
    
      
    What it costs, all in: for light use (about 30 minutes of calls a month), our research estimates roughly $2.50 to $10 a month depending on the path; path A, and path D on LiveKit’s free plan, are at the low end. The phone number is the cheap part, usually $0.50 to $1.15 a month; the speech and model minutes are most of the bill. On Vapi, the free number and $5 starting credit cover your first 40 to 60 minutes.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Two kinds of voice brain
    
      
    
        
    Hear, think, speak
    Three models in a row
    Speech-to-text writes down what you said, a language model decides what to do, and text-to-speech reads the answer aloud. You can use almost any model, and swap each piece separately. Claude always works this way on the phone, because it has no audio API. For voice, use Claude Haiku 5.5 for speed ($0.10 in / $0.50 out per million tokens) or Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10) when it must reason harder.
    
        
    Speech to speech
    One model that listens and talks
    A single "realtime" model hears audio and answers in audio, which makes interruptions and tone feel more natural. Options: OpenAI's gpt-realtime-2.1 (audio $32 in / $64 out per million tokens; the mini version $10 / $20; no official per-minute price), OpenAI's GPT-Live 1 ($0.05 a minute plus the model behind it), and Google's Gemini 3.1 Flash Live in preview (about $0.023 a minute). Claude can still be plugged in as a tool behind one of these.
    
      
    
      
    Update box: older videos use gpt-4o-realtime-preview, which shut down on May 7, 2026. gpt-realtime and its mini version retire on January 20, 2027. Use gpt-realtime-2.1. Pipecat and LiveKit still default to older Claude model names, so set the model explicitly.
    
      
    Sources: Claude models, Claude on Vapi, OpenAI pricing, OpenAI deprecations, GPT-Live 1, Gemini API pricing, Speechmatics: listen, think, speak (0:21).
    
    
    

    
    
      
    What a tool call looks like for the curious and the coders
    
      
    When the AI decides to act, the platform sends your computer a small message and waits for a one-line answer. This is Vapi's format; the other platforms are similar.
    
      
    
        
    1 · The platform sends (HTTP POST to your tunnel, /vapi/tool-calls)
    {
  "message": {
    "type": "tool-calls",
    "toolCallList": [{
      "id": "call_abc123",
      "function": {
        "name": "add_grocery_item",
        "arguments": { "item": "milk" }
      }
    }]
  }
}
    
        
    2 · Your tool server answers (always HTTP 200)
    {
  "results": [{
    "name": "add_grocery_item",
    "toolCallId": "call_abc123",
    "result": "Added milk to the grocery list."
  }]
}
    
      
    
      
    
        
    Three gotchas
    arguments can arrive as an object or as a JSON string, so accept both. Answer with status 200 even when something failed, putting the problem in an "error" field. Keep the result to one line of plain text.
    
        
    Time limits
    Vapi waits 20 seconds by default (a forum post says 120 is the maximum; unconfirmed). ElevenAgents also defaults to 20 seconds (5 to 300). Retell defaults to 120 and allows up to 600. Aim to answer in under about 5 seconds, because the caller is waiting in silence.
    
        
    Testing
    Vapi's dashboard Test button doesn't send the real message, so test with a real call. Accounts created on or after September 23, 2026 must save the server address and secret on the tool itself, or the log shows "credentials withheld".
    
      
    
      
    Can it use MCP instead? Yes on Vapi, ElevenAgents, Retell and Telnyx, which can each load the tools of a remote MCP server. Bland shows no sign of it. But the official filesystem MCP server only runs locally, so a cloud voice platform can't reach it, and a generic "read and write any file" server gives a phone caller far more power than "add an item to the grocery list". For a phone assistant, a few small named actions are the safer design.
    
      
    Sources: Vapi custom tools, Vapi server authentication, Vapi tool settings, ElevenAgents webhook tools, Retell custom functions, Vapi MCP, ElevenAgents MCP, Bland MCP, Kris Torrington: the results format fix (5:10).
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Reaching your home computer, safely benefits, risks, layers
    
      
    This is the link that turns a talking chatbot into an assistant that does real things. It's also the one that, done carelessly, opens your computer to strangers.
    
      
    
        
    At full power
    Your computer, on call
    With a link to your computer, a phone call can do anything you allow: add to lists and notes, send email to people you choose, read a file aloud, start a backup, turn on lights. The most powerful version is a remote MCP server with broad read and write access, so the AI can work across your files like you do. A tunnel means no router settings and no open ports: your computer dials out, so no ports are opened on your router.
    
        
    The honest risks
    A phone number is a public door
    Anyone can call a number, and caller ID can be faked. The tunnel address is public too. A broad file or command tool means a successful trick, from a caller or from text the AI reads, can reach everything that tool can. OpenClaw showed the cost: over 135,000 copies were found exposed online after it listened on all network addresses by default. And when your computer sleeps, the call still connects but every tool fails.
    
      
    
      
    The safety layers, in the order to add them
    
      
    
      
    Which tunnel?
    
      
    
      
    Sources: ngrok overview, ngrok free plan, Cloudflare quick tunnels, Cloudflare named tunnels, Tailscale Funnel, Twilio webhook security, The Register on exposed OpenClaw, OWASP file handling, What a tunnel is (0:23). The phone-specific advice (PIN, caller check, never reading secrets aloud) is our own design guidance: no source or video we found covers phone attacks.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Where the waiting comes from
    
      
    
        
    Deciding you've finished
    The platform waits for a pause before it answers. Too short and it interrupts you; too long and every reply feels slow. LiveKit's defaults wait between half a second and three seconds.
    
        
    Thinking and speaking
    The model's first words and the voice's first sound take time. Instructions over about 2,000 tokens slow every turn; bigger models and premium voices add more. That's why Haiku is the usual pick for live calls.
    
        
    The trip to your computer
    Each tool call crosses the internet and back. Keep tools fast, cover the gap with a neutral "one moment", and let quick saves run in the background while lookups wait for their answer.
    
      
    
      
    No fake numbers here: we found no measured end-to-end delay for any platform, and no published speed figures for Claude on calls. Build it, call it, and judge by ear. If replies feel slow, shorten the instructions first.
    
      
    Sources: LiveKit turn tuning, ElevenLabs prompting guide, Vapi prompting guide, Pipecat with Claude.

    Your own AI assistant · Stop B4 · Build it · about 40 minutes to read, 1–2 hours to build
    
        
    Build your first phone assistant
    
        
    By the end of this stop you'll have a real phone number you can call, a voice that understands you, and a small program on your own computer that does what you ask: adds groceries to a list, saves notes and emails people you've approved. It costs nothing to start, needs no credit card for the number, and every safety rule lives in code, not in a hopeful prompt.
    
      
    
      
    
      
    At this stop you'll learn
    • How the five parts connect: phone, voice platform, tunnel, tool server, your files
    • How to run and test the tool server on Mac or Windows, with checkpoints
    • How to open a safe, stable tunnel to your computer with ngrok
    • How to create the Vapi assistant, number and tools, click by click
    • Which safety layers are already built in, which you add, and what's still missing
    • How to keep it running after a restart, and what it costs
    
    
    
    
    

    
    
      
    What you're building tap a part
    
      
    A call travels through five parts. You'll build them left to right, and each one has its own checkpoint, so you always know which part works.
    
      
    
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
      
    
      
    
        
    
          
    Why this path first. Vapi gives you a free US phone number with no payment method, and $5 of free credit, so your first calls cost nothing. Its dashboard is documented click by click. The only code is a small Python server that was built and tested for this course (72 automated tests pass, and we re-ran them for this page). When you're done, the same server also works with the other build paths on the next stop.
    
          
    What "callable" really means here. When you speak, Vapi turns your words into text, an AI model decides what to do, and if it needs your computer, Vapi sends a small web request through the tunnel to your tool server. The server does the job and answers with one short sentence, which the assistant says back to you.
    
        
    
        
    Honest status, checked Nov 2026
    What's tested and what isn't
    • Tested: the tool server and its safety rules (72 tests, plus a live run with real web requests on the server's own computer, Python 3.13).
    • Not yet tested: a real Vapi phone call, a real ngrok tunnel and a real Gmail send. Nobody has run the Mac or Windows commands below yet; they're written from the official docs.
    • Every step has a checkpoint, so if something differs on your screen you'll know exactly where.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: Vapi phone quickstart, Vapi custom tools, Vapi pricing; this course's tested code and test log.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Before you start gather these
    
      
    
        
    A Mac or Windows computer
    It must stay on while you want the assistant to reach it. You'll install Python 3.11 or newer (3.13 recommended) and ngrok. About 15 minutes.
    
        
    Two free accounts
    Vapi (voice platform and number) and ngrok (tunnel). Neither asks for a card to start. Gmail with 2-Step Verification is only needed for the email step.
    
        
    One to two hours
    Most of the time goes into account setup, not code. You can stop after any checkpoint; your ticks are saved in this browser.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    Your details optional, fills in the commands below
    Saved only in this browser. This page never asks for your secret or passwords; you paste those yourself, on your own computer.
    
        
    
          
          
          
        
    
      
    
    
    

    
    
      
    The build, step by step tick each checkpoint
