    0 of 9 checkpoints
    
        
    

        
      
          
          
    1. 
            
            
      
              
      Python runs the tool server. ngrok gives your computer a stable web address so Vapi can reach it. Use the official install commands below; some older guides point to packages that are years out of date.
      
              
      Terminal (Mac)
      # Needs Homebrew (brew.sh). Then:
brew install python@3.13 ngrok
python3.13 --version
which ngrok
      
              
      PowerShell (Windows)
      # The Python install manager (what python.org now recommends), then Python 3.13
winget install 9NQ7512CXL7T -e --accept-package-agreements --disable-interactivity
# ngrok from the Microsoft Store source (the official command)
winget install ngrok -s msstore
      
              
      Close PowerShell, then in a NEW PowerShell window
      py install 3.13
py -V:3.13 --version
ngrok help
      
              
      What you should see
      Python 3.13.x (anything 3.11 or newer works), and a path ending in /ngrokngrok's list of commands.
      
              
      Gotchas
        
                
      • Python 3.10 won't work. One of the pinned packages needs 3.11 or newer, so the install step fails on 3.10.
        • 
                
      • Don't use winget install Ngrok.Ngrok. That community package is stuck on an old version (3.3.1). Use the -s msstore command above.
        • 
                
      • If you prefer the classic installer, winget install -e --id Python.Python.3.13 also works; it adds Python to your PATH. That installer is deprecated since 3.14 and won't be made for 3.16 or later.
        • 
                
      • Don't touch Apple's built-in /usr/bin/python3; always use python3.13 from Homebrew (or the python.org installer).
        • 
              
      
              
      Sources: Using Python on Windows, Using Python on macOS, ngrok for Windows, ngrok for macOS.
      
              
            
      
          
      2. 

          
          
    2. 
            
            
      
              
      Four files run the assistant, and two more run its tests. Easiest: download the B4 code as one zip (the same tested files plus a README), unzip it, and rename the callable-assistant folder to assistant in your home folder. Or make a folder and copy each file below, saving it under the exact name shown.
      
              
      Download the B4 code (.zip)View files: README.md · assistant_actions.py · tool_server.py · .env.example · tests/test_tool_server.py
      
              
      Terminal (Mac)
      mkdir -p ~/assistant/tests
cd ~/assistant
      
              
      PowerShell (Windows)
      mkdir $HOME\assistant\tests
cd $HOME\assistant
      
              
      
              
      What you should see
      ls -a ~/assistantdir -Force $HOME\assistant lists .env.example, assistant_actions.py, requirements.txt, tool_server.py and a tests folder holding conftest.py and test_tool_server.py.
      
              
      Why read it, even briefly
        
                
      • assistant_actions.py is the only list of things your assistant can do. If an action isn't in its ACTIONS table, it doesn't exist, whatever anyone says on the phone.
        • 
                
      • tool_server.py checks the secret on every request and never shows its own documentation pages to the internet.
        • 
              
      
              
            
      
          
      3. 

          
          
    3. 
            
            
      
              
      3a. Install and run the tests. A virtual environment keeps this project's packages separate from everything else.
      
              
      Terminal (Mac)
      cd ~/assistant
python3.13 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip install pytest==9.2.0 httpx2==2.16.0
python -m pytest -q
      
              
      PowerShell (Windows)
      cd $HOME\assistant
py -V:3.13 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip install pytest==9.2.0 httpx2==2.16.0
python -m pytest -q
      
              
      What you should see
      A row of dots, then 72 passed. Those tests try bad secrets, path tricks, strangers' email addresses and oversized requests, and check that every one is refused.
      
              
      3b. Make your settings file and secret. The secret is a long random password that only Vapi and your server will know.
      
              
      Terminal (Mac)
      cp .env.example .env
python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"
open -e .env
      
              
      PowerShell (Windows)
      Copy-Item .env.example .env
python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"
notepad .env
      
              
      In .env, change three lines and save. Leave the Gmail lines for step 8.
      
              
      .env: the lines to change
      ASSISTANT_FOLDER=~/AssistantInbox
TOOL_SECRET=paste-the-random-string-you-just-made
EMAIL_CONTACTS=me=you@example.com
      
              
      3c. Start the server. Leave this window open; it's your server's log.
      
              
      Same window
      uvicorn tool_server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
      
              
      What you should see
      INFO ... Tool server ready. Folder: /Users/youC:\Users\you/\AssistantInbox. Email contacts: me
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit)
      
              
      3d. Talk to it yourself, from a second window. These are the same requests Vapi will send later.
      
              
      Second Terminal window (Mac)
      cd ~/assistant
export TOOL_SECRET=$(grep '^TOOL_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/add_grocery_item -H "X-Vapi-Secret: $TOOL_SECRET" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"item":"milk","quantity":"2 gallons"}'; echo
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/read_grocery_list -H "X-Vapi-Secret: $TOOL_SECRET" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}'; echo
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/add_grocery_item -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"item":"milk"}'
cat ~/AssistantInbox/groceries.md
      
              
      Second PowerShell window (Windows)
      cd $HOME\assistant
$secret = ((Get-Content .env | Select-String '^TOOL_SECRET=').Line -split '=',2)[1]
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/add_grocery_item -Headers @{"X-Vapi-Secret"=$secret} -ContentType "application/json" -Body '{"item":"milk","quantity":"2 gallons"}'
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/read_grocery_list -Headers @{"X-Vapi-Secret"=$secret} -ContentType "application/json" -Body '{}'
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/add_grocery_item -ContentType "application/json" -Body '{"item":"milk"}'
Get-Content $HOME\AssistantInbox\groceries.md
      
              
      What you should see
      {"result":"Added milk (2 gallons) to the grocery list."}
{"result":"1 item: milk (2 gallons)."}
401(an error saying 401 Unauthorized)
- [ ] milk (2 gallons)  _(added 2026-11-06 10:55)_
      The third request had no secret, so it was refused. That's the lock working. PowerShell shows results as a small table with a result column; the text is the same.
      
              
      Gotchas
        
                
      • "Running scripts is disabled" when activating: run Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser once, then activate again.
        • 
                
      • Windows paths in .env: never put them in double quotes. "C:\new\folder" turns \n into a line break. Write ~/AssistantInbox, an unquoted path, or forward slashes.
        • 
                
      • Server refuses to start: TOOL_SECRET must be 16 characters or more and can't still be the placeholder (anything containing "replace", "change" or "example" is refused), and ASSISTANT_FOLDER can't be your whole home folder or a drive. Both are deliberate.
        • 
                
      • Always --host 127.0.0.1. Several popular videos use 0.0.0.0, which opens the server to every device on your network. The tunnel reaches it fine on 127.0.0.1.
        • 
                
      • Keep .env private. It holds your secret (and later your App Password). Never paste it into a chat, email or screenshot. If you ever put this folder in git or on GitHub, first create a .gitignore file listing .env and .venv/, so they are never uploaded.
        • 
                
      • Keeping the folder outside Desktop, Documents and iCloud avoids macOS privacy prompts later (likely, not confirmed).
        • 
              
      
              
      Sources: this course's test log, Python venv docs.
      
              
            
      
          
      4. 

          
          
    4. 
            
            
      
              
      Your computer dials out to ngrok, and ngrok forwards requests back in. You don't open anything on your router, and a changing home internet address doesn't matter. ngrok's free plan includes one development domain that stays the same every time you restart, which is why it beats a throwaway tunnel for daily use.
      
              
        
                
      1. Sign up at ngrok.com (free) and copy your authtoken from the dashboard.
        2. 
                
      2. Find your free development domain in the dashboard (it looks like some-words-1234.ngrok-free.app) and type it into Your details above.
        3. 
                
      3. With the server from step 3 still running, open a third window:
        4. 
              
      
              
      Third window
      ngrok config add-authtoken "PASTE-YOUR-AUTHTOKEN"
ngrok http 8000 --url https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app
      
              
      Now test from the outside, through the tunnel, in the second window:
      
              
      Second window (Mac)
      curl -s https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app/health; echo
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app/tools/read_grocery_list -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}'
      
              
      Second window (Windows)
      Invoke-RestMethod https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app/health
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app/tools/read_grocery_list -ContentType "application/json" -Body '{}'
      
              
      What you should see
      {"status":"ok"}
401status
------
ok
(then an error saying 401 Unauthorized)
      Your server is now reachable from anywhere, and it still refuses anyone without the secret.
      
              
      Gotchas
        
                
      • ngrok's warning page only appears for web browsers. It doesn't affect Vapi or other programs.
        • 
                
      • Want a free test without an account? cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8000 works, but its address changes every time it restarts, and Cloudflare says it's for testing only. You'd have to re-paste the address into every Vapi tool each time.
        • 
                
      • Ignore old --basic-auth or --oauth flags. They're deprecated; ngrok now uses Traffic Policy. Your secret header already does the job.
        • 
                
      • Never forward a port on your router instead. It exposes your home address, and voice platforms don't come from fixed addresses you could restrict.
        • 
                
      • Debugging tip: while ngrok runs, its local inspector at http://localhost:4040 shows each request that came in (shown in an older ngrok video; the page may look different now).
        • 
              
      
              
      Sources: ngrok free plan limits, ngrok CLI reference, Cloudflare quick tunnels.
      
              
            
      
          
      5. 

          
          
    5. 
            
            
      
              
      Sign up at vapi.ai. New accounts get $5 of free credit and one free US number.
      
              
        
                
      1. Assistants → the down arrow next to Create Assistant → pick any template (you'll replace its words).
        2. 
                
      2. Set the First Message to something like "Hi, it's your assistant. What do you need?"
        3. 
                
      3. Replace the System Prompt with the one below, putting your name in.
        4. 
                
      4. Publish → Next → Publish. Until you publish, your changes stay a draft and calls use the old version.
        5. 
                
      5. Press Talk to test it in your browser. It can chat, but it can't do anything yet.
        6. 
              
      
              
      System prompt (our draft; not yet tried on a live call)
      You are [your name]'s personal phone assistant. Only [your name] should be calling.
Keep every reply to one or two short sentences, because they are spoken aloud.

Tools:
- add_grocery_item: call it once for each item the caller names, then say what was added.
- read_grocery_list: always call it before saying what's on the list. If there are many items, read the first five and ask whether they want the rest.
- save_note: save short notes the caller dictates.
- clear_grocery_list and send_email: first call WITHOUT confirm. Read the summary back and ask "Should I go ahead?"; for send_email, read the whole email back word for word, as the tool's reply says. Call again with confirm=true ONLY after a clear yes. For send_email, also pass the draft_id from the first reply.

Say "One sec" before you use a tool. Afterwards, say what actually happened, using the tool's reply.
You can only email the contact names the tool accepts. Never ask for or spell out an email address.
If a tool fails or doesn't answer, say the home computer seems to be offline and offer to try again later. Never pretend something worked.
Never read out tool names, code, JSON or secrets.
      
              
        
                
      1. Phone Numbers → Create Phone Number → Free Vapi Number → type a 3-digit US area code → Create. Activation can take a few minutes.
        2. 
                
      2. Open the number → Inbound Settings → choose your Assistant → Save.
        3. 
                
      3. Call the number from your phone.
        4. 
              
      
              
      What you should see (hear)
      Your first message, in the assistant's voice. Afterwards, Logs → Calls shows the transcript and why the call ended.
      
              
      Gotchas
        
                
      • The free number only receives calls. It can't call you. Calling out needs an imported Twilio, Telnyx or DIDWW number, which costs money and adds setup.
        • 
                
      • Forgot to Publish? Calls keep using the old draft. It's the most common "my change did nothing" cause.
        • 
                
      • The new-assistant default is a "Balanced" preset for listening, thinking and voice. Leave it while you build; Vapi's docs also list Claude Haiku 5.5, but the dashboard menu wasn't checked (paths B and D on the next stop use Claude).
        • 
              
      
              
      Sources: Vapi phone quickstart, Vapi prompting guide, Vapi Anthropic provider.
      
              
            
      
          
      6. 

          
          
    6. 
            
            
      
              
      6a. Give Vapi the secret. Dashboard → Integrations → Server Configuration → Add Custom Credential → type Bearer Token. Paste your TOOL_SECRET from .env as the token and keep the standard Authorization header with the Bearer prefix on. (The older style, header name X-Vapi-Secret with the prefix off, also works; the server accepts both.)
      
              
      6b. Create five Function tools. Tools → Create Tool → Function tool, once per action. The filler below gives you every field to copy.
      
              
      
              
      6c. Attach and publish. Assistants → your assistant → Tools tab → Add Tool (all five) → Save → Publish.
      
              
      6d. Call it. Keep the server and ngrok running and try these, one at a time:
      
              
      "Add eggs and two gallons of milk.""What's on my list?""Save a note: call the dentist Monday.""Clear the grocery list." (it should ask first)
      
              
      What you should see
      The assistant confirms each one, your server window logs action=add_grocery_item ok, and groceries.md and notes.md in your AssistantInbox folder fill up. Clearing the list renames it to an archive file instead of deleting it.
      
              
      Gotchas
        
                
      • The tool's Test button doesn't send a real call's request, only the parameters you type. Test with a real call, or with the commands from step 3.
        • 
                
      • Async must be off, or the assistant won't wait for the answer.
        • 
                
      • "credentials withheld" in the call log means the server URL wasn't saved on the tool itself. For accounts created on or after 23 Sept 2026, Vapi only sends saved credentials with URLs saved on the tool, assistant or number.
        • 
                
      • "No result returned": check that your server and ngrok are both running, and that the tool's Server URL ends in /vapi/tool-calls.
        • 
                
      • The server already copes with Vapi's quirks: arguments arriving as text or as an object, answers that must be one line, and HTTP 200 even for errors.
        • 
              
      
              
      Sources: Vapi custom tools, Vapi server authentication, Vapi server events; this course's test log and video notes.
      
              
            
      
          
      7. 

          
          
    7. 
            
            
      
              
      Right now anyone who learns your number can talk to your assistant. The server limits what they could do (only your list, your notes and your approved contacts), but you'll add more. Do the first three now; the last two are the next layer.
      
              
      
                
      Keep the number private. Treat it like a house key: don't post it or put it on a card.
      
                
      Cap the call length. In the assistant's call timeout settings, set Maximum Duration (maxDurationSeconds, default 600 s) to about 300, and a Silence Timeout of 20–30 s. A stuck call then can't keep spending your credit.
      
                
      Keep spending capped. Vapi is pre-paid credit; run on your $5 first and add small amounts. If you later import a Twilio number: set Geo Permissions to the US only, add usage alerts, and use an API key instead of your main Auth Token.
      
                
      Next layer: answer only your phone. Put your number in .env as ALLOWED_CALLERS=+15555550100 (E.164; several numbers with commas) and restart the server: tool calls from any other number, and Vapi's dashboard test calls, are then refused with "This line only works for its owner." tested with simulated calls For a spoken refusal before the call even starts, Vapi can also ask your server who's calling (an assistant-request message; your answer must arrive within 7.5 seconds). design, not in the tested code yet
      
                
      Next layer: a spoken PIN. Caller ID can be faked, so before email or anything irreversible, ask for a PIN that your server checks. Never put the PIN in the prompt. design, not in the tested code yet
      
              
      
              
      What you should see
      The new limits saved and published. On a test call that you leave silent, the call ends by itself after your silence timeout.
      
              
      Sources: Vapi call timeout settings, Vapi spam call rejection, Twilio Geo Permissions. The security stop goes deeper on phone-specific attacks.
      
              
            
      
          
      8. 

          
          
    8. 
            
            
      
              
      The assistant can email only the nicknames you list (like me or mom), never an address someone dictates. It always reads the whole email back first (bodies are capped at 1,000 characters so that stays short), and stops after a daily limit. Be clear about what that proves: the server can check that a full read-back happened, but on a call your "yes" is heard and passed on by the AI, so it can't prove you agreed. For a confirmation the AI can't fake, see the approval codes in the head-agent build (B8).
      
              
      Lock it before email: until your server answers only your phone (set ALLOWED_CALLERS from step 7's next layer; the PIN design is in the "Teaching it to do things" stop), anyone who learns the number could ask it to send email to your contacts. Best: add the caller check first, then do this step. Until then, leave GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD blank in .env; the server then refuses every email ("Email is not set up"), while groceries and notes keep working. If you turn email on early anyway, list only me= in EMAIL_CONTACTS and keep MAX_EMAILS_PER_DAY low.
      
              
        
                
      1. On a personal Google account, turn on 2-Step Verification.
        2. 
                
      2. Create an App Password at myaccount.google.com/apppasswords. It's a separate 16-letter password just for this server.
        3. 
                
      3. Fill in the Gmail lines of .env, then stop the server (Ctrl+C) and start it again.
        4. 
              
      
              
      .env: the email lines
      GMAIL_ADDRESS=you@example.com
GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD=the-16-letter-app-password
EMAIL_CONTACTS=me=you@example.com,mom=mom@example.com
MAX_EMAILS_PER_DAY=5
      
              
      Test with an email to yourself. The first command only makes a draft and shows its 6-character id; put that id into the second command, which sends. Without the id, nothing can be sent.
      
              
      Second window (Mac)
      curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/send_email -H "X-Vapi-Secret: $TOOL_SECRET" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"to":"me","subject":"Test","body":"Hello from my assistant"}'; echo
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/send_email -H "X-Vapi-Secret: $TOOL_SECRET" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"to":"me","subject":"Test","body":"Hello from my assistant","confirm":true,"draft_id":"PASTE-THE-ID"}'; echo
      
              
      Second window (Windows)
      Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/send_email -Headers @{"X-Vapi-Secret"=$secret} -ContentType "application/json" -Body '{"to":"me","subject":"Test","body":"Hello from my assistant"}'
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/send_email -Headers @{"X-Vapi-Secret"=$secret} -ContentType "application/json" -Body '{"to":"me","subject":"Test","body":"Hello from my assistant","confirm":true,"draft_id":"PASTE-THE-ID"}'
      
              
      What you should see
      {"result":"Not sent yet (draft 3f9a1c). Read all of this back to the caller, word for word: email to me, subject 'Test', body 'Hello from my assistant'. Then ask if it should be sent. Only if they say yes, call send_email again with the same to, subject and body, confirm=true and draft_id='3f9a1c'."}
{"result":"Email sent to me."}
      …and the email in your inbox, ending "(Sent by my phone assistant.)". Then try it by phone: "Email me my grocery list."
      
              
      Gotchas
        
                
      • "The email login failed on the home computer" means Gmail refused the login (error 535). You probably used your normal password instead of the App Password. Failed tries count toward MAX_EMAILS_PER_DAY, so after a few you'll see "Daily email limit reached" until tomorrow.
        • 
                
      • 401 Unauthorized on these tests? If this is a new window, run the export TOOL_SECRET=…$secret = … line from step 3d again first.
        • 
                
      • No App Password option? They need 2-Step Verification and don't appear for most school or work accounts, or with security-key-only or Advanced Protection settings. Use a personal account.
        • 
                
      • Changed your Google password? That revokes App Passwords. Make a new one.
        • 
                
      • Only the alias list is trusted. Even if a caller (or text the AI read somewhere) says "email this to someone@else.com", the server answers "I can only email these contacts: me, mom."
        • 
              
      
              
      Sources: Google App Passwords, Gmail SMTP settings.
      
              
            
      
          
      9. 

          
          
    9. 
            
            
      
              
      So far the server and tunnel only run while their windows are open. Now make both start by themselves, and stop the computer from sleeping.
      
              
      
                
      Mac: two LaunchAgents. Save each file in ~/Library/LaunchAgents/. No secrets go in them: the server reads .env from its own folder. Replace /opt/homebrew/bin/ngrok with what which ngrok printed.
      
                
      ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.assistant.server.plist
      <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.assistant.server</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key><array>
    <string>/Users/you/assistant/.venv/bin/python</string>
    <string>-m</string><string>uvicorn</string><string>tool_server:app</string>
    <string>--host</string><string>127.0.0.1</string><string>--port</string><string>8000</string>
  </array>
  <key>WorkingDirectory</key><string>/Users/you/assistant</string>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/Users/you/assistant/server.out.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/you/assistant/server.err.log</string>
</dict></plist>
      
                
      ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.assistant.tunnel.plist
      <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.assistant.tunnel</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key><array>
    <string>/opt/homebrew/bin/ngrok</string><string>http</string><string>8000</string>
    <string>--url</string><string>https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app</string>
  </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/Users/you/assistant/tunnel.out.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/you/assistant/tunnel.err.log</string>
</dict></plist>
      
                
      Terminal: close the old windows first (Ctrl+C), then
      launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.assistant.server.plist
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.assistant.tunnel.plist
sudo pmset -c sleep 0 womp 1 autorestart 1
# to stop one later:  launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.assistant.server.plist
# to restart after editing code:  launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.assistant.server
      
                
      The pmset line means: on the charger, never sleep, wake for network access, and restart after a power cut. You can set the same in System Settings → Energy (desktop Macs) or Battery → Options (laptops): "Prevent automatic sleeping…". A closed laptop lid still sleeps. LaunchAgents only run while you're logged in.
      
              
      
              
      
                
      Windows: two small batch files and Task Scheduler. Save both in your assistant folder.
      
                
      C:\Users\you\assistant\run-server.bat
      cd /d C:\Users\you\assistant
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m uvicorn tool_server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
      
                
      C:\Users\you\assistant\run-tunnel.bat
      ngrok http 8000 --url https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app
      
                
      Ordinary PowerShell (no administrator needed)
      schtasks /create /tn "Assistant server" /tr "C:\Users\you\assistant\run-server.bat" /sc onlogon
schtasks /create /tn "Assistant tunnel" /tr "C:\Users\you\assistant\run-tunnel.bat" /sc onlogon
powercfg /change standby-timeout-ac 0
powercfg /change hibernate-timeout-ac 0
      
                
      Optional check · PowerShell as administrator
      powercfg /requests
      
                
      Use the least power that works: only powercfg /requests (which lists what is keeping the computer awake) needs an administrator window. If a line in the first box says "Access is denied", run just that line as administrator.
      
                
      The powercfg lines stop sleep while plugged in; the screen can still turn off. Want crash restarts and log files? Servy (winget install servy) runs any program as a proper Windows service and is actively maintained. Skip NSSM: its last release was in 2017.
      
              
      
              
      What you should see
      Restart the computer, log in, wait a minute, then call. It works with no windows open. And if the computer is off? The call still connects, and the assistant should say your home computer seems offline, because the prompt tells it so.
      
              
      Sources: launchd.plist, launchctl, pmset, Apple: prevent sleep, schtasks, powercfg, Servy.
      
              
            
      
          
      10. 
        
    
        
    All nine checkpoints done. You have a working, callable assistant. The next stop shows other ways to build it, and "Teaching it to do things" adds calendar, texts and more.
    
      
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Try to break it pick an attack
    
      
    Full access first: your assistant can write to your computer and send email in your name, by voice, from anywhere. That's the point, and it's also why it has nine layers. Pick something an attacker (or a confused AI) might try, and watch which layer stops it. Every reply shown is the server's real answer from the tests.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    The honest downsides
    What this setup can't do yet
    • Anyone who learns the number can talk to it, until you add the caller check and PIN. That is why email stays off (blank app password) until the caller check is in place.
    • "Read it back and ask first" depends on the AI following its instructions. The hard limits are the contact list and the daily cap.
    • Vapi keeps call recordings and transcripts; on the free tier, raw data is kept for 14 days.
    • Your computer has to be on and awake, and nothing has been tested end to end on a real call yet.
    
        
    Why it's built this way
    Rules in code, not in the prompt
    A prompt can be talked around: a caller, or text the AI reads, can try to change its mind. So every rule that matters runs in plain Python on your computer, where no conversation can reach it. "The AI checked it" is never treated as a lock.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: this course's test list and live request log; Vapi pricing (data kept 14 days on the free tier).
    
    
    

    
    
      
    What it's good for, starting today
    
      
    
        
    In the kitchen or the car
    "Add olive oil and two cans of tomatoes." The list is on your computer before you've closed the fridge, and you can read it back from the store.
    
        
    Thoughts on the move
    Walking out of a lecture or practice: "Save a note: ask about the lab due date." Every note lands with the date and time in one file.
    
        
    Quick messages to family
    "Email Mom that I'll be home Sunday around five." It reads it back, waits for your yes, and can only reach people you listed.
    
      
    
    
    

    
    
      
    What it costs checked Nov 2026
    
      
    
        
    
          
    Vapi number$0First number free, inbound only
    
          
    Vapi callsabout $0.08–0.13 a minute$0.05/min Vapi fee plus listening, AI and voice at cost
    
          
    Light use, 30 minutes a monthabout $2.50–4 a monthYour first $5 credit covers roughly 40–60 minutes
    
          
    ngrok, Python, Gmail$0Free plan: 20,000 requests a month, far more than you'll use
    
        
    
        
    The per-minute figure comes from Vapi's own estimator (1,000 minutes for $82–129). Prices change, so check the pricing page before you rely on them. The bigger cost is your time: about one to two hours for this build, mostly account setup.
    Sources: Vapi pricing, ngrok free plan.

    Your own AI assistant · Stop B5 · Build it · about 30 minutes
    
        
    Other ways to build it
    
        
    Path A is the quickest start, but it isn't the only good assistant. You can give it Claude as its brain, make it sound more natural, keep every word inside your own home, or skip the tunnel entirely. This stop compares four more ways to build it, tells you which one fits what you care about, and shows exactly what each one asks of you.
    
      
    
      
    
      
    At this stop you'll learn
    • What each path is best at: Claude, natural speech, privacy, no code, or no tunnel
    • How cost, effort, privacy and speed compare, with a recommendation for your priorities
    • The steps and commands for each path, and the traps the videos miss
    • Which locks each path needs so only you can use it
    • How the tool server you built in B4 carries over
    
    
    
    
    

    
    
      
    What the other paths give you
    
      
    Every path ends the same way: you call a number and your assistant does things on your computer. They differ in what does the listening and thinking, who keeps your recordings, and how much you build yourself.
    
      
    
        
    Claude as the brain
    Paths B and D let you pick Claude models, and Vapi (path A) lists Claude Haiku 5.5. Claude has no audio model of its own, so on the phone it always works as listen → Claude → speak. The fast, cheap choice is Haiku 5.5 ($0.10 in / $0.50 out per million tokens, checked Nov 2026).
    
        
    More natural conversation
    Path C uses OpenAI's realtime voice model, which hears and speaks audio directly instead of passing text between three services. You can interrupt it mid-sentence and it stops.
    
        
    Your words stay home
    Path E runs the listening, thinking and speaking on your own hardware, so no company keeps your recordings. It's the most private and the most work.
    
        
    No tunnel to babysit
    With LiveKit (path D), your computer connects out to LiveKit's service, so nothing needs to reach in. That likely removes the tunnel altogether (our reading of the docs, untested).
    
      
    
      
    Sources: Claude models overview, Vapi Anthropic provider, LiveKit phone numbers, Home Assistant private voice assistant.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Compare them pick what matters
    
      
    Choose up to three things you care about most. The paths re-rank, and the top one comes with the reason. The scores are our judgment from the research notes; the facts underneath are sourced.
    
      
    
      
    Prices checked Nov 2026. Build times are estimates for someone who knows a little Python. Sources: Vapi, ElevenAgents, Twilio US voice, OpenAI, LiveKit numbers, Claude.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Path B: ElevenAgents with a Twilio number no code, Claude inside
    
      
    
        
    
          
    Why choose it. ElevenLabs' agent builder (now called ElevenAgents) is the most polished no-code option: excellent voices, Claude available as the brain (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 4.5 are listed), a built-in Tests tab that simulates conversations and checks tool calls, and 15 free call minutes a month to start.
    
          
    The catch. ElevenAgents doesn't sell you a number in anything we could verify; you import one, usually from Twilio. And Twilio's free trial won't work for this: it uses shared Twilio numbers and strips out the audio streaming these platforms rely on. Plan to upgrade Twilio (add a balance) before you start. A US number is $1.15 a month.
    
          
    The good news. Your B4 tool server works here too. Point each webhook tool at the server's plain endpoint, https://YOUR-DOMAIN.ngrok-free.app/tools/add_grocery_item and so on (the same ngrok address as B4), and send the secret as a header.
    
        
    
        
    
          The build, in order
          
      
            
    1. Upgrade Twilio, buy a voice number, and create an API key (safer than your main Auth Token).
      2. 
            
    2. ElevenAgents → new agent from the Blank template. On the Agent tab set the first message and system prompt; choose a Claude model as the LLM; pick a voice on Voice; try Test AI agent.
      3. 
            
    3. Phone Numbers tab → import the Twilio number → assign your agent.
      4. 
            
    4. Add Tool → Webhook for each action: method POST, URL as above, parameters with value type LLM Prompt, and a Secret header Authorization: Bearer your-TOOL_SECRET. Default timeout is 20 s.
      5. 
            
    5. Advanced → Data Retention: lower it. By default ElevenLabs keeps conversations for 2 years.
      6. 
          
    
          
    Not verified: the exact JSON body ElevenAgents sends to a webhook. Our server expects the body to be just the arguments, like {"item":"milk"}. Make one test call and check the server log before relying on it.
    
        
    
      
    
      
    Lock it to you: import the number by SIP trunk and use its Allowed Numbers list, or pass the caller's number into each tool with the dynamic variable {{system__caller_id}} and have your server refuse other numbers. That second way needs a change to the B4 server first (not in the tested code): as written, it rejects any argument it doesn't expect, so an extra caller-ID parameter makes every tool fail. The Twilio "conversation initiation" webhook sees the caller ID but, per the docs we read, can't reject the call.
    
      
    Sources: ElevenAgents quickstart, LLM choice, Twilio import, webhook tools, dynamic variables, retention, Twilio trial.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Path C: Twilio + OpenAI Realtime, in Python the most natural conversation
    
      
    
        
    Benefits
    Speech in, speech out
    One model hears and answers in audio, so turns feel quick and you can cut in. You own the code: one Python file, adapted from Twilio's official sample and tested here with mocks (24 tests, including a full simulated call that runs a tool).
    
        
    Downsides
    Cost and moving parts
    Twilio must be upgraded. Audio tokens are priced at $32 in / $64 out per million for gpt-realtime-2.1 ($10 / $20 for -mini), and OpenAI publishes no per-minute price; our rough estimate is $3–9 a month for light use (untested). It needs a tunnel that supports WebSockets: use ngrok.
    
        
    Built-in locks
    Already in the code
    ALLOWED_CALLERS (only your number), a check that each request really came from Twilio (TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN), a one-time token so strangers can't open the audio stream, and the server bound to 127.0.0.1. The same five actions and limits as B4.
    
      
    
      
    Download the B5 code (.zip)View files: README.md · main_with_tools.py · pipecat_bot.py · livekit_agent.py · assistant_actions.py · .env.example
    
      
    
        
    Run it (in the other-paths folder from the code pack)
    python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
# in .env (copy .env.example first). TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN and ALLOWED_CALLERS are required:
# without them the server won't start and refuses calls.
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
OPENAI_REALTIME_MODEL=gpt-realtime-2.1
ALLOWED_CALLERS=+15555550100
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN=your-twilio-auth-token
PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://your-domain.ngrok-free.app

python main_with_tools.py            # listens on 127.0.0.1:5050
# Stop the B4 tunnel first: your one free ngrok domain can point at only one port at a time
ngrok http 5050 --url https://your-domain.ngrok-free.app
# Twilio Console → Phone Numbers → Manage → Active numbers → your number →
#   "A call comes in" → Webhook → https://your-domain.ngrok-free.app/incoming-call → Save
    
        
    Update box: newer than most videos
    • Use gpt-realtime-2.1. The older gpt-4o-realtime-preview models shut down 7 May 2026, and gpt-realtime retires 20 Jan 2027.
    • Run tools when the response is done and completed (response.done), not on the earlier "arguments done" event, which also fires when you interrupt.
    • The GA session has no temperature setting; old samples that pass one are out of date.
    • Twilio's own sample binds to 0.0.0.0 and leaves the audio stream open; the tested version fixes both.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: Twilio sample repo, OpenAI deprecations, OpenAI pricing, Twilio pricing. Get the code: other-paths.zip (paths C and D, with their own copy of the B4 actions and 53 tests), or read main_with_tools.py in your browser.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Path D: Pipecat or LiveKit, with Claude open source, your rules
    
      
    Both are open-source Python frameworks for voice agents. You pick each piece: a speech-to-text service, Claude, and a voice. The assistant code for both was checked against the current libraries (Pipecat 1.15, LiveKit Agents 1.8.11) and passes unit tests, but no real call has been made.
    
      
    
        
    
          LiveKit Agents
    The easier of the two
    
          
    • Free number: every LiveKit Cloud plan includes one US local number, and the Build plan includes 50 free inbound minutes. It's inbound only.
    • Likely no tunnel: your computer connects out to LiveKit Cloud.
    • Claude: not in LiveKit's built-in model list, so you use the livekit-plugins-anthropic plugin with your own Anthropic key.
    • Gotcha: the agent name in your dispatch rule must match the code (my-agent), or calls ring and nobody answers.
    
          
    Mac / Windows
    # Mac:
brew install livekit-cli
# Windows:
winget install LiveKit.LiveKitCLI
# then, on either (in its own venv, as tested: python3.13 -m venv .venv-livekit,
#   Windows: py -V:3.13 -m venv .venv-livekit, then activate it as in B4 step 3a):
lk cloud auth
lk app env --write --destination .env.local   # writes LIVEKIT_URL, _API_KEY, _API_SECRET
# add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ASSISTANT_FOLDER to .env
python -m pip install -r requirements-livekit.txt
python livekit_agent.py dev
    
          
    Code: livekit_agent.py, in other-paths.zip.
    
        
    
        
    
          Pipecat
    The most control
    
          
    • Pieces: a Twilio number, Deepgram (listening), Claude, Cartesia (voice), each with its own key.
    • Tunnel: needed (ngrok), and Twilio must be upgraded.
    • Current code style: pass the model with AnthropicLLMService.Settings(model=..., system_instruction=...); import tool schemas from pipecat.adapters.llm.schemas. Older tutorials use paths that now warn or break.
    • Lock: set ALLOWED_CALLERS; the bot asks Twilio who is really on the call before starting.
    
          
    Mac / Windows
    # in its own venv, as tested (.venv-pipecat), activated as in B4 step 3a
# .env needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, DEEPGRAM_API_KEY, CARTESIA_API_KEY,
#   TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID, TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN, ASSISTANT_FOLDER
python -m pip install -r requirements-pipecat.txt
ngrok http 7860 --url https://your-domain.ngrok-free.app
python pipecat_bot.py --transport twilio
# Twilio: TwiML Bin with
#  <Response><Connect><Stream url="wss://your-domain.ngrok-free.app/ws"/></Connect></Response>
    
          
    Code: pipecat_bot.py, in other-paths.zip.
    
        
    
      
    
      
    Set the model yourself. Both frameworks still default to an older Claude (Sonnet 4.6). The tested code sets claude-haiku-5-5, the fastest current model, which matters on the phone where every half-second of silence is noticeable.
    
      
    Sources: Pipecat Twilio example, pipecat-ai, LiveKit agent starter, livekit-plugins-anthropic, LiveKit phone numbers.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Path E: fully self-hosted and private for tinkerers
    
      
    
        
    
          
    The big benefit: nothing you say leaves your house. Home Assistant can run the whole chain locally: Whisper or Speech-to-Phrase to listen, a local model through Ollama to think, Piper to speak. It can also control your smart home, which no other path does out of the box.
    
          
    The honest catch: the officially supported "phone" is an old-style analog handset plugged into a small adapter (a Grandstream HT801) on your home network. Reaching it from a real phone number needs an unofficial bridge through Asterisk or FreePBX, and people report one-way audio, calls that don't hang up, and every caller showing up as the same number. That last one breaks caller checks.
    
          
    Models that handle tools well in 2026 hobbyist guides are small ones: Qwen 3.5 (4B or 9B), Llama 3.1 8B, or the Home-Assistant-tuned home-3b.
    
        
    
        
    
          How long until it answers (hobbyist measurements on Home Assistant; secondary source)
          
    Gaming PC with a mid-range NVIDIA card, or a 16 GB Apple-silicon Macabout 2–4 s
    
          
    Mini PC without a graphics cardabout 4–8 s
    
          
    Raspberry Pi 5about 5–10 s, simple commands only
    
          
    A phone call adds its own delay on top. Hardware runs from a $50–80 used mini PC to $800+ for a GPU PC; electricity for an always-on mini PC is a few dollars a month. Several figures come from hobbyist blogs, so treat them as approximate.
    
        
    
      
    
      
    Sources: HA VoIP integration, HA local assistant, HA Ollama, HA community: Asterisk, InsiderLLM local LLM guide (secondary).

    Your own AI assistant · Stop B6 · Making it useful · about 40 minutes
    
        
    Teaching it to do things
    
        
    A voice that only chats is a novelty. Give it a few well-chosen actions and you can add to the grocery list from the car, email yourself a reminder, put a dentist appointment on your calendar or switch off the porch light, all by phoning one number. This stop is a catalogue of those actions: what each one gets you, how it's wired, the real gotchas, and how much freedom to give it. Then it shows how to add your own, and other ways to reach your assistant besides a phone call.
    
      
    
      
    
      
    
        from 14:07n8n · official · Feb 2026n8n Quick Start: Build Your First AI AgentGiving an agent its first tool, and why the tool's description matters.
        
    At this stop you'll learn
    • How an action actually runs, and the three ways to wire one
    • The gate every action sits behind: your number, a PIN and a secret
    • Five safety settings, and which one each action deserves
    • The gotchas that break actions after a week (OAuth, App Passwords, SMS rules)
    • How to add a new action to the tested code, with a test
    • Which channel to add next: Telegram, Siri Shortcuts, Android or SMS
    
      
    
    
    
    
    

    
    
      
    How an action works and three ways to wire one
    
      
    When you say "add milk", the AI doesn't touch anything itself. It picks one tool from a list you gave it and fills in the blanks. Your code does the job and hands back one short sentence to say out loud.
    
      
    
        
    
          
    Each tool has a name, a description the AI reads to decide when to use it, and named arguments (for add_grocery_item: item and an optional quantity). The voice platform sends the AI's choice to a web address you control. Your server checks it, does it, and replies with a short result such as "Added milk to the grocery list."
    
          
    This is the most useful thing to understand about assistants: it can do exactly what's on that list and nothing else. Each tool you add is a new power, and the code behind each tool, not the AI's good behaviour, decides what's allowed.
    
          
    The exact shapes, for Vapi: it POSTs message.toolCallList[], each with an id and function.name / function.arguments (sometimes an object, sometimes a JSON string; accept both). You always answer HTTP 200 with {"results":[{"name","toolCallId","result"}]}, and the result must be a single-line string. Anything else, and the assistant says no result came back.
    
        
    
        
    Speed matters on a call
    Aim for a few seconds
    The platforms allow long waits: ElevenAgents defaults to 20 s (5–300), Retell to 120 s (up to 600), and Vapi's maximum is 120 s according to a support reply, not the docs. But a few seconds of silence on a phone feels broken. Our notes suggest aiming for under about 5 s, and adding a filler line ("One moment, adding that") to every tool that talks to another service. Vapi calls it Request Start, Retell Talk While Waiting, ElevenAgents pre_tool_speech. For anything slow, start it in the background and have it say "I'll let you know when that's done."
    
      
    
      
    
        
    1. A function on your tool server
    Your own Python on your computer, like add_grocery_item in assistant_actions.py from Build path A. Best for: files on your computer and full control; it's the part we have tested (with fakes). Costs you: you maintain it, and your computer and tunnel have to be on.
    
        
    2. A tool on the voice platform
    A webhook or MCP tool plugged straight into Vapi, Retell or ElevenAgents, such as Home Assistant's MCP server or Zapier MCP. Best for: no code. Costs you: your logins live with that service, and a long tool list makes the AI slower and likelier to pick the wrong one.
    
        
    3. An n8n or Zapier workflow
    One tool, say do_task(action, payload), points at a workflow that branches to Gmail, Sheets or Calendar and sends back one sentence. Best for: many cloud apps at once; the hub refreshes your Google sign-in for you. Costs you: the hub becomes a powerful app on the internet that needs its own lock.
    
      
    
      
    In real life: AI voice agents sometimes say they did something they never actually called a tool for. Have the assistant repeat what the tool said back ("Added milk to the grocery list") rather than its own guess, and glance at tool_server.log now and then: every action is logged as ok or refused, without secrets or email bodies.
    
      
    Sources: Vapi custom tools, Vapi server events, Vapi support thread (timeout), Retell custom functions, ElevenAgents tool API; the tested code package in our research notes (Nov 6, 2026).
    
    
    

    
    
      
    The gate in front of every action open each layer
    
      
    Before any action runs, the request should pass through several locks, each enforced by code rather than by asking the AI nicely. Set these up first; every action in the catalogue assumes they're there.
    
      
    
      
    Why both a number check and a PIN? Caller ID can be faked ("spoofed"), so "it's my number" only means "probably me". The PIN covers that gap for anything that changes something. No video or source we found covers phone-specific attacks like this, so the PIN design here is our own reasoning, marked as such. Stop B9 covers the full security picture: prompt injection, phone fraud, the "lethal trifecta" and a pre-launch checklist.
    
      
    Sources: Vapi spam call rejection, Vapi server events (7.5 s limit), Retell inbound webhook, Vapi server authentication, FCC caller ID spoofing guide; the tested code package (Nov 6, 2026).
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Five safety settings from most freedom to none
    
      
    Every action in the catalogue gets one of these settings. The rule of thumb: the harder it is to undo, and the more it reaches other people, the less the assistant decides alone.
    
      
    
        
    Read-only
    It can look but not change anything: weather, your calendar for today, what's on the list. Set it up: give it only a "get" tool (the n8n Quick Start's agent can only search its table, by design) or read-only access. Catch: what it reads (emails, web pages, invitations) may contain hidden instructions. Reading must never lead straight to sending.
    
        
    Auto
    It just does it, because the action only adds to your own stuff, or is easy to undo: add an item, save a note, text you. Set it up: make the action append-only, and archive instead of deleting (the tested clear_grocery_list renames the old list rather than erasing it).
    
        
    Read back and confirm
    The first call to the tool does nothing except return a summary. The AI reads it to you, and only after a clear "yes" does it call again with confirm=true. Set it up: put the check in the code, as the tested send_email does ("Not sent yet. Read this back to the caller…"). A prompt alone can be talked around.
    
        
    Approval code
    A spoken "yes" can be misheard, faked, or come from someone else on the call. For actions you can't take back, a one-time code arrives on a separate channel (a text or an app notification) and must be given back before the action runs. Set it up: the head-agent build in stop B8 does this by text message (tested with fakes). Use it for: new recipients, private data leaving, deleting, sharing files, changing account settings.
    
        
    Never by voice
    Don't give the phone assistant the tool at all. Do these yourself in the app: moving money, unlocking doors, changing passwords. Set it up: leave the tool out, and with Home Assistant, don't "expose" those devices to the assistant. (Our recommendation. The security notes say payments should always be approved by a person.)
    
      
    
      
    Sources: n8n Quick Start (read-only tool design), OpenAI Agents SDK human-in-the-loop, Home Assistant MCP Server; our head-agent security notes and tested code (Nov 6, 2026).
    
    
    

    
    
      
    The action catalogue filter, search, open
    
      
    Twenty-one actions people actually want from a phone assistant. Each shows what it unlocks, how it's wired, what goes wrong, and the safety setting we'd give it. "In the tested code" means it's in the Build path A package and passed its tests with fakes. Nothing here has been tested with real accounts or a real call yet.
    
      
    
        
    
          
    
          
    Wired as
    
          
    Safety
    
          
    Status
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
      
    
      
    Update box (video older than the facts): Kevin Stratvert's n8n tutorial (Jul 2025) is still the clearest demo of "the agent only drafts, a person approves, then the workflow sends" (watch 15:58–18:42 and 20:30–22:51). But it was made on n8n 1.x. Since then the agent-type dropdown has gone, workflows are Published rather than activated, the Gemini preview model it uses is dated, and n8n now has built-in approve/deny for an agent's tool calls in Chat, Slack, Discord, Telegram and others.
    
      
    Sources are listed inside each action. Prices checked Nov 2026.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Add your own action copy, paste, test
    
      
    Adding a power to the tested tool server takes one block of Python, one test and one setting in Vapi. Here's a to-do list action that reuses the package's own safety helpers, so it gets the same limits as the grocery list.
    
      
    
        
    
          
    What the helpers do for you: clean_text strips newlines and enforces a maximum length; safe_path only allows a fixed file name inside your one assistant folder; _file_lock stops two calls writing at once. Registering in ACTIONS, REQUIRED and DESCRIPTIONS is what makes it exist. run_action refuses unknown actions and unexpected arguments automatically.
    
          
    Honest status: we ran this exact block against the tested package on Nov 6, 2026 (Linux, Python 3.13): every test passed, the originals plus the new one, and a live curl to 127.0.0.1 returned "Added to your to-do list: call the dentist (due Friday)." The Mac and Windows commands weren't run on those systems.
    
        
    
        
    For an action that sends or deletes
    Copy the confirm pattern
    Give it a confirm argument and return "Not done yet. Read this back…" unless is_confirmed(confirm) is true, exactly like send_email and clear_grocery_list. Fix the recipient or target on the server (an alias list in .env), never from what the AI says. For anything you can't undo, use an approval code (stop B8) or leave it off the phone.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    1
    Paste this into assistant_actions.py, just above def tool_definitions()
    
          
    assistant_actions.py · new action
    # ---- NEW ACTION: add_todo
TODO_FILE = "todo.md"
MAX_TASK = 200
MAX_DUE = 40


def add_todo(task, due=None) -> str:
    task = clean_text(task, "task", MAX_TASK)
    due = clean_text(due, "due", MAX_DUE, required=False)
    entry = f"{task} (due {due})" if due else task
    with _file_lock:
        path = safe_path(TODO_FILE)
        with path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as fp:
            fp.write(f"- [ ] {entry}  _(added {datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M})_\n")
    return f"Added to your to-do list: {entry}."


ACTIONS["add_todo"] = (add_todo, {
    "task": {"type": "string", "description": "One to-do item, e.g. 'call the dentist'"},
    "due": {"type": "string", "description": "Optional, as the caller said it, e.g. 'Friday'"},
})
REQUIRED["add_todo"] = ["task"]
DESCRIPTIONS["add_todo"] = "Add one item to the user's to-do list on their home computer. Call once per item."
    
        
    2
    Add a test to tests/test_tool_server.py and run the suite
    
          
    tests/test_tool_server.py · add at the end
    def test_add_todo(client, env):
    r = post_vapi(client, ("t1", "add_todo", {"task": "call the dentist", "due": "Friday"}))
    assert r.json()["results"][0]["result"] == "Added to your to-do list: call the dentist (due Friday)."
    assert "call the dentist (due Friday)" in (env / "todo.md").read_text()
    r = post_vapi(client, ("t2", "add_todo", {"task": "x", "path": "../../etc/passwd"}))
    assert "error" in r.json()["results"][0]
    
          
    Then, with your venv active: python -m pytest. You should see every test pass, including test_add_todo.
    
        
    3
    Try it by hand, with the server running
    
          
    
          
    Terminal (Mac)
    curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/add_todo \
  -H "X-Vapi-Secret: PASTE_TOOL_SECRET" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"task":"call the dentist","due":"Friday"}'
    
          
    PowerShell (Windows)
    Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8000/tools/add_todo `
  -Headers @{"X-Vapi-Secret"="PASTE_TOOL_SECRET"} -ContentType "application/json" `
  -Body '{"task":"call the dentist","due":"Friday"}'
    
          
    What you should see: {"result":"Added to your to-do list: call the dentist (due Friday)."}, and a new line in todo.md in your assistant folder. Without the secret header you get {"detail":"unauthorized"}, and nothing is written.
    
        
    4
    Tell Vapi about it
    Run python assistant_actions.py: it prints every tool's name, description and parameters, now including add_todo. In Vapi, create a Function tool with exactly that name and parameters, set its Server URL to https://YOUR-TUNNEL/vapi/tool-calls, attach the same Bearer Token credential (Header Name X-Vapi-Secret, prefix off), add the tool to your assistant and publish. Add one line to the assistant's prompt: "When the caller names a to-do, call add_todo once per item." Vapi's Test button sends only your parameters, not the real envelope, so test with a real call.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: Vapi custom tools, Vapi server authentication, Python venv docs; the tested code package, plus our own test run of this block (Nov 6, 2026).
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Channels beyond the phone pick what matters to you
    
      
    A phone number is the best hands-free option, but it costs per minute and can't easily send you something later. The same actions can sit behind other doors. Tick what you care about: the channels re-rank, and each card shows how it does on every need (ticked ones in bold).
    
      
    
        
    I want…
    
        
    
        
    
      
    
      
    
        
    
          
    Our recommended mix
    
          
    Keep the phone number for the car and hands-free use. Add a Telegram bot as your text and voice-note channel: it's free, it can message you first, and with "long polling" your computer reaches out to Telegram, so no public address or open port is needed. Add one Siri Shortcut (or a Tasker task) for the thing you do most, like adding groceries. Only pay for SMS if you really want texting with no app, about $57 a year in fixed fees by our arithmetic on Twilio's prices (checked Nov 2026).
    
          
    Whatever the channel, the same gate applies: only you (your Telegram chat, your phone's secret), and the same safety setting per action.
    
        
    
        
    iPhone Shortcut "Add groceries" (untested)
    1. Dictate Text
2. Get Contents of URL
     URL:     https://YOUR-TUNNEL/tools/add_grocery_item
     Method:  POST
     Headers: X-Vapi-Secret = YOUR_TOOL_SECRET
     Request Body: JSON
       item = Dictated Text
3. Get Dictionary Value: result  (from Contents of URL)
4. Speak Text: Dictionary Value

Name it so "Hey Siri, add groceries" runs it.
It calls the tested tool server directly, with no AI in between.
Don't share this shortcut: the secret is inside it.
    
      
    
      
    The Shortcut uses Apple's documented Get Contents of URL action (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE; JSON, Form or File body). Apple's page doesn't document custom headers, and some users report header or JSON quirks on some iOS versions, so check that the reply is the "Added…" sentence. That the shortcut's name works as the Siri phrase is unverified.
    
      
    Sources: Telegram Bots FAQ, Telegram Bot API, Twilio A2P 10DLC, Twilio 10DLC fees, Twilio SMS pricing (US), Twilio Sole Proprietor registration, Apple Shortcuts: request your first API, Apple Community thread, Tasker HTTP Request event, TechCrunch on WhatsApp's terms, Meta AI Providers policy, Google Voice linked numbers, Vapi community: Google Voice forwarding.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Your first week of actions tick as you go
    
      
    Start with the reliable ones and add risk slowly. Our notes rank reliability roughly like this: lookups, then adding to your own lists, then emailing yourself, calendar events, smart home, email to others, SMS, and last, calls to businesses. This order follows that ranking.
    
      
    
      
    Sources: our research notes on actions and integrations, and the build order in the research handoff (Nov 6, 2026).
    
    
    

    
    
    
    
  
    

    



    
  
    
    
    
    
    
      
    
        
    Your own AI assistant · Stop B7 · Making it useful · about 35 minutes
    
        
    Making it good to talk to
    
        
    A well-designed phone assistant feels like calling a sharp friend: it answers in a sentence, does the easy things without asking, reads back anything that can't be undone, and never pretends a job is done when it isn't. Here you'll build that personality as a real system prompt you can copy, hear the difference in a bad call and a good call, tune its speed, give it a memory between calls, and test it before you trust it.
    
      
    
      
    
      
    At this stop you'll learn
    • Why talking needs different rules from typing
    • How to assemble a voice system prompt, part by part, and copy it
    • When it should act, read back, or ask you to approve outside the call
    • What makes it feel fast: turn-taking, model choice, tool speed
    • How it remembers you between calls, safely
    • How to test it with simulated callers and a checklist
    
    
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Why talking is different from typing
    
      
    
        
    
          
    On the phone you have no screen. You can't scroll back, skim a list, or see that it misheard "Linda" as "Lindah". Everything it says costs your time, and anything it gets wrong may already have happened by the time you notice. So the same assistant that writes great answers in a chat window can be painful on a call.
    
          
    The good news: the fixes are well known, and every voice platform's own guide agrees on them. Short turns (one or two sentences, one question at a time). Spoken formats (say "five thirty p.m.", never read out symbols or bullet points). Read-backs for exact details. Honest tool talk ("one sec" while it works, "sent" only once it really is). And a few platform settings that no prompt can replace: how long it waits before answering, how long a call can run, what it says while a tool is busy.
    
          
    Done well, it's the most natural way to use an assistant: hands-free while you walk, cook, drive or push a shopping cart.
    
        
    
        
    How Claude hears and speaks
    Claude has no audio of its own. On a phone line it's always a relay: speech-to-text turns your voice into words, Claude reads them and decides what to say or which tool to use, and text-to-speech reads its reply aloud. Vapi, ElevenAgents, Retell, Pipecat and LiveKit all let you pick Claude as the middle step. That's why the prompt has to ask for speakable text: Claude writes it, a voice reads it word for word.
    OpenAI's realtime models (currently gpt-realtime-2.1) hear and speak directly, which can feel snappier. You could still call Claude as a tool from one.
    
      
    
      
    For you: before you write a word of prompt, call your assistant once and just listen. Count how many sentences it says per turn and whether it ever reads you a list. That's your "before" picture.
    
      
    Sources: Vapi prompting guide, ElevenLabs prompting guide, Claude models overview, Pipecat Anthropic, Vapi Anthropic provider.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    The voice prompt workshop build and copy
    
      
    Switch parts on and off and watch the system prompt assemble. Every part comes from a vendor guide (Vapi, OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Retell) or our own tested code. Pick your platform to see the settings you also need to change there, because some behaviour lives outside the prompt.
    
      
    
        
    
          
    
            
            
            
          
    
          
    
            Your platform
            
    
          
    
          
    
            
            
          
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    
            
    Your voice system prompt
    
            
    0 of 11 parts0 words
    
            
    
          
    
          
    
        
    
      
    
      
    Where it goes: paste it into your agent's System prompt box (ElevenAgents: on the Agent tab; Vapi and Retell: the assistant's system prompt field; your own code: the system instruction). Replace the {{…}} placeholders with your platform's variables, and make the tool names match your real tools exactly, or the model will call tools that don't exist.
    
      
    Status: the parts are built from vendor guidance and the confirmation pattern matches our tool server, which passed its tests with fakes and mocks. This exact prompt has not been tested on a real phone call. ElevenLabs warns that prompts over about 2,000 tokens add latency and cost; with everything on this prompt is around 650 words, which should be well under that; check your platform's token count if you add much more.
    
      
    Sources: Vapi prompting guide, OpenAI Realtime prompting guide, ElevenLabs prompting guide, Retell prompt engineering guide, ElevenAgents tool settings, Vapi call timeouts, Retell custom functions, LiveKit turn tuning.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    A bad call and a good call same request, side by side
    
      
    Both assistants get the same request from Alex, walking into the grocery store. The bad one is what a quick demo prompt often produces; the good one runs the full prompt from the workshop. Tap a number to see what went wrong and what fixed it. (Written for this course to show the rules; not a recording.)
    
      
    
        
    
        
    
        
    
      
    
      
    For you: call your own assistant with this exact request (with a test contact instead of Mom). Every one of these nine differences can be checked in about two minutes.
    
      
    Sources for the rules shown: Vapi prompting guide, OpenAI Realtime prompting guide, ElevenLabs prompting guide, Retell prompt engineering guide, Vapi Simulations.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    When it should ask before acting
    
      
    The most capable setup asks as little as possible. OpenAI's own guide says to drop confirmation loops for low-risk tools and let the agent be proactive, and that's what makes an assistant feel effortless. The skill is deciding which actions earn a question.
    
      
    
        
    Just do it
    Easy to undo
    Adding groceries, saving a note, reading your list. No question; say what the tool did ("Eggs and oat milk are on the list"). If it ever starts acting too eagerly, soften that wording.
    
        
    Read back, then "yes"
    Exact or irreversible
    Sending an email, a calendar event, clearing a list. One sentence with the exact details, then "Send it?" Only a clear yes counts. On a correction, change only that detail and read back once more.
    
        
    Approve outside the call
    Big or costly
    Anything you'd hate to see done by a stranger who spoofed your number: money, deleting files, messages to new people. A spoken "yes" isn't enough; you approve with a code sent to you (see the head-agent stop, B8).
    
      
    
      
    
        
    
          
    The honest downside. Voice is the easiest channel to mishear and the hardest to check. A misheard address, or a "yes" to the wrong question, can send an email you can't unsend. And the prompt is only a polite request to the model: Vapi's guide calls it a soft control, not a security boundary. Someone who gets through can try to talk it out of its rules.
    
          
    So put the real checks in code on your own server, where talking can't change them. Layer them like this, from cheapest to strongest.
    
        
    
        
    
          
    1
    Prompt rules
    The "When to ask before acting" part of the workshop. Good manners; easy to talk around.
    
          
    2
    Two-step tools
    Our tool server's send_email refuses to send unless called a second time with confirm=true; the first call returns the summary to read back. Clearing the list works the same way. (Tested with fakes and mocks.)
    
          
    3
    Saved contacts only
    The tool takes a name like "Mom" and the server looks up the address, so nobody ever spells an email on the phone. In the mock tests it refused five tricky addresses, including a look-alike domain and a hidden Bcc.
    
          
    4
    Daily cap
    Set MAX_EMAILS_PER_DAY in the server's .env, so a runaway call can't spam anyone.
    
          
    5
    Passphrase check
    Caller ID can be faked. Before write actions, the assistant asks for a passphrase and a verify_pin tool checks it on the server; never put the passphrase in the prompt. (Design advice; no source covers phone-specific attacks yet.)
    
          
    6
    Your own log
    Log every tool request and result with the call ID. The platform transcript shows what the model said; your log shows what your server actually did.
    
        
    
      
    
      
    Sources: OpenAI Realtime prompting guide, Vapi prompting guide, ElevenLabs prompting guide; our tool server tests (research notes: tested code); caller-check design from our actions and head-agent security notes.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Making it feel fast play the steps
    
      
    The gap after you stop talking comes from three places: deciding you've finished (turn detection, also called endpointing), the model and voice getting their first words out, and any tool round-trips. Click through the relay to see where each delay lives and what you can change.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    
          Try it: how long should it wait?
          
    You say "Add eggs… (short pause) …and oat milk."
    
          
    An illustration with a made-up 0.8-second pause, not a measurement. The thinking and voice time that come after the wait aren't drawn, because our sources have no measured numbers for them.
    
        
    
        
        
    
        
    
        
    LiveKit's defaults: wait at least 0.5 s (endpointing.min_delay), and force the turn closed at 3.0 s (max_delay). Its mode: "dynamic" adapts inside that range from your own pause habits, and adaptive interruption tells a real "wait" from an "mm-hm".
    
      
    
      
    
        
    Pick a fast Claude
    Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5) is Anthropic's fastest, from $0.10 / $0.50 per million tokens in/out up to 100K context (checked Nov 2026). Sonnet 5.5 with low effort is the step up. Avoid Opus 5.5 for live turns: its thinking is always on. Vapi lists claude-haiku-5-5; ElevenAgents' Claude list (Nov 2026) has Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5.5, not Haiku 5.5. Pipecat and LiveKit default to an older Claude, so set the model yourself. Phone and voice minutes, not Claude, are most of the bill.
    
        
    Keep tools quick
    Aim for tool replies under about 5 seconds, even though ElevenAgents waits 20 s by default. Cover slow ones with a neutral line: pre_tool_speech on force (ElevenAgents), a request-start message on the tool (Vapi), or Talk While Waiting (Retell). Let "add to list" run in the background (async), but keep "read my list" waiting, since it needs the answer.
    
        
    Short prompt, close server
    Long prompts are slower: ElevenLabs flags anything over about 2,000 tokens. Move reference material into a knowledge base. Vapi's pre-call webhook must answer within 7.5 s (fixed), so Vapi suggests hosting near us-west-2. A home computer that's asleep, or a free server that has to wake up, causes awkward silences.
    
      
    
      
    Be wary of speed claims. Our sources contain no measured end-to-end numbers (like "under 800 ms"), and none for Haiku vs Sonnet response time. ElevenLabs' advice is the honest one: try two or three models with your real prompt and compare speed, accuracy and tool-calling success yourself.
    
      
    Sources: LiveKit turn-taking tuning, Claude models overview, Claude pricing, Vapi Anthropic provider, ElevenAgents LLMs, ElevenAgents quickstart, Deepgram keyterm prompting, Pipecat Anthropic, ElevenAgents tool settings, Vapi server events, ElevenLabs prompting guide.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Remembering you between calls open each step
    
      
    With memory it can say "Want your usual oat milk?" or "You asked me to remind you about the dentist." None of the platforms do this by magic; it's two small webhooks on your server: one before the call, one after.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    memory/+15555550123.md (example)
    # Alex: memory (keep this short)
Preferences: shops at the corner store; often calls while walking
Usual items: oat milk, eggs, coffee
Open tasks: book the dentist (asked Nov 3)
Last calls:
- Nov 5: added eggs, oat milk; emailed Mom (home Sunday, 6 pm)
- Nov 3: saved a note about the dentist
    
        
    After-call summary prompt
    Here is the transcript of a phone call between me and my assistant, and my current memory file.
1. Summarize the call in 3 to 5 short bullets: what was asked and what the tools actually did (use the tool results, not what the assistant said).
2. List any changed facts: new preferences, open tasks added or finished.
3. Return the updated memory file. Keep only the last 3 call summaries and keep it under about 300 words.
Never store passwords, passphrases, codes or account numbers.
    
      
    
      
    Status: this pattern is built from the platforms' documented webhooks; it has not been run end to end. The 300–500 token memory size and the 3-call history are our suggestions, not vendor numbers.
    
      
    Sources: Vapi server events, ElevenAgents Twilio personalization, ElevenAgents dynamic variables, ElevenAgents post-call webhooks, ElevenAgents data retention.
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Test it before you trust it tick as you go
    
      
    All three big platforms can now phone your assistant with a simulated caller and grade the result. The loop is the same everywhere: iterate fast in text chat, check in a browser voice call, confirm on a real phone call, and re-run the same tests after every prompt change.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    Your personal test list
    0 of 11
    
        
    Saved in this browser. Run the risky ones with tools mocked first (ElevenAgents' tests can mock tools), and while testing, save only your own address as a contact.
    
        
    
        
    
      
    
      
    The trap to avoid: Vapi's docs put it plainly: a tool reporting success doesn't prove the outside system changed. After each test, look at the grocery file, the sent-mail folder or the calendar itself.
    
      
    Sources: Vapi Simulations, Vapi Evals and Simulations, ElevenAgents agent testing, Retell testing, ElevenLabs prompting guide, Retell prompt engineering guide.
